questions.x: Stored spring energy becomes kinetic energy: ½kx² = ½ × 400 × 0.0025 = 0.5 J. Then ½(0.1)v² = 0.5, so v² = 10 and v ≈ 3.2 m/s. Remember to take the square root at the end and to keep the ½ on both sides.

questions.q: Which of the following forces is nonconservative?
o: Kinetic friction
Correct: friction's work depends on path and turns mechanical energy into heat.
Gravity
Gravity's work depends only on endpoints.
An ideal spring force
Spring work depends only on endpoints.
The electrostatic force
Electrostatic work depends only on endpoints.
questions.x: A force is conservative if its work depends only on the start and end points, so it does zero work around any closed loop. Gravity, ideal springs and electrostatic forces meet this test, so each has a potential energy. Kinetic friction does more work the longer the path and always takes mechanical energy away as heat.

questions.q: During running, the Achilles tendon (effective k ≈ 2 × 10⁵ N/m) stretches about 1 cm. How much elastic energy does it store?
o: Forgets the ½.
Uses x = 0.1 m instead of 0.01 m.
Uses kx (the force) as the energy.
questions.note: Tendons return stored energy, improving running economy.
questions.x: A spring stores energy U = ½kx². With x = 0.01 m, x² = 10⁻⁴ m², so U = ½ × 2 × 10⁵ × 10⁻⁴ = 10 J. Convert centimeters to meters before squaring: leaving x as 0.1 m inflates the answer 100-fold. Using kx gives the tendon force in newtons, not an energy.

questions.q: A rock is dropped from rest off a 45 m cliff. Ignoring air resistance, how fast is it moving just before impact (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: 45 m/s
Equates speed numerically with height.
30 m/s
Correct: v = √(2gh) = √900.
About 21 m/s
Uses √(gh), dropping the factor of 2.
Forgets the square root.
questions.x: Energy conservation gives mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 45) = 30 m/s. Mass cancels. The kinematics formula v² = 2gh gives the same result. Dropping the 2 or forgetting the final square root are the usual slips.

questions.q: A roller coaster car starts from rest 30 m above the ground. Ignoring friction, what is its speed when it is 10 m above the ground (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: About 24 m/s
Uses the full 30 m drop.
About 14 m/s
Uses only a 10 m drop.
20 m/s
Correct: drop of 20 m; v = √(2 × 10 × 20) = 20 m/s.
10 m/s
Uses √(gh) with h = 10 m.
questions.note: Only the height dropped matters.
questions.x: Only the height dropped turns into kinetic energy. The car falls 30 − 10 = 20 m, so v = √(2gh) = √400 = 20 m/s. Using the full 30 m height pretends the car reached the ground. The shape of the track does not matter without friction.

questions.q: A 50 kg sledder starts from rest at the top of a 10 m high hill and reaches 10 m/s at the bottom. How much energy was lost to friction (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: mgh = 5000 J; KE = ½(50)(100) = 2500 J; lost 2500 J.
That is the total initial PE.
Adds KE to PE instead of subtracting.
0 J
The final KE is less than the initial PE, so energy was dissipated.
questions.x: Energy at the start is mgh = 50 × 10 × 10 = 5000 J. At the bottom, KE = ½ × 50 × 10² = 2500 J. The missing 2500 J was turned into heat by friction (W_friction = −2500 J). Energy lost is always the difference between the initial and final mechanical energy.

questions.q: Two identical balls are thrown from the same rooftop at the same speed, one horizontally and one straight down. Ignoring air resistance, how do their speeds compare just before they land?
o: They are equal
Correct: same initial KE and same PE drop give the same final KE.
The downward ball is faster
Direction of launch doesn't change energy.
The horizontal ball is faster
Both gain the same KE from the same drop.
It depends on their mass
Mass cancels in the energy equation.
questions.x: Kinetic energy is a scalar, so the launch direction does not matter. Both balls start with the same KE and drop the same height, so they gain the same energy and land at the same speed. The ball thrown downward lands sooner, but not faster.

questions.q: A horizontal mass–spring system oscillates on a frictionless surface. At the equilibrium position, which quantity is at its maximum?
o: Elastic potential energy
Spring PE is maximum at the turning points.
Restoring force
F = −kx is zero at x = 0.
Kinetic energy
Correct: spring PE is zero there, so all mechanical energy is kinetic.
Acceleration
a = −kx/m is zero at equilibrium.
questions.x: At equilibrium, x = 0, so the spring force (−kx), the acceleration and the elastic PE (½kx²) are all zero. All the mechanical energy is then kinetic, so the speed is greatest. At the turning points it is the reverse: maximum PE, force and acceleration, and zero speed.

questions.q: A ball dropped from 2.0 m rebounds to 1.5 m. What fraction of its mechanical energy was lost in the bounce?
o: That is the fraction retained.
Correct: PE ∝ height, and the height fell from 2.0 to 1.5 m.
Assumes energy halves with each bounce.
About 13%
Uses the square root of the height ratio (a speed ratio).
questions.x: Gravitational PE is proportional to height, so the fraction of energy kept is 1.5/2.0 = 75%. That means 25% was lost to heat and sound in the bounce. Using the square root of the height ratio gives a speed ratio, not an energy ratio.

questions.q: A cart rolls down a 2 m ramp, losing 4.0 J of gravitational PE, and has 3.2 J of kinetic energy at the bottom. What is the average friction force along the ramp?
o: Gives the energy lost, not the force.
Multiplies the lost energy by distance.
Divides the full 4.0 J of PE by the distance.
Correct: 0.8 J lost ÷ 2 m = 0.4 N.
questions.x: Of the 4.0 J of PE lost, only 3.2 J became KE, so friction removed 0.8 J. Friction work is force × distance, so f = 0.8 J ÷ 2 m = 0.4 N. Dividing the full 4.0 J by the distance treats all the PE as lost to friction.

questions.q: Total mechanical energy of a system is conserved when:
o: The net force is zero
Net force can be nonzero (e.g., free fall) while energy is conserved.
Friction is present but small
Any friction dissipates some mechanical energy.
The object moves at constant speed
A block sliding at constant speed down a rough ramp loses mechanical energy.
Only conservative forces do work
Correct: nonconservative forces (friction, drag) convert mechanical energy to other forms.
questions.x: Mechanical energy (KE + PE) stays constant when only conservative forces, such as gravity and springs, do work. Friction, drag and muscles do nonconservative work and change it. A nonzero net force is fine: in free fall gravity is the net force, yet mechanical energy is conserved.

questions.q: A pole vaulter runs at 10 m/s. If all of her kinetic energy became gravitational PE, how high could she raise her center of mass (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Forgets the factor of 2.
5 m
Correct: h = v²/(2g) = 100/20.
Divides by 4g.
1 m
Divides speed by g.
questions.note: Mass cancels in v²/2g.
questions.x: Setting ½mv² = mgh gives h = v²/(2g) = 100/20 = 5 m. Mass cancels, so the speed alone sets the ideal height. Real vaulters clear about 6 m because their center of mass starts about 1 m above the ground and they push with their arms.

questions.q: A pendulum with a 1.8 m string is released from rest at 60° from vertical. What is its speed at the lowest point (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: About 4.2 m/s
6 m/s
Uses the full string length as the height drop.
3 m/s
Uses h = 0.45 m, half the true drop.
About 5.6 m/s
Uses h = L sin 60° ≈ 1.56 m.
questions.x: The bob drops h = L − L cos θ = 1.8(1 − 0.5) = 0.9 m. Then v = √(2gh) = √18 ≈ 4.2 m/s. The tricky step is the geometry: the vertical drop is L(1 − cos θ), not L and not L sin θ.

questions.q: A block slides down a rough incline at constant speed. What happens to its mechanical energy?
o: It stays constant because speed is constant
Constant KE but falling PE means total mechanical energy drops.
It increases as PE turns into KE
KE doesn't increase at constant speed.
It decreases as thermal energy is produced
Correct: PE drops while KE stays constant; friction converts the difference to heat.
It is converted entirely into kinetic energy
KE stays the same.
questions.x: Constant speed means KE does not change, but the block keeps losing height and therefore PE. So the total mechanical energy goes down, and kinetic friction turns the lost PE into thermal energy. Constant speed means the forces balance; it does not mean energy is conserved.

questions.q: In a lab, a solid ball rolling without slipping down a ramp consistently has about 30% less translational KE at the bottom than mgh predicts. What best explains this?
o: The ball's mass was too large
Mass cancels in comparing KE to mgh.
The local value of g is larger than assumed
A larger g would increase the KE.
Some energy goes into the ball's rotational kinetic energy
Correct: for a solid sphere, 2/7 of the energy (≈ 29%) is rotational.
The ramp height was underestimated
Underestimating h would make KE seem too large.
questions.x: A ball rolling without slipping has to spin as well as move forward. Part of mgh becomes rotational KE (½Iω²), so less is left for translational KE. For a solid sphere, I = ⅖mr², so 2/7 (≈29%) of the energy goes into rotation, which matches the data. Mass cancels, so mass cannot be the explanation.

questions.q: Two people of equal mass climb the same staircase, one in half the time of the other. How do their work and power compare?
o: The faster person does twice the work
Work depends on height and weight, not time.
Same work; the faster person has twice the power
Correct: work = mgh is equal; power = work/time.
Same power; different work
Equal work in half the time means double power.
Same work and same power
Power depends on time.
questions.x: Work done against gravity is mgh, which depends only on weight and height, so both climbers do the same work. Power is work divided by time, so finishing in half the time means twice the power. Work and power are different: power is how fast the work is done.

questions.q: A motor lifts a 100 kg load at a constant 0.5 m/s. What power does it deliver (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: P = Fv = 1000 N × 0.5 m/s.
Uses mass instead of weight.
Divides force by velocity.
Off by a factor of 10.
questions.x: At constant speed, the lifting force equals the weight, 1000 N. Power is P = Fv = 1000 × 0.5 = 500 W. Equivalently, the motor adds 500 J of potential energy each second. Using the mass (100 kg) instead of the weight gives the wrong answer.

questions.q: How much energy does a 100 W lamp use in 1 minute?
o: That is the energy used in 1 s.
Divides power by time.
That is the energy used in 1 hour.
Correct: E = Pt = 100 J/s × 60 s.
questions.x: A watt is one joule per second, so E = Pt = 100 J/s × 60 s = 6000 J. Always convert time to seconds before multiplying. A kilowatt-hour, the unit on power bills, is 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

questions.q: A car's engine delivers 30 kW to the wheels while the car moves at a constant 15 m/s. What is the driving force?
o: Correct: F = P/v = 30,000/15.
Multiplies power by velocity.
Inverts the ratio, dividing speed by power in kW.
Treats watts as newtons.
questions.x: For constant velocity, P = Fv, so the driving force is F = P/v = 30,000 W ÷ 15 m/s = 2000 N. At steady speed this force exactly balances drag and rolling resistance. Convert kW to W before dividing, or the force comes out 1000 times too small.

questions.q: Skeletal muscle converts chemical energy to mechanical work with about 25% efficiency. To produce 200 W of mechanical power, what metabolic power is required?
o: Multiplies by 0.25 instead of dividing.
Adds 25% to the output.
Correct: 200 W ÷ 0.25.
Gives only the heat produced, not the total input.
questions.note: The other 75% becomes heat.
questions.x: Efficiency = useful output ÷ input, so input = 200 W ÷ 0.25 = 800 W. The other 600 W is released as heat, which is why exercise warms the body. Multiplying by 0.25 instead of dividing gets the direction of the relationship backward.

questions.q: A resting adult has a metabolic power of about 100 W. Roughly how much energy is this per day (1 kcal ≈ 4200 J)?
o: About 200 kcal
Off by 10.
About 2000 kcal
About 20,000 kcal
Off by 10 in the other direction.
About 100 kcal
Confuses watts with kcal per day.
questions.x: A day has 86,400 s, so 100 W × 86,400 s ≈ 8.6 × 10⁶ J. Dividing by 4200 J/kcal gives about 2000 kcal, which matches typical daily food intake. A handy rule is that 100 W ≈ 2000 kcal/day.

questions.q: What is the momentum of a 0.15 kg baseball moving at 40 m/s?
o: 120 kg·m/s
Computes ½mv², the KE in joules.
60 kg·m/s
Off by a factor of 10.
0.6 kg·m/s
Off by a factor of 10.
6 kg·m/s
Correct: p = mv = 0.15 × 40.
questions.x: Momentum is p = mv = 0.15 × 40 = 6 kg·m/s. It is a vector that depends linearly on velocity. Kinetic energy depends on v² and has units of joules: here ½mv² = 120 J, a completely different quantity.

questions.q: On a graph of force versus time, the area under the curve equals the object's:
o: Change in momentum
Correct: impulse = ∫F dt = Δp.
Change in kinetic energy
That is the area under force versus displacement.
Power
Power is the rate of doing work.
Acceleration
Acceleration is F/m at an instant.
questions.x: Force multiplied by the time it acts is impulse, and the impulse–momentum theorem says impulse = Δp. So the area under an F–t graph gives the change in momentum. The area under an F–x graph gives work, which equals ΔKE.

questions.q: Why does an airbag reduce injury to a driver in a collision?
o: It reduces the driver's change in momentum
The driver still goes from moving to stopped.
It reduces the impulse delivered to the driver
Impulse equals Δp, which is unchanged.
It converts the driver's momentum into heat
Momentum is not converted to heat; kinetic energy is dissipated.
It lengthens the stopping time, lowering the average force for the same impulse
Correct: FΔt = Δp is fixed; larger Δt means smaller F.
questions.x: The driver's change in momentum, from moving to stopped, is the same with or without an airbag, so the impulse FΔt is the same too. The airbag makes the stop take longer, which lowers the average force, F = Δp/Δt. It also spreads that force over a larger area.

questions.q: A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s collides with and sticks to a 1 kg cart at rest. What is their speed afterward?
o: 3 m/s
Ignores the added mass.
2 m/s
Correct: 2 × 3 = 3 × v gives v = 2 m/s.
1 m/s
Divides the initial speed by the total mass (3/3), ignoring the moving cart's mass.
Averages the two velocities.
questions.x: In a perfectly inelastic (sticking) collision, momentum is conserved: 2 × 3 = (2 + 1)v, so v = 2 m/s. The same momentum is now carried by more mass, so the speed drops. Kinetic energy is not conserved here, so you cannot set the KEs equal.

questions.q: A 4 kg cart at 2 m/s collides with and couples to an identical cart at rest. How much kinetic energy is lost?
o: 0 J
Kinetic energy isn't conserved in a perfectly inelastic collision.
8 J
Assumes all KE is lost; the carts keep moving.
4 J
Correct: v_f = 1 m/s; KE goes from 8 J to ½(8)(1) = 4 J.
2 J
Miscomputes the final KE as 6 J.
questions.note: Momentum is conserved; KE is not, in sticking collisions.
questions.x: Momentum conservation gives 4 × 2 = 8v, so v = 1 m/s. KE drops from ½(4)(4) = 8 J to ½(8)(1) = 4 J, so 4 J is lost to deformation and heat. When equal masses stick and one started at rest, half the KE is always lost.

questions.q: In a perfectly elastic collision, which quantities are conserved?
o: Both momentum and kinetic energy
Correct: elastic collisions conserve both.
Momentum only
That describes inelastic collisions.
Kinetic energy only
Momentum is conserved in all isolated collisions.
Neither
Isolated collisions always conserve momentum.
questions.x: In any isolated collision, momentum is conserved, because the internal forces are an equal-and-opposite third-law pair. An elastic collision is one where kinetic energy is also conserved, with none turned into heat or deformation. Inelastic collisions conserve momentum but not KE.

questions.q: A moving billiard ball strikes an identical stationary ball head-on in a perfectly elastic collision. What happens?
o: Both move forward at half the original speed
That conserves momentum but loses KE (inelastic).
The first ball stops; the second moves off with the first's velocity
Correct: equal masses exchange velocities in a 1-D elastic collision.
The first ball bounces back at its original speed
That would violate momentum conservation.
Both stop
Momentum would not be conserved.
questions.x: For a 1-D elastic collision between equal masses, conserving both momentum and KE leads to one solution: the balls swap velocities. The striker stops and the target moves off at the original speed. Both moving at half speed conserves momentum but only keeps half the KE.

questions.q: A 5 kg squid at rest expels 0.5 kg of water backward at 10 m/s. With what speed does the squid move forward (squid mass after expulsion ≈ 5 kg)?
o: 10 m/s
Assumes the squid matches the water's speed.
Off by a factor of 10.
Multiplies the ratio instead of dividing.
1 m/s
Correct: total momentum stays zero: 5v = 0.5 × 10.
questions.note: Jet propulsion is recoil: momentum conservation.
questions.x: The squid and water start at rest, so the total momentum stays zero: the water's backward momentum (0.5 × 10 = 5 kg·m/s) equals the squid's forward momentum. So 5v = 5 and v = 1 m/s. Recoil and rocket propulsion work the same way.

questions.q: A 0.2 kg ball moving at 10 m/s bounces straight back at 10 m/s after 0.01 s of contact with a wall. What is the average force on the ball?
o: Ignores the reversal; uses Δv = 10 m/s.
0 N
Speed is unchanged but velocity reverses, so momentum changes.
Correct: Δp = 0.2 × 20 = 4 kg·m/s; F = 4/0.01.
Off by a factor of 20.
questions.note: Trap: a rebound doubles Δp.
questions.x: Momentum is a vector, so a rebound reverses it. Δp = 0.2(10) − 0.2(−10) = 4 kg·m/s, and F = Δp/Δt = 4/0.01 = 400 N. Using only a 10 m/s change ignores the reversal and halves the force.

questions.q: An object at rest explodes into two pieces. Which statement is true?
o: Total momentum stays zero, while total kinetic energy increases
Correct: internal forces conserve momentum; chemical energy becomes KE.
Both momentum and kinetic energy stay zero
The pieces move, so KE is positive.
Total momentum increases along with kinetic energy
No external force acts, so momentum is conserved.
The pieces move in the same direction
They must move oppositely to keep total momentum zero.
questions.x: An explosion involves only internal forces, so the total momentum stays at its initial value of zero. The pieces move in opposite directions with equal and opposite momenta. Kinetic energy rises from zero because stored chemical energy is released, so KE is not conserved.

questions.q: A 1 kg puck moving east at 3 m/s collides and sticks to a 1 kg puck moving north at 3 m/s. What is the velocity of the combined pucks?
o: 3 m/s toward the northeast
Adds the speeds then divides incorrectly.
About 2.1 m/s toward the northeast
Correct: p = (3, 3) kg·m/s; divided by 2 kg gives (1.5, 1.5), magnitude ≈ 2.1 m/s.
About 4.2 m/s toward the northeast
Forgets to divide by the combined mass.
0 m/s
Perpendicular momenta don't cancel.
questions.note: Conserve each momentum component separately.
questions.x: Conserve momentum separately in each direction: 3 kg·m/s east and 3 kg·m/s north. Dividing by the combined 2 kg gives 1.5 m/s in each direction, with magnitude 1.5√2 ≈ 2.1 m/s toward the northeast. Perpendicular momenta add as vectors, never cancel, and never add as plain numbers.

questions.q: Cart A (1 kg) moves at 4 m/s toward stationary cart B (1 kg). Afterward, A moves at 1 m/s and B at 3 m/s, both forward. How should this collision be classified?
o: Perfectly elastic
KE drops from 8 J to 5 J.
Perfectly inelastic
The carts move at different speeds, so they didn't stick.
Impossible, because momentum isn't conserved
1(1) + 1(3) = 4 kg·m/s, matching the initial momentum.
Inelastic, but not perfectly inelastic
Correct: momentum 4 → 4 is conserved, but KE falls from 8 J to 5 J and the carts separate.
questions.x: Check momentum first: 4 kg·m/s before, and 1 + 3 = 4 kg·m/s after, so it is conserved. KE drops from 8 J to 0.5 + 4.5 = 5 J, so the collision is not elastic. The carts separate, so it is not perfectly inelastic either. It falls in the general inelastic category.

questions.q: A force sensor records a triangular force pulse on a ball that peaks at 400 N and lasts 0.01 s. What impulse was delivered?
o: 4 N·s
Uses the peak force for the whole duration.
40 N·s
Off by 10 and ignores the ½.
2 N·s
Correct: triangle area = ½ × 400 × 0.01.
Off by a factor of 10.
questions.x: Impulse is the area under the F–t graph. For a triangular pulse, that is ½ × peak force × duration = ½ × 400 × 0.01 = 2 N·s, which equals the ball's change in momentum. Using the peak force for the whole duration doubles the answer.

questions.q: Two carts collide on a frictionless track with no external horizontal forces. What happens to the velocity of the system's center of mass?
o: It drops to zero at the moment of impact
Internal forces can't change the center of mass's motion.
It increases if the collision is elastic
Elasticity affects KE, not total momentum.
It remains constant
Correct: with no external force, total momentum and center-of-mass velocity don't change.
It reverses direction
That would require an external impulse.
questions.x: The center-of-mass velocity is the total momentum divided by the total mass. With no external force, the total momentum is constant, so the center-of-mass velocity stays the same no matter how violent or elastic the collision is. Internal forces redistribute momentum between the carts but cannot change the total.

questions.q: A lever has an effort arm of 1.2 m and a load arm of 0.3 m. What is its ideal mechanical advantage?
o: Correct: IMA = effort arm ÷ load arm = 1.2/0.3.
Inverts the ratio.
Multiplies the arms.
Adds the arms.
questions.x: The ideal mechanical advantage of a lever is effort arm ÷ load arm = 1.2/0.3 = 4. Balancing torques, F_effort × 1.2 = F_load × 0.3, so the effort is one-quarter of the load. The effort end moves four times as far, so the work is the same.

questions.q: An ideal pulley system with 4 rope segments supporting the movable block lifts an 800 N load. What effort force is required?
o: That would be a single fixed pulley.
Correct: IMA = 4, so effort = 800/4.
Multiplies by the MA instead of dividing.
Uses an MA of 2.
questions.x: In an ideal pulley system, the load is shared equally by the rope segments holding up the movable block, so IMA = 4. The effort is 800/4 = 200 N, but you must pull 4 m of rope for each meter the load rises. A single fixed pulley only changes the direction of the force (IMA = 1).

questions.q: A simple machine with an ideal mechanical advantage of 5 raises a load 0.2 m. How far must the effort force move?
o: Divides by MA; the effort moves farther, not shorter.
Assumes equal distances.
5 m
Uses the MA as the distance.
1 m
Correct: work in = work out, so effort distance = 5 × 0.2 m.
questions.note: Force is traded for distance.
questions.x: An ideal machine conserves work: F_in × d_in = F_out × d_out. With IMA = 5, the effort is one-fifth of the load, so it must move 5 times as far: 5 × 0.2 = 1 m. A smaller force means a longer distance, never a shorter one.

questions.q: An ideal simple machine lets a person lift a load with a smaller effort force. Compared with lifting the load directly, which quantity is unchanged?
o: The effort force
It is smaller; reducing it is the purpose of the machine.
The work required
Correct: W = Fd; the smaller force acts over a proportionally longer distance.
The distance the effort must move
It is larger; a smaller force must act over a longer distance.
The ratio of load force to effort force
That ratio, the mechanical advantage, rises above 1.
questions.note: Machines trade force for distance, never saving work.
questions.x: An ideal machine cannot create energy, so the work needed to lift the load (mgh) is the same with or without it. It reduces the force by making the effort act over a proportionally longer distance, F_in d_in = F_out d_out. Real machines need slightly more input work because of friction.

questions.q: A pulley system with an ideal mechanical advantage of 4 requires a 250 N effort to lift an 800 N load. What is its efficiency?
o: Divides effort by load.
Inverts AMA/IMA; efficiency can't exceed 100%.
Divides effort by half the load (250/400).
questions.x: Actual mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort = 800/250 = 3.2. Efficiency = AMA ÷ IMA = 3.2/4 = 80%, with the rest lost to friction. Equivalently, the useful work output is 80% of the work input. Any efficiency above 100% signals an inverted ratio.

questions.q: The biceps and forearm form a third-class lever. What is the main consequence of this arrangement?
o: The muscle force is less than the load
That would require MA > 1.
The muscle force equals the load
Lever arms differ greatly.
No torque is needed at the elbow
Holding a load requires balancing torques.
The muscle force exceeds the load, but the hand moves farther and faster
Correct: MA < 1 trades force for speed and range of motion.
questions.x: In a third-class lever, the effort (biceps) attaches between the fulcrum (elbow) and the load (hand). The muscle's short lever arm means it must pull much harder than the load (MA < 1). In exchange, a small contraction moves the hand a long way quickly, so speed and range of motion are gained at the cost of force.

questions.q: Nodding the head uses the atlanto-occipital joint between the neck muscles behind and the head's weight in front. What class of lever is this?
o: Second class
Second class has the load between fulcrum and effort.
Third class
Third class has the effort between fulcrum and load.
First class
Correct: the fulcrum lies between the effort and the load.
It is not a lever
A rigid body rotating about a joint is a lever.
questions.x: Lever class depends on what sits in the middle: in first class it is the fulcrum, in second class the load, in third class the effort. In nodding, the atlanto-occipital joint (fulcrum) lies between the neck extensors behind and the head's center of mass in front, like a seesaw. So it is first class.

questions.q: A ramp is 6 m long and rises 1.5 m. What is its ideal mechanical advantage?
o: Correct: IMA = length ÷ height = 6/1.5.
Inverts the ratio.
Multiplies length and height.
Adds length and height.
questions.x: For a ramp, IMA = length ÷ height = 6/1.5 = 4. The work mgh is the same either way, so pushing along a 6 m path needs only a quarter of the force of lifting the load straight up 1.5 m. Inverting the ratio gives an MA below 1, which would make the ramp pointless.

questions.q: Lifting a box with a bent back, the erector spinae act about 5 cm behind the lumbar discs, while the upper body and box weight act about 40 cm in front. Why are disc forces so large?
o: The weight of the box acts directly on the discs only
Muscle force dominates the disc load.
Bending reduces the muscles' lever arm to zero
The lever arm is small but not zero.
Gravity is stronger when the back is bent
g is unchanged; lever arms change.
The short muscle lever arm requires a muscle force many times the load
Correct: about 8× the load (40/5), which adds compressive force on the discs.
questions.note: Bend the knees to bring the load closer.
questions.x: Taking torques about the disc, the back muscles' 5 cm lever arm must balance a load acting 40 cm in front. So the muscle force is about 8 times the load. The discs carry that muscle force plus the weight, which is why lifting with a bent back is dangerous. Keeping the load close shortens its lever arm.

questions.q: A saline solution has a density of 1200 kg/m³. What is its specific gravity?
o: Inverted ratio: water density divided by the solution density.
Correct: specific gravity = ρ/ρ(water) = 1200/1000, a dimensionless ratio.
This is the density itself; specific gravity divides by water's 1000 kg/m³.
1.2 kg/m³
Specific gravity is a ratio of densities, so it has no units.
questions.x: Specific gravity compares a substance's density with water's (1000 kg/m³ or 1 g/cm³), so the units cancel and only a pure number remains. Here 1200/1000 = 1.2, meaning the saline is 1.2 times as dense as water. A handy check: in g/cm³ the density and specific gravity are numerically equal, which is why attaching kg/m³ to 1.2 or reporting 1200 are both wrong.

questions.q: A fluid has a density of 0.9 g/cm³. Expressed in SI units, its density is:
o: 9000 kg/m³
Multiplied by 10⁴ instead of 10³.
0.9 kg/m³
Treats g/cm³ and kg/m³ as equal; they differ by a factor of 1000.
90 kg/m³
Off by a factor of 10 in the unit conversion.
900 kg/m³
Correct: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, so 0.9 g/cm³ = 900 kg/m³.
questions.x: Converting g/cm³ to kg/m³ multiplies by 1000: a gram is 10⁻³ kg, but a cubic centimeter is 10⁻⁶ m³, so the net factor is 10³. Water at 1 g/cm³ is 1000 kg/m³, so a fluid slightly less dense than water must be just under 1000 kg/m³. Anchoring to water's value catches the factor-of-10 and factor-of-1000 slips.

questions.q: A 3 kg solid sphere occupies 0.002 m³. When placed in fresh water, it will:
o: Sink, because its density is 1500 kg/m³
Correct: ρ = 3/0.002 = 1500 kg/m³, greater than water's 1000 kg/m³.
Float, because its density is 667 kg/m³
Divided volume by mass instead of mass by volume.
Remain suspended at any depth
Neutral buoyancy requires density exactly equal to water's.
Float with half its volume submerged
Only objects less dense than water float; this one is denser.
questions.x: Whether a solid object sinks or floats depends only on comparing its average density with the fluid's. Density is mass over volume: 3 kg ÷ 0.002 m³ = 1500 kg/m³, which exceeds water's 1000 kg/m³, so the weight exceeds the maximum buoyant force and the sphere sinks. Inverting the ratio (V/m) gives a number below 1000 and the false conclusion that it floats.

questions.q: Whole blood has a specific gravity of about 1.06. What is the approximate mass of 5 L of blood?
o: 5.0 kg
Uses the density of water rather than blood.
53 kg
Off by a factor of 10 in the liter-to-m³ conversion.
5.3 kg
4.7 kg
Divided by the specific gravity instead of multiplying.
questions.x: Mass equals density times volume. A specific gravity of 1.06 means blood's density is 1060 kg/m³, and 5 L is 0.005 m³ (1 L = 10⁻³ m³), so m = 1060 × 0.005 = 5.3 kg. Because blood is only slightly denser than water, its mass must be slightly more than the 5 kg that 5 L of water would have, which rules out both 5.0 kg and anything below it.

questions.q: A patient's urine specific gravity rises from 1.005 to 1.030 after a day without drinking. This change indicates that the urine:
o: Contains more water per unit solute
That dilution would lower specific gravity toward 1.000.
Has a lower mass per unit volume
A higher specific gravity means a higher mass per unit volume.
Contains more dissolved solute per unit volume
Correct: added solute mass per volume raises density and thus specific gravity.
Has become less dense than water
Any specific gravity above 1 means denser than water.
questions.x: Urine specific gravity measures how much dissolved solute it carries per unit volume, since solutes add mass with little added volume. When the body conserves water, the kidneys excrete the same solutes in less water, so density and specific gravity rise toward 1.030. Values nearer 1.000 indicate dilute urine, so the rise means more solute per volume, not more water.

questions.q: Equal masses of two liquids with densities 800 kg/m³ and 1200 kg/m³ are mixed (volumes additive). The mixture's density is:
o: 960 kg/m³
1040 kg/m³
Weights toward the denser liquid; equal masses mean more volume of the lighter one.
2000 kg/m³
Densities are not additive; the sum of the two is meaningless.
1000 kg/m³
This simple average applies to equal volumes, not equal masses.
questions.x: For a mixture, density is total mass divided by total volume, not the average of the densities. With equal masses, the less dense liquid occupies more volume, so the mixture's density is pulled below the simple average of 1000 kg/m³ (it equals the harmonic mean, 2·800·1200/2000 = 960). A simple average is only correct when equal volumes are mixed.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes specific gravity?
o: It equals mass divided by volume, in kg/m³
That is density, which has units.
It is the buoyant force on an object per unit mass
Buoyant force depends on displaced fluid, not this definition.
It is the weight of a substance per unit volume, in N/m³
That is specific weight, ρg, which has units.
It is a dimensionless ratio of a substance's density to water's density
Correct: the units cancel, leaving a pure number.
questions.x: Specific gravity is ρ(substance)/ρ(water), a dimensionless ratio. Density (kg/m³) and specific weight (ρg, in N/m³) are related quantities but both carry units. A specific gravity above 1 means the substance sinks in water and below 1 means it floats, which is why it is a quick, unit-free way to compare materials.

questions.q: What is the gauge pressure 10 m below the surface of a freshwater lake? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²)
o: 2×10⁵ Pa
This is absolute pressure; gauge pressure excludes the atmosphere.
1×10⁴ Pa
Dropped one factor of 10 from ρgh.
1×10⁵ Pa
Correct: P(gauge) = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 10 = 1×10⁵ Pa.
1×10³ Pa
Omits g from ρgh.
questions.x: Gauge pressure is the pressure above atmospheric, and in a static fluid it equals ρgh. At 10 m in water: 1000 × 10 × 10 = 1×10⁵ Pa, roughly one extra atmosphere for every 10 m of depth. Adding the 1×10⁵ Pa of air above the surface would give absolute pressure (2×10⁵ Pa), which is a different quantity than the question asks for.

questions.q: A diver is 20 m below the surface of fresh water. What is the absolute pressure on the diver? (Patm ≈ 1×10⁵ Pa)
o: 3×10⁵ Pa
Correct: Patm + ρgh = 1×10⁵ + 2×10⁵ = 3×10⁵ Pa.
1×10⁵ Pa
Ignores the weight of the water column entirely.
2×10⁶ Pa
Multiplied ρgh by an extra factor of 10.
2×10⁵ Pa
This is only gauge pressure; absolute adds the atmosphere.
questions.x: Absolute pressure at depth is the atmospheric pressure on the surface plus the weight of the fluid column: P = Patm + ρgh. At 20 m, ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 20 = 2×10⁵ Pa, and adding 1×10⁵ Pa gives 3×10⁵ Pa (about 3 atm). The common error is reporting only ρgh, which is the gauge pressure.

questions.q: Three open containers of different shapes and widths are filled with water to the same height. How do the pressures at their bottoms compare?
o: Greatest in the container that holds the most mass
Total weight affects force on a scale, not pressure at a depth.
Greatest in the narrowest container
Narrowness does not concentrate pressure; depth alone matters.
Greatest in the widest container
More total water does not raise pressure at a given depth.
They are equal
Correct: hydrostatic pressure depends only on ρ, g and depth, not on container shape.
questions.x: Hydrostatic pressure P = P₀ + ρgh depends only on fluid density, g and vertical depth below the surface. Container shape does not matter (the hydrostatic paradox): the walls of a flared or narrowing container supply the extra or missing force. A container holding more water weighs more in total, but its pressure at the same depth is identical.

questions.q: In a standing adult, the feet are about 1.2 m below the heart. Approximately how much greater is arterial pressure in the feet than at the heart? (ρ(blood) ≈ 1000 kg/m³)
o: Off by a factor of 100 from ρgh.
Dropped a factor of 10 from ρgh.
Correct: ΔP = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 1.2 = 1.2×10⁴ Pa (about 90 mmHg).
That is more than one atmosphere; too large by a factor of 10.
questions.x: In a continuous fluid column, pressure increases by ρgh with vertical distance below a reference point. Blood in the feet sits 1.2 m below the heart, so arterial pressure there is higher by 1000 × 10 × 1.2 = 1.2×10⁴ Pa, about 90 mmHg (1 mmHg ≈ 133 Pa). This is why blood pressure is measured at heart level and why dependent tissues see high pressures.

questions.q: An IV line must overcome a venous gauge pressure of 1300 Pa. What is the minimum height of the fluid bag above the insertion site? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³)
o: 1.3 cm
Too low by a factor of 10; check h = P/(ρg).
13 cm
Forgot to divide by g.
Off by a factor of 100.
questions.x: A gravity-fed IV works because the fluid column's height creates pressure ρgh at the insertion site. To exceed a venous pressure of 1300 Pa, h = P/(ρg) = 1300/(1000 × 10) = 0.13 m, or 13 cm. Raising the bag higher increases flow; a useful sanity check is that 10 cm of water exerts about 1000 Pa.

questions.q: A tire gauge at sea level reads 200 kPa. Taking atmospheric pressure as 100 kPa, the absolute pressure in the tire is:
o: 2 kPa
Divided the gauge reading by atmospheric pressure.
200 kPa
Gauges read pressure above atmospheric, not absolute pressure.
300 kPa
Correct: absolute = gauge + atmospheric = 200 + 100 kPa.
100 kPa
Subtracted atmospheric pressure instead of adding it.
questions.x: Most pressure gauges, including tire gauges, read gauge pressure: the pressure above the surrounding atmosphere. To get absolute pressure you add atmospheric pressure, so 200 + 100 = 300 kPa. Taking the gauge reading as absolute is the main trap; a flat tire reads 0 on the gauge but still holds about 100 kPa of air.

questions.q: A barometer at sea level holds a 760 mm column of mercury. If water (13.6 times less dense) were used instead, the column would be about:
o: 5.6 cm
Divided by 13.6; a less dense fluid needs a taller column.
76 cm
This is the mercury height; water must rise higher.
Correct: 0.76 m × 13.6 ≈ 10.3 m, since h = P/(ρg).
Too large by a factor of 10.
questions.x: A barometer column balances atmospheric pressure, so ρgh is the same for any liquid used: h is inversely proportional to density. Water is 13.6 times less dense than mercury, so its column must be 13.6 times taller: 0.76 m × 13.6 ≈ 10.3 m. Dividing by 13.6 instead would wrongly predict a shorter column for a lighter fluid.

questions.q: An open-ended mercury manometer is attached to a gas tank. The mercury on the open side stands 20 cm higher than on the tank side. The gauge pressure of the gas is about: (ρ(Hg) = 13,600 kg/m³)
o: That is the absolute pressure, not the gauge pressure.
A higher column on the open side means the gas pressure exceeds atmospheric.
Correct: the gas pushes mercury up the open arm; ρgh = 13,600 × 10 × 0.2 ≈ 2.7×10⁴ Pa above atmospheric.
Used the density of water instead of mercury.
questions.x: An open-tube manometer reads gauge pressure as the height difference between its two mercury surfaces: P(gas) − Patm = ρgh. If the open side is higher, the gas has pushed mercury toward the atmosphere, so the gas pressure exceeds atmospheric: 13,600 × 10 × 0.2 ≈ 2.7×10⁴ Pa. If the tank side were higher, the gauge pressure would be negative.

questions.q: At a given point inside a fluid at rest, the pressure:
o: Acts only perpendicular to the free surface
Pressure acts normal to any surface it contacts, in any orientation.
Is greatest in the horizontal direction
There is no preferred direction for static pressure.
Acts only downward, due to gravity
Fluid pressure pushes on surfaces in every orientation.
Acts equally in all directions
Correct: static fluid pressure is isotropic; it is a scalar.
questions.x: At any point in a static fluid, pressure is the same in every direction; it is a scalar, not a vector. The force a fluid exerts on a surface is always perpendicular to that surface, whatever its orientation. Gravity makes pressure increase with depth, but it does not make pressure at a given point act only downward.

questions.q: A diver descends from 10 m to 20 m in fresh water. By what factor does the absolute pressure on the diver increase?
o: Correct: absolute pressure goes from 2 atm (1 + 1) to 3 atm (1 + 2).
Pressure is linear in depth, not quadratic.
Only the gauge pressure doubles; absolute includes 1 atm of air.
Compares 3 atm with 1 atm at the surface, not with 10 m depth.
questions.x: Absolute pressure in water rises by about 1 atm per 10 m, starting from 1 atm at the surface. At 10 m it is 2 atm and at 20 m it is 3 atm, so the ratio is 3/2 = 1.5. Gauge pressure does double (1 to 2 atm), but the diver's body and gas spaces respond to absolute pressure, which includes the atmosphere.

questions.q: A tank holds a 2 m layer of oil (ρ = 800 kg/m³) floating on 3 m of water. What is the gauge pressure at the bottom of the tank?
o: Treated the oil as if it were water.
Ignored the weight of the oil layer.
Treated the water as if it were oil.
questions.x: With layered fluids, each layer adds its own ρgh to the pressure beneath it. The oil contributes 800 × 10 × 2 = 16,000 Pa and the water 1000 × 10 × 3 = 30,000 Pa, for a gauge pressure of 46,000 Pa at the bottom. Treating the entire 5 m column as water overestimates the result because the oil is less dense.

questions.q: An open beaker of water sits in an elevator accelerating upward at 2 m/s². What is the gauge pressure 1 m below the water surface?
o: That would be for downward acceleration (g − a).
This ignores the elevator's acceleration.
Correct: effective g = 10 + 2 = 12 m/s², so P = 1000 × 12 × 1 = 12,000 Pa.
Doubled g instead of adding the 2 m/s² acceleration to it.
questions.x: Hydrostatic pressure comes from supporting the fluid above a point, so it depends on the effective gravity in the fluid's frame. Accelerating upward at a requires each layer to push harder, giving g(eff) = g + a = 12 m/s² and P = ρ(g + a)h = 12,000 Pa. Downward acceleration would reduce it to g − a, and free fall would make the gauge pressure zero.

questions.q: A hypodermic needle pierces skin easily because, for the same applied force, its small tip area produces:
o: A larger buoyant force
Buoyancy is unrelated to piercing.
A smaller pressure that spreads more evenly
Smaller area increases, not decreases, pressure.
A much larger force
The force is the same; only the area changes.
A much larger pressure
Correct: P = F/A, so a tiny area gives a large pressure.
questions.x: Pressure is force per area, P = F/A. A needle tip has a tiny area, so the same push produces an enormous pressure that exceeds the strength of skin. The force itself is not increased; only its concentration is. This is also why snowshoes spread weight over a large area to reduce pressure.

questions.q: A blood pressure cuff is placed on an arm raised well above the level of the heart. Compared with a reading taken at heart level, the reading will be:
o: Unchanged, because pressure is transmitted equally
Pascal's principle adds to, but does not erase, hydrostatic differences.
Higher, because gravity adds to pressure above the heart
Gravity adds pressure below the reference point, not above it.
Higher, because blood must be pumped uphill
Pressure decreases, not increases, with height in a fluid column.
Lower, because the arm is higher in the blood column
Correct: pressure falls by ρgh with height above the heart.
questions.x: Blood in the vessels behaves like a connected fluid column, so pressure falls by ρgh for each height above the heart and rises below it. A cuff on a raised arm sits higher in the column and reads lower than at heart level. Pascal's principle transmits pressure changes but does not cancel the hydrostatic difference between heights.

questions.q: Prolonged standing can cause ankle swelling. Which fluid-mechanical change best explains this?
o: Decreased hydrostatic pressure in leg veins
Venous pressure in the feet rises, not falls, when standing.
Increased plasma oncotic pressure in the lower legs
Higher oncotic pressure would pull fluid into vessels, reducing swelling.
Lower blood density in dependent tissues
Blood density does not change with posture.
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure in the lower legs
Correct: the blood column above raises capillary pressure, pushing fluid into tissue.
questions.x: When standing, the weight of the blood column adds ρgh to the pressure in the leg veins and capillaries. Higher capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes more fluid out into the interstitial space than oncotic pressure pulls back, producing edema in the ankles. Raising plasma oncotic pressure would do the opposite and pull fluid into vessels.

questions.q: Pressure is defined as:
o: Mass divided by volume
That is density.
Energy divided by time
That is power.
Force perpendicular to a surface divided by the surface area
Correct: P = F⊥/A, in pascals (N/m²).
Force multiplied by area
Pressure divides by area; F × A has units N·m².
questions.x: Pressure is the perpendicular (normal) component of force divided by the area it acts on: P = F⊥/A, with SI unit the pascal (1 Pa = 1 N/m²). Spreading the same force over a larger area lowers the pressure. Multiplying force by area gives units of N·m², which is not pressure.

questions.q: Pascal's principle states that a pressure change applied to an enclosed incompressible fluid is:
o: Transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and its container
Correct: this is the basis of hydraulic systems.
Reduced in proportion to the distance from the point of application
The change is undiminished, not attenuated.
Converted into an equal increase in the fluid's density
An incompressible fluid's density does not change.
Transmitted only in the direction of the applied force
Pressure changes spread in all directions.
questions.x: Pascal's principle says a pressure change applied anywhere in an enclosed, incompressible fluid appears undiminished at every point in the fluid and on the container walls. Because the fluid does not compress, its density and volume stay fixed. This principle underlies hydraulic lifts and brakes, where equal pressure acts on pistons of different areas.

questions.q: A hydraulic press has pistons of area 0.01 m² and 0.5 m². A 200 N force on the small piston produces what force on the large piston?
o: 4 N
Divided by the area ratio instead of multiplying.
Pressure, not force, is equal on both pistons.
Off by a factor of 10 in the area ratio.
Correct: F₂ = F₁(A₂/A₁) = 200 × 50 = 10,000 N.
questions.x: In a hydraulic press the pressure is the same on both pistons, so F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂. The force is multiplied by the area ratio: 200 N × (0.5/0.01) = 200 × 50 = 10,000 N. Equal pressure, not equal force, is the key; the price of the larger output force is that the large piston moves a smaller distance.

questions.q: In a hydraulic system, the small piston has a radius of 2 cm and the large piston a radius of 10 cm. By what factor is the input force multiplied?
o: Used the radius ratio instead of the area ratio.
Doubled the radius ratio (5 × 2) instead of squaring it.
Cubed the radius ratio; area goes as r².
Correct: force scales with area, so (10/2)² = 25.
questions.x: Hydraulic force multiplication equals the ratio of piston areas, and area scales with the radius squared (A = πr²). A radius ratio of 10/2 = 5 gives an area ratio of 5² = 25, so the force is multiplied 25 times. Using the radius ratio directly (5) forgets that the pressure acts over the whole circular face.

questions.q: In a hydraulic lift with an area ratio of 1:25, the small piston is pushed down 50 cm. How far does the large piston rise?
o: 10 cm
Used the radius ratio (5) instead of the area ratio.
Multiplied by 25; the large piston moves less, not more.
2 cm
Correct: equal volumes are displaced, so d₂ = 50 cm/25; work in equals work out.
50 cm
Equal distances would violate volume conservation.
questions.x: An incompressible fluid transfers volume: the volume pushed out by the small piston equals the volume that raises the large piston, so A₁d₁ = A₂d₂. With an area ratio of 1:25, the large piston moves 50 cm/25 = 2 cm. This matches energy conservation: the force is 25 times larger but the distance is 25 times smaller, so work in equals work out.

questions.q: Ignoring gravity, cerebrospinal fluid pressure at the skull rises by 20 mmHg. What change would a lumbar spinal needle in the same continuous fluid space register?
o: No change, because the needle is far from the skull
Distance does not diminish a transmitted pressure change.
An increase of 20 mmHg
Correct: by Pascal's principle the change is transmitted undiminished.
An increase much smaller than 20 mmHg
Pressure changes are not attenuated in an enclosed fluid.
An increase much larger than 20 mmHg
Pascal's principle transmits, not amplifies, pressure.
questions.x: Pascal's principle states that a pressure change in an enclosed, continuous fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout. Cerebrospinal fluid fills a connected space from skull to lumbar spine, so a 20 mmHg rise at the skull also appears at the lumbar needle. This is why lumbar puncture opening pressure can reflect intracranial pressure; distance does not attenuate the change.

questions.q: An air bubble in a car's hydraulic brake line makes the brakes feel spongy. Why?
o: Gas is compressible, so part of the pedal stroke compresses it instead of moving the fluid
Correct: Pascal-based hydraulics assume an incompressible fluid.
The bubble increases the area of the output piston
Piston area is fixed by the hardware.
Air raises the fluid's viscosity, slowing flow
Viscosity is not the issue in a static hydraulic line.
Air is denser than brake fluid and blocks the line
Air is far less dense than brake fluid.
questions.x: Hydraulic systems rely on the fluid being nearly incompressible, so pushing the pedal immediately raises pressure everywhere in the line. A gas bubble compresses easily, so part of the pedal travel just squeezes the bubble rather than transmitting pressure to the brake pistons. The pedal feels soft and travels farther; viscosity and density are not the issue.

questions.q: A hydraulic jack lifts a 2000 kg car using a large piston of area 0.2 m² and a small piston of area 0.004 m². What minimum force on the small piston is needed?
o: Forgot to multiply the mass by g to get the car's weight.
Used an area ratio of 20 instead of 50.
That is the car's full weight; the jack multiplies force.
questions.x: The jack must balance the car's weight on the large piston: mg = 2000 × 10 = 20,000 N. Since pressure is equal on both pistons, F(small) = 20,000 × (0.004/0.2) = 20,000/50 = 400 N. The common slip is using mass (2000) rather than weight, which makes the answer ten times too small.

questions.q: According to Archimedes' principle, the buoyant force on a submerged object equals:
o: The weight of the fluid the object displaces
Correct: F(b) = ρ(fluid)·V(displaced)·g.
The pressure at the object's depth times its volume
Units of pressure × volume are energy, not force.
The weight of the object
True only for a floating object, not in general.
The mass of the displaced fluid
Force equals a weight (mg), not a mass.
questions.x: Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced, F(b) = ρ(fluid)·V(submerged)·g. It arises because pressure is greater on the bottom of an object than on the top. It equals the object's own weight only when the object is floating in equilibrium, and it is a force (a weight), not a mass.

questions.q: A block of volume 0.002 m³ is fully submerged in water. What buoyant force acts on it? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³)
o: 2 N
Forgot to multiply by g.
Off by a factor of 10.
It depends on the block's density
Buoyant force depends on the fluid displaced, not the object's material.
questions.x: The buoyant force on a fully submerged object is ρ(fluid)·V·g, which depends only on the fluid and the displaced volume. Here 1000 × 0.002 × 10 = 20 N. The block's material matters only for deciding whether it sinks or floats, not for the size of the buoyant force when fully submerged.

questions.q: A 5 kg object with volume 0.001 m³ hangs from a scale while fully submerged in water. What does the scale read?
o: Correct: weight 50 N minus buoyant force 1000 × 0.001 × 10 = 10 N.
Added the buoyant force instead of subtracting it.
Ignores the buoyant force.
That is the buoyant force, not the apparent weight.
questions.x: A submerged object's apparent weight is its true weight minus the buoyant force. True weight is 5 × 10 = 50 N; buoyant force is 1000 × 0.001 × 10 = 10 N; so the scale reads 40 N. Buoyancy acts upward, reducing the tension the scale must supply, so adding it or ignoring it gives the wrong reading.

questions.q: An ice block floats in fresh water and is then moved to denser seawater. In seawater, the block:
o: Floats higher, with a smaller fraction submerged
Correct: fraction submerged = ρ(ice)/ρ(fluid), which falls as fluid density rises.
Sinks, because seawater is denser
Denser fluid makes floating easier, not harder.
Floats at the same level
The submerged fraction depends on fluid density.
Floats lower, with a larger fraction submerged
A denser fluid supports the same weight with less displaced volume.
questions.x: For a floating object, buoyant force equals weight, so the fraction submerged equals ρ(object)/ρ(fluid). Seawater is denser than fresh water, so less volume must be displaced to support the same weight, and the ice rides higher. A denser fluid makes floating easier, not harder, which rules out the idea that the block sinks.

questions.q: An object weighs 30 N in air and 20 N when fully submerged in water. What is its density?
o: 1500 kg/m³
Used 20 N rather than the 10 N buoyant force in the ratio.
2000 kg/m³
Divided the submerged weight by the buoyant force.
3000 kg/m³
Correct: F(b) = 10 N gives V = 10⁻³ m³; mass 3 kg / 10⁻³ m³ = 3000 kg/m³.
667 kg/m³
Inverted the ratio; an object that sinks must be denser than water.
questions.x: The loss of weight in water equals the buoyant force: 30 − 20 = 10 N, which corresponds to a displaced volume of 10/(1000 × 10) = 10⁻³ m³. The mass is 30/10 = 3 kg, so density = 3/10⁻³ = 3000 kg/m³. Equivalently, specific gravity = true weight/weight loss = 30/10 = 3. Using the 20 N apparent weight in place of the buoyant force is the main trap.

questions.q: A solid of density 900 kg/m³ floats in an unknown liquid with exactly 60% of its volume submerged. What is the liquid's density?
o: 540 kg/m³
Multiplied by 0.6; a smaller submerged fraction means a denser liquid.
900 kg/m³
A liquid of equal density would leave the object fully submerged.
1500 kg/m³
Correct: fraction submerged = ρ(obj)/ρ(liq), so ρ(liq) = 900/0.6.
1000 kg/m³
Assumed the liquid was water without using the data.
questions.x: For a floating object, ρ(object)/ρ(liquid) = fraction submerged. With 60% submerged, ρ(liquid) = 900/0.6 = 1500 kg/m³. The less of an object sits below the surface, the denser the liquid must be; an object in a liquid of equal density would be fully submerged, so the liquid cannot be 900 kg/m³.

questions.q: A rock sinks from 2 m to 10 m below the surface of a lake. Treating water as incompressible, the buoyant force on the rock:
o: Increases slightly with each meter
This would only occur if the water became denser.
Stays the same
Correct: it depends on displaced volume and fluid density, not depth.
Increases fivefold
Pressure rises with depth, but so does pressure on the top face; the difference is constant.
Decreases
Nothing about the displaced volume changes.
questions.x: Buoyant force equals ρ(fluid)·V(displaced)·g, so for an incompressible fluid and a rigid object it does not change with depth. Pressure does rise with depth, but it rises equally on the top and bottom faces, so their difference (the buoyant force) stays constant. Only a change in fluid density or displaced volume would alter it.

questions.q: An ice cube floats in a glass of fresh water filled to the brim. When the ice melts completely, the water level:
o: Rises, then falls back as it cools
No temperature effect is needed to reach the answer.
Stays the same
Correct: floating ice displaces its own weight of water, exactly the volume its meltwater fills.
Rises and overflows
The above-water portion is offset by ice being less dense than water.
Falls
Melted ice fills exactly the volume it was displacing.
questions.x: Floating ice displaces a mass of water equal to its own mass. When it melts, that same mass becomes liquid water that occupies exactly the volume the ice was displacing, so the level does not change. The portion of ice above the surface is compensated by ice being less dense than water, so the brimful glass does not overflow.

questions.q: A helium balloon rises when released because:
o: The buoyant force from displaced air exceeds the balloon's total weight
Correct: the balloon's average density is less than air's.
Helium pressure inside pushes the balloon upward
Internal pressure acts equally in all directions.
Air pressure is greater above the balloon than below it
Pressure is lower above; the higher pressure below gives lift.
Helium molecules repel the Earth's gravity
Gravity attracts helium too; buoyancy explains the rise.
questions.x: Any object in a fluid feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces. A helium balloon's total weight (helium plus rubber) is less than the weight of the air it displaces because its average density is lower than air's, so the net force is upward. The lift comes from higher air pressure below the balloon than above it.

questions.q: A boat floating in a closed pool carries a large rock. The rock is dropped overboard and sinks. The pool's water level:
o: Falls
Correct: in the boat, the rock displaced its weight of water; sunk, it displaces only its smaller volume.
Rises
A sunken dense rock displaces less water than when floating in the boat.
Rises, then returns to the original level
The final level is lower, not unchanged.
Stays the same
This would be true only if the rock had the density of water.
questions.x: A floating object displaces its weight of water, while a sunken object displaces only its own volume. In the boat, the dense rock displaced water equal to its weight, which is more than its volume of water. Once it sinks, it displaces only its volume, so the total displaced water decreases and the pool level falls.

questions.q: Two people weigh the same in air. One has a higher body fat percentage. During underwater weighing, the person with more body fat will have:
o: The same apparent weight, because their masses are equal
Apparent weight depends on volume as well as mass.
A higher apparent weight, due to a smaller buoyant force
More fat means more volume, which increases buoyancy.
A higher apparent weight, because fat absorbs water
Absorption is not the principle behind hydrostatic weighing.
A lower apparent weight, due to a larger volume and buoyant force
Correct: fat is less dense, so the same mass occupies more volume.
questions.x: Hydrostatic weighing works because apparent weight = true weight − buoyant force, and buoyant force depends on body volume. Fat is less dense than lean tissue, so at equal mass the fattier person has more volume, displaces more water, and has a lower apparent weight underwater. Equal true weights do not imply equal apparent weights.

questions.q: A wooden block floating in water is moved to oil, which is less dense than water but denser than the wood. Compared with water, in oil the buoyant force is:
o: Smaller, and the block sinks
The block still floats because oil is denser than the wood.
Unchanged, and more of the block is submerged
Correct: a floating object's buoyant force equals its weight; lower ρ needs more displaced volume.
Smaller, and less of the block is submerged
Buoyant force must still balance the weight for floating.
Larger, and less of the block is submerged
A less dense fluid requires more, not less, displaced volume.
questions.x: A floating object is in equilibrium, so the buoyant force always equals its weight, regardless of which fluid it floats in. In a less dense fluid, more volume must be submerged to displace the same weight of fluid. As long as the oil is still denser than the wood, the block floats, just lower, with the same buoyant force.

questions.q: A fish inflates its gas-filled swim bladder. The most likely effect is that the fish:
o: Sinks, because it now contains more gas mass
The added gas mass is negligible compared with the volume gained.
Rises, because its average density decreases
Correct: larger volume at the same mass lowers density, increasing net buoyancy.
Stays at the same depth, because its mass is unchanged
Buoyancy depends on volume, which increased.
Sinks, because pressure inside the bladder rises
Bladder pressure does not determine whole-body density.
questions.x: Buoyancy depends on displaced volume, while weight depends on mass. Inflating the swim bladder increases the fish's volume with almost no added mass, lowering its average density and increasing the buoyant force relative to its weight. The fish therefore rises; deflating the bladder has the opposite effect and lets it sink.

questions.q: A 0.001 m³ block of wood (density 600 kg/m³) is held fully under water by a string tied to the bottom of the tank. What is the tension in the string?
o: 4 N
Correct: buoyant force 10 N minus weight 6 N leaves 4 N of tension.
Added the weight to the buoyant force; they act in opposite directions.
That is the buoyant force alone.
6 N
That is the block's weight, not the string tension.
questions.x: For an object held underwater, the forces balance: buoyant force (up) = weight (down) + string tension (down). Buoyant force = 1000 × 0.001 × 10 = 10 N, and weight = 600 × 0.001 × 10 = 6 N, so T = 10 − 6 = 4 N. The string pulls down because the wood would float if released; adding the forces instead treats them as acting in the same direction.

questions.q: The continuity equation, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, for an incompressible fluid is a consequence of conservation of:
o: Momentum
Momentum is not what equates volume flow rates.
Mass
Correct: the mass entering a section per second must leave it.
Charge
Charge conservation applies to electric current.
Energy
Energy conservation gives Bernoulli's equation.
questions.x: The continuity equation says the volume (and so mass) of an incompressible fluid entering a pipe section each second must leave it, so Q = Av is constant along the pipe. It is a mass-conservation statement. Energy conservation is a separate idea that gives Bernoulli's equation, which is why the two are often paired but should not be confused.

questions.q: Fluid flows from a tube into a section with three times the radius. The flow speed in the wide section is:
o: 1/3 the original speed
Used the radius ratio instead of the area ratio.
3 times the original speed
Speed falls, not rises, as area increases.
9 times the original speed
Inverted the relationship between area and speed.
1/9 the original speed
Correct: area rises by 3² = 9, so speed falls by a factor of 9.
questions.x: Continuity requires A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so speed is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Area depends on radius squared, so tripling the radius multiplies area by 9 and cuts speed to 1/9. Using the radius ratio directly (1/3) is the classic error; always convert radius changes to area changes first.

questions.q: Blood moves through a 3 cm² section of aorta at an average speed of 30 cm/s. What is the volume flow rate?
o: 10 cm³/s
Divided speed by area instead of multiplying.
33 cm³/s
Not a valid combination; flow rate is the product A × v, not a ratio.
90 cm³/s
Correct: Q = Av = 3 cm² × 30 cm/s.
900 cm³/s
Off by a factor of 10.
questions.x: Volume flow rate is cross-sectional area times average speed: Q = Av. Here 3 cm² × 30 cm/s = 90 cm³/s, and the units confirm it (cm² × cm/s = cm³/s). Dividing one by the other gives the wrong units, so a quick unit check rules out the distractors built from division.

questions.q: Blood leaves the aorta (area 4 cm²) at 25 cm/s. The total cross-sectional area of all systemic capillaries is about 2500 cm². What is the average speed of blood in the capillaries?
o: 625 cm/s
Multiplied by the area ratio instead of dividing.
25 cm/s
Speed must fall when total area increases.
Correct: Q = 100 cm³/s; v = 100/2500 = 0.04 cm/s.
0.4 cm/s
Off by a factor of 10 in the division.
questions.x: By continuity, flow rate is conserved across the whole circulation, so v depends on the total cross-sectional area of each vessel level. Aortic flow Q = 4 × 25 = 100 cm³/s; spread over 2500 cm² of capillaries, v = 0.04 cm/s. Even though each capillary is tiny, their combined area is huge, so blood moves slowest there, allowing time for exchange.

questions.q: An artery divides into 4 identical branches, each with half the parent's radius. Compared with the parent, the average flow speed in each branch is:
o: Four times larger
Considered one branch's area only, ignoring that flow is shared.
Twice as large
Used radius rather than area in the calculation.
Half as large
Doubled the total area by mistake.
The same
Correct: total branch area = 4 × (1/2)² = 1 times the parent area.
questions.x: Continuity applies to the total area of parallel branches, not the area of a single branch. Each branch has (1/2)² = 1/4 the parent's area, and four of them together equal the parent's area, so the average speed is unchanged. Considering one branch alone, or using radius instead of area, gives a false speed change.

questions.q: Placing a thumb partly over the end of a running garden hose makes the water spray farther because:
o: The smaller opening increases the water's exit speed
Correct: by continuity, reduced area means higher speed for the same flow.
The volume flow rate increases
Flow rate does not rise (it usually drops slightly); exit speed rises because area falls.
The water's density increases
Water is essentially incompressible.
The thumb adds energy to the water
No energy is added by the thumb.
questions.x: For a given flow rate, continuity (Q = Av) means shrinking the exit area forces the water out faster, and a faster jet travels farther. The thumb does not add energy or increase flow; in fact, the extra resistance usually reduces total flow slightly. What changes is how the existing flow is converted into exit speed.

questions.q: Bernoulli's equation for an ideal fluid is fundamentally a statement of:
o: Conservation of charge
Charge is irrelevant to fluid flow.
Conservation of energy per unit volume
Correct: pressure, kinetic and potential energy densities sum to a constant.
Newton's third law
Bernoulli's equation is not an action-reaction statement.
Conservation of mass
That is the continuity equation.
questions.x: Bernoulli's equation, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant, expresses conservation of energy per unit volume for an ideal fluid along a streamline. Pressure acts as energy density from work done by the surrounding fluid, ½ρv² is kinetic energy density, and ρgh is potential energy density. Conservation of mass, by contrast, is the continuity equation.

questions.q: In a Venturi meter, vertical tubes rise from a wide section and a narrow throat of a horizontal pipe. Compared with the tube over the wide section, the fluid column over the throat is:
o: Higher, because the throat pushes fluid upward
Column height reflects static pressure, which is lower in the throat.
Higher, because the faster fluid has higher pressure
Bernoulli: faster flow at the same height has lower pressure.
Lower, because the faster fluid in the throat has lower pressure
Correct: higher speed in the throat means lower static pressure.
The same height, because the pipe is horizontal
Horizontal pipes still show pressure changes with speed.
questions.x: In a Venturi meter, continuity forces the fluid to speed up in the narrow throat, and Bernoulli's equation then requires its static pressure to drop there (at constant height). The vertical tubes measure static pressure, so the column above the throat is lower. Many students wrongly assume faster fluid pushes harder, but higher speed means lower static pressure.

questions.q: Water in a horizontal pipe speeds up from 1 m/s to 3 m/s at a constriction. What is the pressure drop? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³)
o: Used (v₂ − v₁)² instead of v₂² − v₁².
Correct: ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = 500 × (9 − 1).
Used only v₂², ignoring the initial speed.
Forgot the factor of ½.
questions.x: For a horizontal pipe, Bernoulli gives P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²). Here that is ½ × 1000 × (9 − 1) = 4000 Pa. The key is to subtract the squared speeds, not to square the difference in speeds: (3 − 1)² = 4 gives only 2000 Pa, a common mistake.

questions.q: An open tank has a small hole 5 m below the water surface. Neglecting viscosity, how fast does water exit the hole?
o: 5 m/s
Equated v numerically with h; exit speed goes as √(2gh), not h.
7 m/s
Used v = √(gh), forgetting the factor of 2.
10 m/s
Correct: Torricelli's law, v = √(2gh) = √(100).
Forgot to take the square root.
questions.x: Torricelli's law, derived from Bernoulli with both the surface and the jet at atmospheric pressure, gives v = √(2gh). With h = 5 m, v = √(2 × 10 × 5) = √100 = 10 m/s. This is the same speed an object would reach falling freely through 5 m, since the water's potential energy becomes kinetic energy.

questions.q: A segment of the aorta has dilated into an aneurysm. Compared with the adjacent normal segment, blood in the aneurysm has:
o: Lower speed and higher lateral pressure
Correct: larger area slows flow, and by Bernoulli slower flow has higher pressure.
Lower speed and lower lateral pressure
Bernoulli links lower speed with higher pressure.
Higher speed and lower lateral pressure
This describes a narrowing, not a dilation.
Higher speed and higher lateral pressure
Speed and pressure trade off in Bernoulli's equation.
questions.x: In an aneurysm the cross-sectional area increases, so by continuity the blood slows. By Bernoulli's equation, slower flow at the same height has higher lateral (static) pressure. On the MCAT, dilation pairs with lower speed and higher pressure, and stenosis pairs with higher speed and lower pressure; speed and pressure move in opposite directions.

questions.q: Blood flowing through a narrowed (stenotic) artery speeds up. The resulting change in lateral pressure at the narrowing tends to:
o: Decrease, which can let the vessel wall partly collapse
Correct: faster flow lowers lateral pressure, favoring wall collapse.
Increase, which pushes the wall outward
Faster flow lowers, not raises, lateral pressure.
Increase, because resistance is higher
Bernoulli predicts a drop where speed is high.
Stay constant, because flow rate is unchanged
Constant Q still implies a speed change and a pressure change.
questions.x: At a stenosis, continuity forces blood to speed up, and Bernoulli's equation says the lateral (static) pressure on the wall drops where speed is highest. Lower internal pressure means less outward push on the wall, which can let the vessel partly collapse and worsen the narrowing. A higher resistance does not raise local pressure at the constriction.

questions.q: During a storm, strong wind blowing horizontally across a flat roof lifts the roof off a house. This is best explained by:
o: Lower pressure in the fast-moving air above the roof
Correct: by Bernoulli's principle, faster air over the roof has lower pressure than the still air inside.
Buoyancy of the roof in the surrounding air
The roof's buoyant force is tiny and does not change with wind speed.
Wind pushing directly upward on the roof surface
A horizontal wind exerts no direct upward push on a flat roof.
Higher pressure in the fast-moving air above the roof
Faster-moving air has lower static pressure, not higher.
questions.note: Faster flow means lower static pressure.
questions.x: Bernoulli's principle links fast-moving air with lower static pressure. Wind racing over a roof lowers the pressure above it, while the still air inside the building stays near atmospheric, so a net upward force acts on the roof. A horizontal wind cannot directly push a roof upward, and buoyancy is unchanged by wind and far too small to lift it.

questions.q: Water flows at constant speed upward through a vertical pipe of uniform diameter. Neglecting viscosity, the pressure at a point 2 m higher is:
o: The same, because speed is constant
Constant speed removes the kinetic term, not the height term.
Higher by 2×10⁴ Pa
Pressure decreases with height in a fluid.
Lower by 2×10³ Pa
Off by a factor of 10.
Lower by 2×10⁴ Pa
Correct: with equal speeds, ΔP = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 2.
questions.x: Bernoulli's equation: P + ½ρv² + ρgh is constant. With uniform diameter, continuity keeps the speed constant, so the kinetic term cancels and any rise in height must be paid for by a drop in pressure: ΔP = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 2 = 2×10⁴ Pa. Constant speed removes only the velocity term, not the height term.

questions.q: Bernoulli's equation would be LEAST accurate for describing:
o: Water draining slowly from a large tank
Torricelli's law, from Bernoulli, works well here.
Turbulent jets through a severely narrowed heart valve
Correct: Bernoulli assumes steady, nonviscous, nonturbulent flow.
Air flowing smoothly over a wing at low speed
Smooth, low-speed airflow fits Bernoulli well.
Slow, steady water flow in a short, wide pipe
This closely approximates ideal flow.
questions.x: Bernoulli's equation assumes steady, incompressible, nonviscous, laminar flow along a streamline. A turbulent jet through a severely narrowed valve loses much of its energy to eddies and viscous dissipation, so energy is not conserved in the simple form. Slow, smooth flows like gentle draining or low-speed airflow are close to ideal and fit well.

questions.q: Echocardiographers estimate a pressure gradient as ΔP (mmHg) ≈ 4v², with v in m/s. A jet across a narrowed valve measures 4 m/s. What is the estimated gradient?
o: 16 mmHg
Omitted the factor of 4 in the formula.
32 mmHg
Used 2v² instead of 4v².
64 mmHg
Correct: 4 × 4² = 64 mmHg.
256 mmHg
Used (4v)² = 16² instead of 4v².
questions.x: The simplified Bernoulli equation used in echocardiography is ΔP ≈ 4v², with v in m/s and ΔP in mmHg; it comes from ½ρv² converted to mmHg. For v = 4 m/s, ΔP = 4 × 16 = 64 mmHg. Square only the velocity, then multiply by 4; squaring the product (4v)² instead gives 256.

questions.q: A Venturi oxygen mask passes a fast O₂ jet through a narrow opening, which draws room air in through side ports. Room air enters because:
o: Oxygen is denser than room air and sinks
Density differences do not drive this entrainment.
The jet raises the pressure inside the mask
Higher internal pressure would push air out, not in.
Oxygen diffuses outward, leaving a vacuum
Diffusion is too slow and does not create a vacuum.
The fast jet creates a region of pressure below atmospheric
Correct: high speed lowers static pressure, entraining air (Venturi effect).
questions.x: A Venturi mask uses Bernoulli's principle: the high-speed O₂ jet through the narrow opening has low static pressure, below atmospheric. Room air at atmospheric pressure is pushed in through the side ports and mixes with the oxygen, setting a predictable O₂ fraction. Raising internal pressure would push air out of the ports, the opposite of what is observed.

questions.q: By Poiseuille's law, if a vessel's radius decreases by 10% with all else constant, the flow rate becomes approximately:
o: 90% of the original
Flow depends on r⁴, not r.
81% of the original
Used r² instead of r⁴.
66% of the original
Correct: (0.9)⁴ ≈ 0.66.
60% of the original
Subtracted 10% four times instead of multiplying.
questions.x: Poiseuille's law gives Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL), so flow scales with the fourth power of radius. A 10% decrease gives (0.9)⁴ = 0.81² ≈ 0.66, so flow drops to about two-thirds. This steep dependence is why small changes in vessel radius have large effects, and why using r or r² badly underestimates the drop.

questions.q: According to Poiseuille's law, doubling the length of a tube while keeping the pressure difference constant will:
o: Decrease the flow rate 16-fold
The fourth power applies to radius, not length.
Not change the flow rate
Resistance depends on length.
Double the flow rate
Longer tubes add resistance.
Halve the flow rate
Correct: resistance R = 8ηL/(πr⁴) doubles with L, so Q halves.
questions.x: Poiseuille's law: Q = ΔP/R with R = 8ηL/(πr⁴), so resistance is directly proportional to length. Doubling L doubles R, and at constant ΔP the flow halves. The fourth-power dependence belongs only to radius; length enters linearly, which rules out the 16-fold answer.

questions.q: A patient with polycythemia has blood viscosity twice normal. If the pressure gradient and vessel dimensions are unchanged, blood flow:
o: Is unchanged
Viscosity is in the denominator of Poiseuille's law.
Halves
Correct: Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL), so Q is inversely proportional to η.
Doubles
Higher viscosity lowers, not raises, flow.
Falls to one-sixteenth
The fourth power applies to radius, not viscosity.
questions.x: In Poiseuille's law, Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL), viscosity appears to the first power in the denominator. Doubling viscosity doubles resistance, so at the same pressure gradient and vessel dimensions, flow halves. This is one reason polycythemia strains the heart. The fourth-power effect applies only to radius, not viscosity.

questions.q: Mean arterial pressure is 100 mmHg, right atrial pressure is near 0, and cardiac output is 5 L/min. Total peripheral resistance is:
o: 0.05 mmHg·min/L
Divided flow by pressure instead of pressure by flow.
20 mmHg·min/L
Correct: R = ΔP/Q = 100/5.
95 mmHg·min/L
Subtracted instead of dividing.
500 mmHg·min/L
Multiplied ΔP by Q instead of dividing.
questions.x: The circulatory analog of Ohm's law is ΔP = Q × R, so R = ΔP/Q. With a pressure drop of 100 − 0 = 100 mmHg and cardiac output of 5 L/min, R = 100/5 = 20 mmHg·min/L. Resistance is the pressure difference needed per unit flow, so multiplying or subtracting the values does not give resistance.

questions.q: Two identical vessels, each with resistance R, are connected in parallel. Their combined resistance is:
o: 2R
That is the result for vessels in series.
R²
Resistances never multiply this way.
R
Adding a parallel path lowers total resistance.
Correct: 1/R(total) = 1/R + 1/R = 2/R.
questions.x: Vessels in parallel combine like resistors in parallel: 1/R(total) = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂. For two identical vessels, 1/R(total) = 2/R, so R(total) = R/2. Adding parallel pathways always lowers total resistance because flow has more routes, whereas vessels in series add their resistances (2R).

questions.q: A vessel's radius is halved. To keep blood flow constant, the pressure difference across it must increase by a factor of:
o: Flow depends on r⁴, not r.
Used r² instead of r⁴.
Used r³ instead of r⁴.
Correct: resistance rises by 2⁴ = 16, so ΔP must rise 16-fold.
questions.x: Resistance in Poiseuille flow scales as 1/r⁴. Halving the radius increases resistance by 2⁴ = 16, and since Q = ΔP/R, keeping Q constant requires ΔP to rise 16-fold. Using r² (4) or r³ (8) are typical slips; the fourth power is what makes narrowing so costly.

questions.q: Arterioles are the main site where the body regulates vascular resistance. This is effective because resistance depends on:
o: The inverse fourth power of vessel radius
Correct: small radius changes cause large resistance changes.
Blood density
Density does not appear in Poiseuille's law.
The square of vessel length
Resistance is proportional to length, not length squared.
The inverse of vessel wall thickness
Wall thickness is not a term in Poiseuille's law.
questions.x: Because resistance is proportional to 1/r⁴, a small change in radius produces a large change in resistance, and arterioles have smooth muscle that can adjust radius.
