A 20% constriction, for example, more than doubles resistance. Length and blood density are not easily adjustable and length enters only linearly, so radius is the effective control.

questions.q: Which is an assumption of Poiseuille's law?
o: Turbulent flow through a flexible tube
Turbulence and wall flexibility violate the law's assumptions.
Flow of a fluid with zero viscosity
Poiseuille's law is built on viscosity; η is in the formula.
Compressible gas flow at high speed
The law assumes incompressible, slow, laminar flow.
Laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a rigid cylindrical tube
Correct: the law requires steady laminar flow with constant viscosity.
questions.x: Poiseuille's law is derived for steady, laminar flow of an incompressible Newtonian fluid (constant viscosity) through a long, rigid, cylindrical tube. Turbulence, flexible walls, compressibility or a non-Newtonian fluid all break those assumptions. It also requires viscosity, since the law describes flow resisted by viscous friction; a zero-viscosity fluid has no Poiseuille resistance.

questions.q: Two vessel segments of equal length are in series; the second has half the radius of the first. Approximately what fraction of the total pressure drop occurs across the narrow segment?
o: Equal drops would require equal resistances.
Treated resistance as scaling with 1/r.
Treated resistance as scaling with 1/r².
Correct: R₂ = 16R₁, so the narrow segment takes 16/17 ≈ 94% of ΔP.
questions.x: In series, the same flow passes through both segments, so each segment's pressure drop is proportional to its resistance (ΔP = QR). Halving the radius raises resistance by 2⁴ = 16, so the drops are in the ratio 1:16, and the narrow segment takes 16/17 ≈ 94%. This is why most pressure loss occurs at the narrowest points, such as arterioles.

questions.q: Two IV catheters have the same length, but one has 1.5 times the internal radius of the other. At the same pressure, the wider catheter delivers about:
o: 1.5 times the flow
Flow depends on r⁴, not r.
2.25 times the flow
Used r² instead of r⁴.
3.4 times the flow
Used r³ instead of r⁴.
5 times the flow
questions.x: At the same pressure and length, Poiseuille flow scales as r⁴. A 1.5-fold wider catheter gives 1.5⁴ = (2.25)² ≈ 5 times the flow, which is why large-bore IVs are used for rapid fluid resuscitation. Using r² (2.25) or r (1.5) underestimates the benefit of a wider catheter.

questions.q: In steady laminar flow through a cylindrical tube, the fluid velocity is:
o: Greatest at the wall and zero at the center
The no-slip condition makes velocity zero at the wall.
Random from point to point
That describes turbulent eddies, not laminar flow.
Greatest at the center and zero at the wall
Correct: the profile is parabolic, with no slip at the wall.
Uniform across the tube's diameter
Viscosity creates a velocity gradient from wall to center.
questions.x: In laminar flow through a tube, the no-slip condition fixes the fluid at the wall at zero velocity, and viscous drag between layers produces a parabolic velocity profile with the maximum at the center. A uniform (plug) profile would require no viscosity, and random point-to-point velocities describe turbulence.

questions.q: Viscosity is best described as a fluid's:
o: Tendency to minimize its surface area
That is surface tension.
Internal resistance to flow, arising from friction between fluid layers
Correct: viscosity measures resistance to shear, in Pa·s.
Resistance to compression
That is the bulk modulus.
Mass per unit volume
That is density.
questions.x: Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to shear, the internal friction between adjacent layers moving at different speeds, measured in Pa·s. Honey is highly viscous and water is not. It is distinct from surface tension (a surface property), density (mass per volume) and compressibility (resistance to volume change).

questions.q: As the temperature of a liquid such as honey increases, its viscosity:
o: Stays constant
Liquid viscosity is strongly temperature dependent.
Decreases
Correct: thermal energy weakens intermolecular attractions in liquids.
First increases, then decreases
Liquid viscosity falls steadily as temperature rises.
Increases
That is the trend for gases, not liquids.
questions.x: Liquid viscosity comes mainly from intermolecular attractions that resist molecules sliding past each other. Heating gives molecules more kinetic energy to overcome these attractions, so viscosity falls, which is why warm honey pours easily. Gases behave oppositely, with viscosity rising with temperature, because their viscosity comes from molecular momentum transfer.

questions.q: Unlike liquids, the viscosity of a gas increases with temperature. The best explanation is that, at higher temperature, gas molecules:
o: Become more densely packed
At constant pressure, heating lowers gas density.
Form temporary hydrogen-bonded clusters
Heating breaks, rather than forms, such clusters.
Move faster and transfer more momentum between layers
Correct: gas viscosity comes from momentum exchange, which rises with speed.
Attract each other more strongly
Intermolecular attractions are weak and do not grow with temperature.
questions.x: In a gas, molecules are far apart and attractions are negligible; viscosity arises because molecules moving between layers carry momentum and drag neighboring layers along. Heating speeds up the molecules and increases this momentum transfer, so gas viscosity rises. In liquids, heating disrupts intermolecular attractions and lowers viscosity, the opposite trend.

questions.q: The Reynolds number is Re = ρvD/η. Which condition makes turbulent blood flow MOST likely?
o: Severe anemia, with low viscosity and high flow speed
Correct: lower η and higher v both raise Re.
Polycythemia, with high viscosity
Higher viscosity lowers Re, favoring laminar flow.
Cooled blood with increased viscosity
Higher viscosity lowers Re.
Slow flow in a narrow capillary
Small D and low v give a very low Re.
questions.x: Turbulence becomes likely when the Reynolds number, Re = ρvD/η, is high. Anemia lowers blood viscosity and the body compensates with higher cardiac output and faster flow, so both changes raise Re; this is why anemia can produce flow murmurs. Higher viscosity, slower flow or smaller diameter all lower Re and favor laminar flow.

questions.q: While a blood pressure cuff is deflated between systolic and diastolic pressure, Korotkoff sounds are heard. These sounds arise because flow through the partly compressed artery is:
o: Turbulent
Correct: high-speed flow through the narrowed artery becomes turbulent and noisy.
Flowing backward
Flow in the artery remains forward.
Completely stopped
With no flow there is no sound; that occurs above systolic pressure.
Laminar
Laminar flow is silent; it returns once cuff pressure falls below diastolic and the sounds stop.
questions.x: Between systolic and diastolic pressure, the cuff partly compresses the artery, so blood spurts through a narrowed opening at high speed. This raises the Reynolds number enough for turbulence, which produces audible Korotkoff sounds. Above systolic no blood flows, and below diastolic the artery stays open with quiet laminar flow, so sounds start and stop at those pressures.

questions.q: For laminar flow, flow rate is proportional to the pressure gradient. For fully turbulent flow, flow rate is roughly proportional to √ΔP. Doubling ΔP in turbulent flow increases flow by about:
o: 1.4 times
Correct: √2 ≈ 1.4; turbulence wastes energy in eddies.
16 times
Confused with the r⁴ dependence of Poiseuille's law.
2 times
That is the laminar result.
4 times
Squared instead of taking the square root.
questions.x: In laminar flow Q ∝ ΔP, but in turbulent flow much of the driving energy is lost to eddies, so Q grows only about as √ΔP. Doubling ΔP raises turbulent flow by √2 ≈ 1.4 times rather than 2 times. This loss of efficiency is one reason turbulence increases cardiac workload; the r⁴ factor relates to radius, not pressure.

questions.q: Blood (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, η = 0.004 Pa·s) flows at 0.5 m/s through a 2 cm diameter vessel. Taking turbulence as likely above Re ≈ 2000, the flow is:
o: Likely turbulent, Re = 2500
Likely laminar, Re = 250
Off by a factor of 10 in the calculation.
Likely laminar, Re = 1250
Used the radius (1 cm) instead of the diameter.
Likely turbulent, Re = 25,000
Misplaced a decimal, using η = 0.0004 Pa·s.
questions.x: The Reynolds number, Re = ρvD/η, compares inertial to viscous forces and uses the diameter. Here Re = 1000 × 0.5 × 0.02 / 0.004 = 10/0.004 = 2500, which is above the ~2000 threshold, so turbulence is likely. Using the radius instead of the diameter halves Re to 1250 and wrongly predicts laminar flow.

questions.q: Laminar flow is characterized by:
o: A uniform velocity at every point across a tube
Laminar flow has a parabolic velocity profile.
Chaotic eddies and swirling motion
That is turbulent flow.
Smooth parallel layers of fluid with little mixing between them
Correct: laminar layers slide past one another without eddies.
Flow that occurs only at high speeds
High speeds favor turbulence, not laminar flow.
questions.x: In laminar flow, fluid moves in smooth, parallel layers (laminae) that slide past each other with little mixing, and the velocity profile in a tube is parabolic. It occurs at low Reynolds numbers, meaning low speeds, small diameters or high viscosity. Chaotic eddies are the signature of turbulent flow, which high speeds favor.

questions.q: An ideal fluid, as assumed in Bernoulli's equation, is:
o: Compressible and highly viscous
Both properties violate the ideal-fluid model.
Incompressible and has zero viscosity
Correct: no density changes and no internal friction.
Incompressible and highly viscous
Ideal fluids have no viscosity.
Compressible with zero viscosity
Ideal fluids are incompressible.
questions.x: An ideal fluid is incompressible (constant density) and nonviscous (no internal friction), and its flow is assumed steady and laminar. These assumptions let Bernoulli's equation treat mechanical energy as conserved. Viscosity would dissipate energy and compressibility would change density along the flow, both of which break the simple Bernoulli relation.

questions.q: Blood is a shear-thinning (non-Newtonian) fluid. As the shear rate increases, for example during fast flow, blood's apparent viscosity:
o: Increases, as red cells collide more often
That would describe a shear-thickening fluid.
Decreases, as red cells disaggregate and align with flow
Correct: shear-thinning fluids become less viscous at higher shear.
Is unchanged, as with water
Water is Newtonian; blood is not.
Drops to zero
Viscosity falls but never reaches zero.
questions.x: Blood's apparent viscosity depends on shear rate, making it non-Newtonian. At low shear, red cells aggregate into stacks (rouleaux) that resist flow; at high shear these break up and the cells deform and align with the flow, so viscosity falls (shear thinning). A shear-thickening fluid does the opposite, and a Newtonian fluid such as water has constant viscosity.

questions.q: Surface tension in a liquid arises mainly from:
o: Gravity pulling surface molecules downward
Gravity is far weaker than intermolecular forces at this scale.
Atmospheric pressure pressing on the surface
Atmospheric pressure acts uniformly and does not create tension.
Unbalanced cohesive forces on molecules at the surface
Correct: surface molecules are pulled inward, so the surface resists stretching.
Adhesion between the liquid and the air
Air-liquid adhesion is negligible.
questions.x: Molecules inside a liquid are pulled equally in all directions by cohesive forces, but molecules at the surface have fewer neighbors above them and feel a net inward pull. The surface therefore behaves like a stretched elastic film that resists being enlarged, which is surface tension. Gravity and atmospheric pressure do not create this effect.

questions.q: A carefully placed steel needle rests on a water surface even though steel is about 8 times denser than water. The needle is supported mainly by:
o: Viscosity
Viscosity resists motion but does not support static weight.
Surface tension
Correct: the stretched surface film supports the small weight.
Atmospheric pressure
Air pressure acts on all sides and gives no net support.
Buoyancy
A solid denser than water cannot float by buoyancy alone.
questions.x: Surface tension makes the water surface act like a stretched elastic membrane. A light needle laid gently on the surface depresses it slightly, and the upward components of surface tension along the dimple support the needle's small weight. Buoyancy alone could never support steel, which is about 8 times denser than water, as shown when the film is broken and the needle sinks.

questions.q: Water rises in a glass capillary tube. If a tube with half the radius is used instead, the water rises:
o: To the same height
Capillary rise depends on tube radius.
About four times as high
Capillary height scales with 1/r, not 1/r².
About half as high
Narrower tubes produce greater rise.
About twice as high
Correct: capillary rise h ∝ 1/r.
questions.x: Capillary rise h = 2γcosθ/(ρgr) is inversely proportional to tube radius, because the upward surface-tension force scales with circumference (∝ r) while the weight of the lifted column scales with area (∝ r²). Halving the radius therefore doubles the rise. Assuming a 1/r² dependence gives the tempting but wrong fourfold answer.

questions.q: Mercury in a narrow glass tube forms a convex meniscus and sits below the outside level. This happens because:
o: Adhesion to glass exceeds cohesion
That produces a concave meniscus and capillary rise, as in water.
Cohesion among mercury atoms exceeds their adhesion to glass
Correct: strong cohesion causes depression and a convex meniscus.
Mercury has zero surface tension
Mercury has a very high surface tension.
Mercury is denser than water
Density alone does not determine meniscus shape.
questions.x: Meniscus shape reflects the balance between cohesion (liquid-liquid attraction) and adhesion (liquid-wall attraction). Mercury atoms attract each other far more strongly than they attract glass, so mercury pulls away from the walls, forming a convex meniscus and sinking below the outside level. Water wets glass because adhesion dominates, giving a concave meniscus and capillary rise.

questions.q: By the law of Laplace (P = 2γ/r), if two connected alveoli had equal surface tension, the smaller alveolus would:
o: Expand until it matches the larger one
Higher pressure in the small one causes it to shrink.
Have a higher internal pressure and tend to empty into the larger one
Correct: smaller r gives larger P, driving air toward the larger alveolus.
Have the same pressure as the larger one
Pressure depends on radius when γ is equal.
Have a lower internal pressure and fill from the larger one
Pressure is inversely proportional to radius.
questions.x: The law of Laplace for a sphere, P = 2γ/r, means that at equal surface tension the smaller bubble has the higher internal pressure. If two alveoli were connected, air would flow from the small one into the large one, collapsing the small one. Surfactant prevents this by lowering surface tension more in smaller alveoli, stabilizing alveoli of different sizes.

questions.q: Pulmonary surfactant helps keep alveoli open mainly by:
o: Raising alveolar surface tension
Higher tension would favor collapse.
Lowering the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli
Correct: reduced surface tension lowers collapsing pressure and work of breathing.
Raising the partial pressure of oxygen
Surfactant does not change gas composition.
Increasing the viscosity of alveolar air
Surfactant acts at the liquid surface, not on air.
questions.x: Surfactant, secreted by type II pneumocytes, reduces the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli. By Laplace's law (P = 2γ/r), lower surface tension means less collapsing pressure, so alveoli stay open more easily and less work is needed to inflate the lungs. Deficiency, as in premature infants, causes alveolar collapse and respiratory distress.

questions.q: A small alveolus has radius 0.1 mm and lining surface tension 0.05 N/m. By Laplace's law (P = 2γ/r), the pressure needed to keep it open is:
o: 10 Pa
Off by a factor of 100 in converting mm to m.
100 Pa
Off by a factor of 10.
500 Pa
Omitted the factor of 2.
questions.x: Laplace's law for a sphere, P = 2γ/r, gives the pressure difference needed to keep a curved liquid-lined surface from collapsing. Converting 0.1 mm to 1×10⁻⁴ m, P = 2 × 0.05 / 10⁻⁴ = 1000 Pa. Unit conversion is the main trap: leaving r in mm or dropping the factor of 2 gives wrong answers. Smaller alveoli need more pressure, which surfactant helps offset.

questions.q: A needle floating on water sinks after a drop of detergent is added. The detergent:
o: Increases the needle's mass
Detergent does not add meaningful mass to the needle.
Increases the water's density
A tiny drop barely changes density, and higher density would aid floating.
Lowers the water's surface tension
Correct: surfactants weaken the surface film that supported the needle.
Raises the water's surface tension
A stronger film would hold the needle better, not worse.
questions.x: A floating needle is held up by surface tension, not buoyancy. Detergent is a surfactant: its molecules gather at the surface and disrupt the cohesive hydrogen bonding between water molecules, lowering surface tension. The weakened film can no longer support the needle's weight, so it sinks. A higher surface tension would support it better.

questions.q: By the law of Laplace for a cylindrical vessel (wall tension T = P·r), why are large aneurysms more likely to rupture?
o: Blood viscosity rises in wider vessels
Viscosity is not the explanation here.
Wall tension falls as the radius increases
T is proportional to r.
Wall tension rises as the radius increases at the same pressure
Correct: larger r means greater T, which favors further dilation.
Pressure inside falls to zero as the radius grows
Pressure does not vanish; tension rises with radius.
questions.x: For a cylindrical vessel, the law of Laplace gives wall tension T = P·r. At the same blood pressure, a wider aneurysm has a larger radius and therefore greater wall tension, which stretches the wall further, enlarging r again in a vicious cycle toward rupture. The internal pressure does not fall to zero; tension grows with radius.

questions.q: A syringe of gas is compressed from 60 mL to 20 mL at constant temperature. The pressure of the gas:
o: Increases ninefold
The relationship is inverse, not inverse-square.
Falls to one-third
Pressure and volume are inversely related.
Triples
Correct: Boyle's law, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂; volume ÷ 3 means pressure × 3.
Is unchanged
Pressure must change when volume changes at constant T.
questions.x: Boyle's law: at constant temperature and amount of gas, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so pressure is inversely proportional to volume. Reducing volume from 60 mL to 20 mL is a factor of 3, so pressure triples. The relationship is a simple inverse, not inverse-square, so a ninefold increase is wrong.

questions.q: A balloon is heated at constant pressure from 27°C to 127°C. Its volume becomes:
o: About 4.7 times the original
Used Celsius temperatures; gas laws need kelvin.
4/3 of the original
Correct: V ∝ T in kelvin; 400 K/300 K = 4/3.
3/4 of the original
Volume increases with temperature.
The same as the original
At constant P, volume changes with temperature.
questions.x: Charles's law: at constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature. Converting to kelvin, 27°C = 300 K and 127°C = 400 K, so V₂/V₁ = 400/300 = 4/3. Using Celsius gives the absurd ratio 127/27 ≈ 4.7; gas laws always require kelvin because volume extrapolates to zero at 0 K, not 0°C.

questions.q: What volume do 2 mol of an ideal gas occupy at STP (0°C, 1 atm)?
o: Correct: 2 × 22.4 L/mol.
That is the volume of 1 mol.
That is the volume of 0.5 mol.
That uses 24.5 L/mol, the value near 25°C, not STP.
questions.x: At STP (0°C, 1 atm), one mole of any ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L, so 2 mol occupy 44.8 L. Molar volume depends only on temperature and pressure, not on the identity of the gas. The 24.5 L/mol figure applies near 25°C, not at STP, so it gives a slightly larger, incorrect volume here.

questions.q: At the same temperature and pressure, which gas has the greatest density?
o: He
He (4 g/mol) has the lowest density of these.
N₂
N₂ (28 g/mol) is lighter than O₂ and CO₂.
O₂
O₂ (32 g/mol) is lighter than CO₂.
CO₂
Correct: ρ = PM/RT, and CO₂ has the largest molar mass (44 g/mol).
questions.x: From PV = nRT, gas density is ρ = PM/(RT), so at the same T and P density is proportional to molar mass. CO₂ (44 g/mol) is heaviest of these, followed by O₂ (32), N₂ (28) and He (4). This is why CO₂ pools in low places and helium balloons rise.

questions.q: Real gases deviate MOST from ideal behavior under which conditions?
o: High temperature at any pressure
High temperature reduces the effect of attractions.
Low pressure and low temperature
Low pressure keeps molecules far apart.
Low pressure and high temperature
These conditions make gases behave most ideally.
High pressure and low temperature
Correct: molecules are crowded and slow, so volume and attractions matter.
questions.x: The ideal gas model assumes negligible molecular volume and no intermolecular forces. At high pressure, molecules are crowded so their own volume matters; at low temperature, they move slowly so attractions matter. Both effects are greatest at high pressure and low temperature. Low pressure and high temperature make gases behave most ideally.

questions.q: At very high pressure, a real gas often occupies a larger volume than the ideal gas law predicts. The main reason is that:
o: Gas molecules have a finite volume of their own
Correct: excluded molecular volume becomes significant when gas is compressed.
Collisions with the walls become elastic
Ideal gases already assume elastic collisions.
Intermolecular attractions pull molecules together
Attractions make the volume smaller, not larger.
Molecules move faster at high pressure
Speed depends on temperature, not pressure.
questions.x: Real molecules take up space, so the volume actually available for motion is less than the container volume. At very high pressure the molecules are packed closely and this excluded volume becomes significant, making the real volume larger than PV = nRT predicts (the b term in van der Waals). Attractions push the other way, making volume smaller, and dominate at moderate pressures and low temperatures.

questions.q: Balloon A holds 2 g of H₂ and balloon B holds 32 g of O₂, both at the same temperature and pressure. How do their volumes compare?
o: B is 16 times larger
Volume depends on moles, not mass.
They are equal
Correct: each holds 1 mol, and equal moles occupy equal volumes (Avogadro).
B is 4 times larger
Took the square root of the 16-fold mass ratio; volume depends only on moles.
A is 16 times larger
Both contain 1 mol, so neither is larger.
questions.x: Avogadro's law states that at the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gas contain equal numbers of moles. 2 g of H₂ (2 g/mol) and 32 g of O₂ (32 g/mol) are each 1 mol, so the balloons have equal volumes. Gas volume depends on moles, not mass, which rules out the 16-fold answer based on mass.

questions.q: During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and thoracic volume increases. By Boyle's law, alveolar pressure:
o: Falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in
Correct: larger volume gives lower pressure, creating an inward gradient.
Rises, pushing air out
That describes expiration.
Rises above atmospheric pressure, so air flows in
Air flows from high to low pressure, so alveolar pressure must fall.
Stays equal to atmospheric pressure throughout
A pressure gradient is required for airflow.
questions.x: Air flows from high to low pressure. When the diaphragm contracts, thoracic and lung volume increase, and by Boyle's law alveolar pressure falls slightly below atmospheric, so air flows in. During expiration volume decreases and alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric, pushing air out. Without a pressure gradient there would be no airflow.

questions.q: A diver fills her lungs to 2 L at 20 m depth (about 3 atm absolute), then holds her breath and ascends to the surface. Her lung gas would expand to about:
o: 4 L
Used gauge pressure (2 atm) instead of absolute pressure.
2 L
Gas volume changes with pressure.
6 L
Correct: Boyle's law, 3 atm × 2 L = 1 atm × V, so V = 6 L, risking barotrauma.
Gas expands, not compresses, as pressure falls.
questions.x: Boyle's law uses absolute pressure: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. At 20 m the absolute pressure is about 3 atm, and at the surface 1 atm, so 3 × 2 L = 1 × V gives V = 6 L, enough to overexpand and rupture lungs. This is why divers must exhale while ascending. Using gauge pressure (2 atm) underestimates the expansion.

questions.q: By Graham's law, about how many times faster does He (4 g/mol) effuse than O₂ (32 g/mol)?
o: Forgot the square root.
Squared the molar mass ratio.
Correct: rate ratio = √(32/4) = √8 ≈ 2.8.
Inverted the ratio; the lighter gas effuses faster.
questions.x: Graham's law: effusion rate is inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass, rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁). For He versus O₂, √(32/4) = √8 ≈ 2.8, so helium effuses about 2.8 times faster. Lighter molecules move faster at the same temperature; forgetting the square root gives 8.

questions.q: How many moles of ideal gas occupy 8.2 L at 2 atm and 400 K? (R = 0.082 L·atm/(mol·K))
o: 0.5 mol
0.05 mol
Off by a factor of 10 in the arithmetic.
2 mol
Inverted the ratio, computing RT/PV instead of PV/RT.
0.25 mol
Dropped the factor of 2 atm.
questions.x: Rearranging the ideal gas law gives n = PV/(RT). Here PV = 2 × 8.2 = 16.4 L·atm and RT = 0.082 × 400 = 32.8 L·atm/mol, so n = 0.5 mol. Choosing numbers that are multiples of R simplifies the arithmetic; inverting the ratio (RT/PV) gives 2 mol, a common slip.

questions.q: When gas volume at constant pressure is plotted against temperature in °C, the straight line extrapolates to zero volume at about:
o: Correct: this is absolute zero, 0 K.
No special significance for ideal gases.
That is close to absolute zero in °F, not °C.
0°C is 273 K; real gases still have volume there.
questions.x: For an ideal gas at constant pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature (Charles's law). Plotting V against T in °C gives a straight line that extrapolates to zero volume at about −273°C, which defines absolute zero (0 K). That is why gas law calculations require kelvin: 0°C is 273 K, not zero.

questions.q: A 3 L gas sample at 1 atm and 300 K is changed to 2 atm and 400 K. Its new volume is:
o: Inverted both ratios: 3 × 2 × 3/4.
8 L
Multiplied by the pressure ratio instead of dividing.
Inverted the temperature ratio: 3 × 1/2 × 3/4.
2 L
questions.x: The combined gas law, P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, gives V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁). Doubling pressure halves volume and raising T from 300 to 400 K multiplies it by 4/3, so V₂ = 3 × 1/2 × 4/3 = 2 L. A good check is direction: higher pressure shrinks the gas and higher temperature expands it.

questions.q: Which assumption is part of the ideal gas model?
o: Gas molecules occupy most of the container's volume
Ideal molecules have negligible volume.
Gas molecules exert no attractive or repulsive forces on one another
Correct: ideal molecules interact only through elastic collisions.
Collisions between molecules lose kinetic energy
Ideal collisions are perfectly elastic.
Molecular speed is independent of temperature
Average speed rises with temperature.
questions.x: The ideal gas model treats molecules as point particles with negligible volume that exert no attractive or repulsive forces on one another and collide perfectly elastically. Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature, so speed rises with temperature. Real gases deviate when molecular volume or attractions become significant.

questions.q: Dalton's law of partial pressures states that the total pressure of a gas mixture equals:
o: The product of the component partial pressures
Partial pressures add, not multiply.
The partial pressure of the most abundant gas
All components contribute.
The average of the component partial pressures
Partial pressures add; they are not averaged.
The sum of the partial pressures of each component gas
Correct: P(total) = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + ...
questions.x: Dalton's law states that in a mixture of non-reacting gases, each gas exerts its own partial pressure as if it alone filled the container, and the total pressure is the sum of these partial pressures. Each partial pressure equals the gas's mole fraction times the total pressure. Partial pressures add; they are not multiplied or averaged.

questions.q: A container holds 3 mol N₂ and 1 mol O₂ at a total pressure of 2 atm. What is the partial pressure of O₂?
o: 0.5 atm
Correct: X(O₂) = 1/4, so P = 0.25 × 2 atm.
2 atm
That is the total pressure.
1.5 atm
That is the partial pressure of N₂.
0.67 atm
Used the mole ratio 1:3 as a fraction (1/3).
questions.x: By Dalton's law, a gas's partial pressure equals its mole fraction times the total pressure. O₂ is 1 of 4 total moles, so X(O₂) = 0.25 and P(O₂) = 0.25 × 2 atm = 0.5 atm. A common error is using the mole ratio (1:3, or 1/3) instead of the mole fraction (1/4), which uses total moles in the denominator.

questions.q: Air (21% O₂) is inhaled at sea level (760 mmHg) and fully humidified at body temperature, where water vapor pressure is 47 mmHg. The PO₂ of the humidified air is about:
o: 100 mmHg
That is alveolar PO₂, which also reflects CO₂ and O₂ uptake.
160 mmHg
Ignores water vapor; 0.21 × 760 ≈ 160 mmHg.
150 mmHg
113 mmHg
Took 21% of 760 and then subtracted all 47 mmHg of vapor from the O₂ alone.
questions.x: In the airways, inspired air becomes saturated with water vapor at body temperature, and water vapor takes up 47 mmHg of the total pressure. The remaining dry-gas pressure is 760 − 47 = 713 mmHg, and O₂ is 21% of that: ≈150 mmHg. Alveolar PO₂ is lower still (~100 mmHg) because O₂ is taken up and CO₂ is added.

questions.q: A patient breathes 100% O₂ in a hyperbaric chamber at 3 atm absolute. Ignoring water vapor, the inspired PO₂ is about:
o: 760 mmHg
That is 100% O₂ at 1 atm.
480 mmHg
Multiplied by 0.21, but the gas is pure O₂.
160 mmHg
That is room air at sea level.
2280 mmHg
Correct: 1.00 × 3 × 760 mmHg.
questions.x: Partial pressure equals the gas fraction times the total absolute pressure. Pure O₂ (fraction 1.00) at 3 atm gives 3 × 760 = 2280 mmHg, which greatly increases dissolved O₂ in the blood. Multiplying by 0.21 would apply only if the patient breathed air, not pure oxygen.

questions.q: Helium is pumped into a rigid, sealed container of air at constant temperature, doubling the total pressure. The partial pressure of O₂ in the container:
o: Halves
O₂'s mole fraction halves, but total pressure doubles, so P(O₂) is constant.
Falls to zero
Helium does not remove O₂.
Doubles
Only total pressure doubles; O₂ amount did not change.
Is unchanged
Correct: O₂ moles, volume and T are unchanged, so its partial pressure is too.
questions.x: Each gas's partial pressure depends only on its own moles, the volume and the temperature (P = nRT/V), as if it filled the container alone. Adding helium to a rigid container raises the total pressure but leaves O₂'s moles, the volume and the temperature unchanged, so P(O₂) is constant. O₂'s mole fraction halves, but the total pressure doubles, and the two effects cancel.

questions.q: A gas is collected over water at a total pressure of 760 mmHg; water vapor pressure is 24 mmHg. The pressure of the dry collected gas is:
o: 736 mmHg
Correct: P(gas) = P(total) − P(H₂O) = 760 − 24.
24 mmHg
That is the water vapor pressure itself.
784 mmHg
Added the vapor pressure instead of subtracting it.
760 mmHg
Ignored the contribution of water vapor.
questions.x: Gas collected over water is a mixture of the gas and water vapor, and by Dalton's law the total pressure is the sum of the two partial pressures. So P(dry gas) = 760 − 24 = 736 mmHg. Ignoring the vapor overstates the amount of gas collected; adding it gets Dalton's law backwards.

questions.q: A diver breathes a mix that is 32% O₂ at 40 m depth (5 atm absolute). The PO₂ of the gas being breathed is:
o: 1.28 atm
Used gauge pressure (4 atm) instead of absolute.
0.32 atm
Used surface pressure rather than pressure at depth.
5 atm
That is total pressure, not O₂'s share.
1.6 atm
Correct: 0.32 × 5 atm.
questions.x: Inspired partial pressure equals the gas fraction times the total absolute pressure. At 40 m depth, absolute pressure is about 1 + 4 = 5 atm, so PO₂ = 0.32 × 5 = 1.6 atm, a level near the limit for oxygen toxicity. Using gauge pressure (4 atm) would ignore the atmosphere pressing on the water surface.

questions.q: At an altitude where atmospheric pressure is 380 mmHg, the fraction of O₂ in dry air is still 21%. The PO₂ of the dry air is about:
o: 40 mmHg
Halved the sea-level value twice.
380 mmHg
That is the total pressure, not O₂'s share.
160 mmHg
That is PO₂ at sea level.
80 mmHg
Correct: 0.21 × 380 ≈ 80 mmHg; the fraction is constant, the total falls.
questions.x: The fraction of O₂ in dry air stays about 21% at all altitudes; what falls is the total barometric pressure. At 380 mmHg, PO₂ = 0.21 × 380 ≈ 80 mmHg, half the sea-level value of about 160 mmHg. Hypoxia at altitude results from this lower partial pressure, not from a lower percentage of oxygen.

questions.q: Henry's law states that, at constant temperature, the concentration of a gas dissolved in a liquid is proportional to:
o: The volume of the liquid
Concentration does not depend on how much liquid there is.
The liquid's viscosity
Viscosity does not set equilibrium solubility.
The partial pressure of that gas above the liquid
Correct: C = k·P(gas).
The total pressure of all gases above the liquid
Each gas dissolves according to its own partial pressure.
questions.x: Henry's law: at constant temperature, the amount of a gas dissolved in a liquid is proportional to that gas's own partial pressure above the liquid, C = k·P(gas). Each gas dissolves according to its own partial pressure, not the total pressure of the mixture. Concentration is independent of how much liquid is present.

questions.q: A scuba diver ascends too quickly and develops joint pain from gas bubbles in tissues. This occurs because:
o: Falling ambient pressure lowers N₂ solubility, so dissolved N₂ comes out of solution
Correct: Henry's law; rapid decompression forms bubbles.
Rising ambient pressure forces N₂ into the joints
Ascent lowers, not raises, ambient pressure.
O₂ is consumed faster at the surface
Bubbles in decompression sickness are mainly N₂.
Cold water makes N₂ less soluble
The trigger is rapid pressure loss, not temperature.
questions.x: At depth, high ambient pressure raises the partial pressure of inhaled N₂, so more N₂ dissolves in tissues (Henry's law). If the diver ascends too fast, ambient pressure drops and N₂ solubility falls faster than the excess gas can be exhaled, so N₂ comes out of solution as bubbles in joints and tissues. Slow ascents let it leave gradually through the lungs.

questions.q: Across the alveolar membrane, the PO₂ gradient is about 60 mmHg while the PCO₂ gradient is only about 6 mmHg, yet CO₂ exchange is not limited. The best explanation is that CO₂:
o: Is far more soluble in water and tissue than O₂
Correct: CO₂'s solubility is about 20 times O₂'s, offsetting its small gradient.
Is actively transported across the membrane
Gas exchange is passive diffusion.
Has a lower molar mass than O₂
CO₂ (44 g/mol) is heavier than O₂ (32 g/mol).
Has a higher partial pressure in air than O₂
Atmospheric PCO₂ is far below PO₂.
questions.x: Diffusion rate across a membrane depends on the partial pressure gradient times the gas's solubility (Fick's law), among other factors. CO₂ is about 20 times more soluble than O₂ in water and tissue, so a small PCO₂ gradient moves as much CO₂ as a large PO₂ gradient moves O₂. CO₂ is actually heavier than O₂, so molar mass does not explain its fast exchange.

questions.q: O₂ solubility in plasma is about 0.003 mL O₂ per dL of blood per mmHg. At a PaO₂ of 100 mmHg, the dissolved O₂ content is:
o: 20 mL O₂/dL
That approximates total content, mostly bound to hemoglobin.
0.3 mL O₂/dL
Correct: 0.003 × 100 by Henry's law.
3 mL O₂/dL
Off by a factor of 10.
0.03 mL O₂/dL
Off by a factor of 10 in the other direction.
questions.x: Henry's law says dissolved gas concentration equals the solubility constant times partial pressure. At PaO₂ = 100 mmHg, dissolved O₂ = 0.003 × 100 = 0.3 mL/dL. This is tiny compared with the roughly 20 mL/dL carried on hemoglobin, which is why hemoglobin is essential for oxygen transport.

questions.q: An opened bottle of carbonated water goes flat over time because:
o: The water evaporates, concentrating the CO₂
Evaporation is not why the drink loses fizz.
CO₂ reacts with oxygen in the air
CO₂ does not react with O₂ under these conditions.
Atmospheric pressure pushes CO₂ deeper into solution
The CO₂ leaves the solution; it is not pushed in.
The CO₂ partial pressure above the liquid drops, so dissolved CO₂ leaves
Correct: by Henry's law, less CO₂ stays dissolved at lower partial pressure.
questions.x: Carbonated drinks are bottled under high CO₂ pressure, so a lot of CO₂ dissolves (Henry's law). Once opened, the CO₂ above the liquid escapes and its partial pressure falls to the very low atmospheric level, so the equilibrium amount of dissolved CO₂ drops and the excess gas leaves the solution. Atmospheric pressure does not push CO₂ in.

questions.q: A warm can of soda fizzes more when opened than a cold one. This shows that, for most gases, solubility in water:
o: Depends only on total pressure
Temperature and partial pressure both matter.
Increases as temperature increases
This is the opposite of the observed behavior.
Decreases as temperature increases
Correct: warmer liquid holds less dissolved gas.
Is independent of temperature
The difference in fizzing shows a temperature dependence.
questions.x: For most gases, dissolving in water releases heat, and warmer molecules have more kinetic energy to escape the liquid, so gas solubility decreases as temperature rises. A warm soda therefore holds less CO₂ at equilibrium, so more gas bursts out when it is opened. Solids often show the opposite trend, which is a common source of confusion.

questions.q: Raising a patient's PaO₂ from 100 to 600 mmHg increases arterial O₂ content only modestly. Why?
o: Extra O₂ lowers plasma solubility
Solubility is a constant at a given temperature.
Henry's law stops applying above 100 mmHg
Dissolved O₂ keeps rising linearly with PO₂.
Hemoglobin is already nearly saturated, and dissolved O₂ rises only by a small amount
Correct: dissolved O₂ climbs linearly but stays small relative to Hb-bound O₂.
High PO₂ causes hemoglobin to release O₂
Higher PO₂ favors O₂ binding, not release.
questions.x: Arterial O₂ content is mostly hemoglobin-bound O₂, plus a small dissolved fraction (0.003 mL/dL per mmHg). At PaO₂ 100 mmHg hemoglobin is already about 98% saturated, so raising PaO₂ to 600 mmHg adds little bound O₂ and only about 1.5 mL/dL dissolved O₂. Henry's law still applies linearly; the dissolved amount is simply small.

questions.q: Plasma equilibrates with alveolar gas at PO₂ = 100 mmHg and PCO₂ = 40 mmHg. Comparing dissolved gases, the plasma contains:
o: More dissolved CO₂ than O₂, despite CO₂'s lower partial pressure
Correct: CO₂'s ~20× higher solubility outweighs its lower partial pressure.
Equal concentrations of both gases
Equal concentrations would require equal solubility × pressure.
No dissolved CO₂, since it is all converted to bicarbonate
Some CO₂ always remains physically dissolved.
More dissolved O₂ than CO₂, because PO₂ is higher
Concentration depends on solubility as well as partial pressure.
questions.x: Dissolved gas concentration equals solubility times partial pressure (Henry's law). CO₂ is about 20 times more soluble than O₂, so even at 40 mmHg its dissolved concentration (∝ 20 × 40 = 800) exceeds that of O₂ at 100 mmHg (∝ 1 × 100). Partial pressure alone does not determine how much gas dissolves.

questions.q: Disease doubles alveolar membrane thickness and halves the surface area available for exchange. With the same partial pressure gradient, the diffusion rate becomes:
o: 4 times normal
Inverted the effect of both changes.
1/4 of normal
Correct: rate ∝ A/T, so (1/2)/(2) = 1/4.
1/2 of normal
Accounted for only one of the two changes.
Unchanged
The two changes both reduce the rate; they do not cancel.
questions.x: Fick's law of diffusion says the rate of gas transfer is proportional to surface area and partial pressure gradient, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness. Halving area halves the rate, and doubling thickness halves it again, so the rate falls to 1/4. The two changes both reduce diffusion and compound rather than cancel.

questions.q: Alveolar PO₂ is about 100 mmHg, and blood entering the pulmonary capillaries has a PO₂ of about 40 mmHg. Oxygen therefore moves:
o: From the blood into the alveoli
That would be against the gradient.
From the alveoli into the blood
Correct: gases diffuse down their partial pressure gradient.
In neither direction until active transport begins
Gas exchange is passive.
From the blood into the alveoli, then back
Net movement follows the gradient into the blood.
questions.x: Gases diffuse passively from regions of higher partial pressure to lower partial pressure. Alveolar PO₂ (~100 mmHg) exceeds the PO₂ of incoming pulmonary blood (~40 mmHg), so O₂ moves into the blood. CO₂ moves the opposite way because its partial pressure is higher in the blood than in the alveoli; no active transport is involved.

questions.q: A stab wound opens the pleural space to the atmosphere, and the lung on that side collapses. The best explanation is that:
o: Intrapleural pressure falls further below atmospheric
Air rushing in raises pleural pressure.
Intrapleural pressure rises to atmospheric, removing the pressure gradient that held the lung expanded
Correct: normally subatmospheric pleural pressure keeps the lung inflated.
Air enters the alveoli directly through the wound
Air enters the pleural space, not the alveoli.
Alveolar surface tension drops to zero
Surface tension still acts, which helps collapse the lung.
questions.x: The lung's elastic recoil pulls it inward, while subatmospheric intrapleural pressure holds it expanded against the chest wall. A wound that opens the pleural space lets air rush in until intrapleural pressure equals atmospheric, removing the transpulmonary pressure gradient. The lung then recoils and collapses (pneumothorax).

questions.q: Blood flow through a vessel is driven by:
o: The density of the blood alone
Density does not drive horizontal flow.
The pressure difference between the vessel's ends
Correct: Q = ΔP/R; flow needs a gradient, not just high pressure.
The absolute pressure inside the vessel
High pressure with no gradient produces no flow.
The vessel's wall thickness
Wall thickness is not a driving force.
questions.x: Flow requires a pressure difference: Q = ΔP/R, the fluid analog of Ohm's law. Blood moves from the high-pressure arterial end to the lower-pressure venous end of a vessel. A vessel at high absolute pressure but with equal pressure at both ends would have no flow, which is why the gradient, not the pressure level, drives flow.

questions.q: Veins hold about two-thirds of the blood volume at low pressure. This is mainly because, compared with arteries, veins have greater:
o: Wall stiffness
Stiffer walls would reduce compliance.
Resistance to blood flow
Veins have low, not high, resistance.
Compliance, a larger volume change per unit pressure change
Correct: compliance = ΔV/ΔP, so veins store volume at low pressure.
Flow velocity
Velocity does not explain volume storage.
questions.x: Compliance is the change in volume per change in pressure, C = ΔV/ΔP. Veins have thin, distensible walls, so they accommodate large volumes with little pressure rise, acting as the circulation's blood reservoir and holding about two-thirds of the blood. Arteries are stiffer and less compliant, so they store less volume at higher pressure.

questions.q: The pulmonary and systemic circuits carry the same flow, but the pressure drop across the pulmonary circuit is about 10 mmHg versus about 90 mmHg systemically. Pulmonary vascular resistance is therefore about:
o: 1/9 of systemic resistance
Correct: R = ΔP/Q, and Q is equal, so 10/90.
Equal to systemic resistance
Equal flows with unequal drops require unequal resistances.
9 times systemic resistance
Inverted the ratio; a smaller drop means lower resistance.
1/81 of systemic resistance
Squared the pressure ratio without basis.
questions.x: Because the two circuits are in series, they carry the same flow (cardiac output). With R = ΔP/Q, resistance is proportional to the pressure drop, so R(pulmonary)/R(systemic) = 10/90 = 1/9. The pulmonary circuit's low resistance lets the right ventricle pump the same flow at a much lower pressure than the left.

questions.q: In a pulmonary capillary, blood PO₂ normally reaches alveolar PO₂ within the first third of the capillary. If the membrane thickens, the most likely result during exercise, when transit time shortens, is that:
o: Blood may leave the capillary before PO₂ fully equilibrates
Correct: slower diffusion plus shorter transit can prevent equilibration.
CO₂ will move from alveoli into the blood
CO₂ still moves from blood to alveoli.
Equilibration will happen faster than normal
A thicker membrane slows diffusion.
Blood PO₂ will exceed alveolar PO₂
Diffusion cannot raise blood PO₂ above alveolar PO₂.
questions.x: Normally pulmonary blood equilibrates with alveolar O₂ within the first third of the capillary, leaving a large safety margin. A thickened membrane slows diffusion (Fick's law), and exercise shortens the time each red cell spends in the capillary. Together these can leave blood PO₂ below alveolar PO₂ at the capillary's end, producing exercise-induced hypoxemia.

questions.q: Gases diffuse across the alveolar–capillary membrane by:
o: Bulk flow driven by blood pressure
Bulk flow moves air in airways, not gas across the membrane.
Passive diffusion down partial pressure gradients
Correct: no energy input is needed for O₂ and CO₂ exchange.
Facilitated diffusion through gas-specific channels
O₂ and CO₂ cross lipid membranes without specific carriers.
Primary active transport using ATP
No pumps are involved in respiratory gas exchange.
questions.x: O₂ and CO₂ cross the alveolar-capillary membrane by simple passive diffusion, moving down their partial pressure gradients with no energy input. Both are small, nonpolar enough to pass through lipid membranes without carriers. Bulk flow moves air through the airways, but transfer across the membrane itself is diffusion.

questions.q: An experimenter measures flow through a rigid tube at several pressure differences. Flow doubles when ΔP doubles at low ΔP, but at high ΔP, doubling ΔP raises flow by only about 40%. The best interpretation is that:
o: The fluid's viscosity fell at high ΔP
Lower viscosity would increase, not reduce, the flow gain.
The tube's radius increased at high ΔP
The tube is rigid; a wider tube would raise flow.
Poiseuille's law holds at all pressures
Poiseuille predicts doubling, which was not observed.
Flow became turbulent at high ΔP
Correct: turbulent flow scales roughly with √ΔP (√2 ≈ 1.4).
questions.x: Poiseuille's law predicts flow proportional to ΔP for laminar flow, matching the low-pressure data. At high ΔP, flow rose only about 40% (√2 ≈ 1.4) when ΔP doubled, which is the signature of turbulence, where energy is lost to eddies and Q ∝ √ΔP. A rigid tube rules out widening, and lower viscosity would increase rather than decrease the flow gain.

questions.q: Two point charges are a distance r apart and exert a force F on each other. If the distance is doubled, what is the new force?
o: Treats the force as 1/r rather than 1/r².
2F
Force falls with distance; it does not grow.
4F
Inverts the inverse-square relationship.
Correct: Coulomb force scales as 1/r², so doubling r divides F by 4.
questions.note: Inverse square: 2× distance → 1/4 force.
questions.x: Coulomb's law, F = kq₁q₂/r², is an inverse-square law: the force depends on 1/r², not 1/r. Doubling r multiplies r² by 4, so the force drops to one quarter. The tempting F/2 comes from treating the dependence as linear in 1/r.

questions.q: Both charges in an isolated pair are doubled, and their separation is also doubled. How does the electrostatic force change?
o: It doubles
Counts only one charge doubling and ignores the distance term.
It quadruples
Accounts for the charges but forgets the 1/r² factor.
It stays the same
Correct: q₁q₂ rises 4× and r² rises 4×, so the effects cancel.
It halves
Counts only one charge doubling, then divides by the 4× rise in r².
questions.x: The force is proportional to the product q₁q₂ and inversely proportional to r². Doubling both charges multiplies q₁q₂ by 4, and doubling r multiplies r² by 4, so the two changes cancel exactly. Choosing 4× means only the numerator was updated and the squared distance was forgotten.

questions.q: Which of the following could NOT be the net charge on an isolated object? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
o: Correct: this is 1.5e; charge comes only in whole multiples of e.
This is 2e, an allowed whole-number multiple.
This is 3e, an allowed whole-number multiple.
This is 10e, an allowed whole-number multiple.
questions.note: Charge is quantized in units of e.
questions.x: Charge is quantized: any isolated object carries an integer multiple of the elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Dividing each value by e gives 2, 3 and 10 for the allowed choices, but 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is 1.5e, which is impossible. Quarks carry fractional charge, but they never appear isolated.

questions.q: A +2 μC charge and a −3 μC charge are 0.3 m apart. What is the force between them? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²)
o: 0.6 N, attractive
Correct: F = (9 × 10⁹)(6 × 10⁻¹²)/0.09 = 0.6 N; opposite signs attract.
0.6 N, repulsive
Right magnitude, but opposite charges attract.
0.18 N, attractive
Divides by r instead of r².
6 N, attractive
Decimal slip: 0.054/0.09 is 0.6, not 6.
questions.x: Use magnitudes in F = k|q₁q₂|/r² and decide direction from the signs separately. Here (9 × 10⁹)(2 × 10⁻⁶)(3 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.054 N·m², and dividing by r² = 0.09 m² gives 0.6 N. Because the charges are opposite, the force is attractive; dividing by 0.3 instead of 0.09 gives the 0.18 N trap.

questions.q: Excess negative charge is placed on a solid metal sphere. Once equilibrium is reached, where is the excess charge?
o: Spread over the outer surface
Correct: like charges repel to maximize separation, ending up on a conductor's surface.
Concentrated at the center
Repulsion drives charge outward, not inward.
Uniformly throughout the volume
That describes a charged insulator, not a conductor.
At the single point where it was added
Charges move freely in a metal and redistribute.
questions.x: In a conductor charges move freely, and any field inside would push them until it vanishes. At equilibrium E = 0 inside, so by Gauss's law no net charge can sit in the interior; the excess ends up on the outer surface. A uniform volume distribution only happens in an insulator, where charges cannot move.

questions.q: A positively charged rod is held near a neutral metal sphere. The sphere is briefly grounded, the ground is removed, and then the rod is taken away. What is the sphere's final charge?
o: Negative
Correct: the rod draws electrons up from ground; they are trapped when ground is cut.
Positive
Induction gives a charge opposite to the inducing rod.
Neutral
Grounding while the rod is near lets net charge flow in.
Positive near the rod, net neutral
That is polarization without grounding; grounding adds net charge.
questions.note: Charging by induction leaves the opposite sign of the inducing charge.
questions.x: The positive rod attracts electrons toward the sphere; grounding provides a path for electrons from the earth to flow onto it. Breaking the ground connection first traps those extra electrons, so removing the rod leaves the sphere net negative. Without grounding, the sphere would only polarize and remain neutral overall.

questions.q: A charge +q sits at x = 0 and a charge +4q sits at x = 3 m. At what position would a small test charge feel zero net electrostatic force?
o: The midpoint balances only equal charges.
x = 2 m
Places the point closer to the larger charge; it must be closer to the smaller one.
x = 1 m
Correct: q/x² = 4q/(3 − x)² gives 3 − x = 2x, so x = 1 m.
x = −1 m, left of +q
Outside the pair, both repulsive forces point the same way and cannot cancel.
questions.x: The null point for two like charges lies between them, closer to the smaller charge, where the two repulsive forces point in opposite directions. Setting kq/x² = k(4q)/(3 − x)² and taking square roots gives 3 − x = 2x, so x = 1 m. The midpoint only works for equal charges, and points outside the pair cannot balance because both forces point the same way there.

questions.q: Which property distinguishes the electrostatic force from the gravitational force?
o: It follows an inverse-square law
Both forces follow inverse-square laws.
It acts along the line joining the objects
Both are central forces along the connecting line.
It depends on a property of each object
Both depend on a product: q₁q₂ or m₁m₂.
It can be either attractive or repulsive
Correct: charge comes in two signs; mass has only one.
questions.x: Coulomb's law and Newton's law of gravitation share the same form: both are central, inverse-square forces proportional to a product of a property of each body. The key difference is that charge comes in two signs, so electric forces can attract or repel, while mass is only positive and gravity only attracts.

questions.q: Two identical metal spheres carry +6 μC and −2 μC. They are touched together and separated. What is the charge on each?
o: +4 μC
That is the total, not each sphere's share.
+3 μC
Ignores the −2 μC on the second sphere.
+2 μC
Correct: total +4 μC is shared equally between identical spheres.
+8 μC
Subtracts the charges with the wrong sign.
questions.note: Identical conductors in contact share total charge equally.
questions.x: Charge is conserved, and identical conductors in contact reach the same potential, so they split the total charge equally. The net charge is +6 + (−2) = +4 μC, giving +2 μC each. Picking +4 μC confuses the total with each sphere's share.

questions.q: The ratio of electric force to gravitational force between two protons is about 10³⁶. How does this ratio change if the protons are moved twice as far apart?
o: It decreases by a factor of 4
Both forces drop by 4, so the ratio does not change.
It increases by a factor of 4
Neither force weakens more slowly than the other.
It decreases by a factor of 2
Neither force goes as 1/r, and they share the same r-dependence.
It stays the same
Correct: both forces scale as 1/r², so their ratio is independent of distance.
questions.x: Coulomb's law (kq²/r²) and Newton's gravitation (Gm²/r²) both fall off as 1/r². Doubling r cuts each force by the same factor of 4, so their ratio is unchanged at any separation. The ratio depends only on the particles' charges and masses, which is why gravity is negligible at atomic scales.

questions.q: The direction of the electric field at a point is defined as the direction of the force on which object placed there?
o: A small negative test charge
A negative charge feels force opposite to E.
A small positive test charge
Correct: E = F/q with q positive by convention.
An electron moving along the field
An electron is negative; its force opposes E.
A neutral dipole at rest
A dipole in a uniform field feels torque, not a net force defining E.
questions.x: The electric field is defined as E = F/q₀ for a small positive test charge q₀, so E points the way a positive charge would be pushed. A negative charge, such as an electron, feels a force opposite to E. The test charge must be small so it does not disturb the source charges.

questions.q: What is the magnitude of the electric field 3 m from a +4 μC point charge? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²)
o: Divides by r instead of r².
Forgets to divide by r² at all.
Divides by r³ instead of r².
questions.x: The field of a point charge is E = kq/r². Here kq = (9 × 10⁹)(4 × 10⁻⁶) = 3.6 × 10⁴ N·m²/C, and dividing by r² = 9 m² gives 4000 N/C. Dividing by r alone (12,000 N/C) mixes up the field with the potential, which goes as kq/r.

questions.q: An electron is placed in a uniform electric field that points east. In which direction does the electron accelerate?
o: East
That is the direction a positive charge would accelerate.
North
Electric force is parallel or antiparallel to E, not perpendicular.
It does not accelerate
Any charge in a nonzero field feels a force qE.
West
Correct: negative charges feel a force opposite the field direction.
questions.x: The force on a charge in a field is F = qE, so its direction depends on the sign of q. An electron's negative charge makes the force, and thus the acceleration, point opposite E, toward the west. East would be correct only for a positive charge such as a proton.

questions.q: Two identical positive point charges are fixed a distance d apart. What is the electric field at the midpoint between them?
o: 8kq/d², toward either charge
That is the result for opposite charges, whose fields add.
Zero
Correct: equal fields point in opposite directions and cancel.
4kq/d², pointing away from the line
Fields from collinear charges lie along the line at the midpoint.
2kq/d², along the line
Fields from equal like charges cancel exactly here.
questions.x: Electric field is a vector. At the midpoint each positive charge produces a field of the same magnitude, kq/(d/2)², but each points away from its own source, so the two vectors are opposite and cancel. The potential there is not zero (it is 4kq/d); only E vanishes.

questions.q: Charges +q and −q are a distance d apart. What is the electric field at the midpoint?
o: Zero
Fields of opposite charges add at the midpoint; potential is zero there.
4kq/d², pointing toward +q
Fields point away from + and toward −, and both contributions add.
8kq/d², pointing toward −q
Correct: each gives kq/(d/2)² = 4kq/d², both pointing toward −q.
2kq/d², pointing toward −q
Uses d instead of d/2 for each distance.
questions.note: Trap: V = 0 at a dipole's midpoint, but E is not.
questions.x: At a dipole's midpoint the field from +q points away from +q, and the field from −q points toward −q: both point toward −q, so they add. Each has magnitude kq/(d/2)² = 4kq/d², giving 8kq/d². The trap is answering zero: the scalar potential cancels there, but the field vectors do not.

questions.q: On an electric field line diagram, what indicates a region of stronger field?
o: Lines that are longer
Line length carries no information about strength.
Lines that curve more sharply
Curvature shows direction change, not magnitude.
Lines that point to the right
Direction and magnitude are independent.
Lines drawn closer together
Correct: line density is proportional to field strength.
questions.x: Field-line diagrams encode magnitude by density: the number of lines crossing a unit area is proportional to field strength. Where lines crowd together the field is strong, and where they spread out it is weak. Line length, curvature and drawing direction convey nothing about magnitude.

questions.q: A proton and an electron are released from rest in the same uniform electric field. Which statement is true?
o: The proton feels a larger force because it is heavier
F = qE depends on charge, not mass.
The forces have equal magnitude, but the electron accelerates far more
Correct: |q| is equal, and a = qE/m is larger for the much lighter electron.
Both have the same acceleration in opposite directions
Equal forces on unequal masses give unequal accelerations.
The electron feels a larger force because it is smaller
Size does not enter F = qE; charges have equal magnitude.
questions.x: The force in a field is F = qE, and the proton and electron have charges of equal magnitude, so the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction. Acceleration is a = F/m, and the electron is about 1800 times lighter, so it accelerates about 1800 times more. Mass affects acceleration, not the electric force itself.

questions.q: A hollow metal box is placed in a strong external electric field. Once charges settle, what is the field inside the box's empty interior?
o: Equal to the external field
Conductors shield their interiors; the field does not pass through unchanged.
Twice the external field
Induced charges cancel the field inside rather than reinforce it.
Equal and opposite to the external field
The net interior field is zero, not reversed.
Zero
Correct: surface charges rearrange until they cancel the field inside a conductor.
questions.note: This is the Faraday cage effect.
questions.x: Free charges in a conductor shift in an external field until the field they create exactly cancels the external field inside the metal. For a closed conducting shell with no charge inside the cavity, the cavity field is also zero, which is why a Faraday cage shields its contents. The field is cancelled, not reversed or reflected.

questions.q: An oil drop of mass 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg hangs motionless in an upward electric field of 1 × 10⁵ N/C. What is its charge? (g = 10 m/s²)
o: −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (one extra electron)
A negative charge would be pushed down, opposite the upward field.
+3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (two electrons missing)
Doubles the weight; mg is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N.
+1.6 × 10⁻²⁰ C (one-tenth of e)
Power-of-ten slip; the result is exactly one elementary charge.
+1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (one electron missing)
Correct: qE = mg gives q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴/10⁵; upward force with upward E means positive.
questions.x: For the drop to hang still, the electric force must balance gravity: qE = mg. Here mg = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵)(10) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, so |q| = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 10⁵ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. The electric force must point up, the same direction as E, so the charge is positive (one electron missing).

questions.q: The newton per coulomb (N/C), the unit of electric field, is equivalent to which unit?
o: Volt per meter
Correct: V/m = (J/C)/m = (N·m/C)/m = N/C.
Volt per coulomb
V/C has units of 1/capacitance, not field.
Volt·meter
Field is potential divided by distance, not multiplied.
Joule per coulomb
J/C is the volt, the unit of potential.
questions.x: Field can be written either as force per charge (E = F/q) or as potential change per distance (E = ΔV/d), so the units must match. A volt is a J/C, and a joule is a N·m, so V/m = N·m/(C·m) = N/C. J/C alone is the volt, a unit of potential, not field.

questions.q: How much work does the electric field do on a charge moved along an equipotential surface?
o: Zero
Correct: W = −qΔV and ΔV = 0 along an equipotential.
qEd, positive
The field is perpendicular to the path, so it does no work.
It depends on the path length
Electric work depends only on endpoints' potentials.
Negative, equal to −qV
Work depends on the change in V, which is zero here.
questions.x: The work done by the electric field on a charge is W = −qΔV, which depends only on the potentials of the start and end points. Along an equipotential ΔV = 0, so no work is done, however long the path. Equivalently, E is perpendicular to an equipotential, so the force has no component along the motion.

questions.q: A proton starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 1000 V. What kinetic energy does it gain?
o: Correct: KE = qΔV = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(1000 V) = 1000 eV.
Uses 1 C instead of the proton charge.
That is 1 eV; it forgets the 1000 V.
Divides by e instead of multiplying.
questions.x: A charge accelerated through a potential difference gains kinetic energy equal to |q|ΔV. For a proton, (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(1000 V) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J, which is 1000 eV by definition of the electronvolt. Writing 1000 J treats the proton as carrying one coulomb rather than one elementary charge.

questions.q: What is the electric potential 0.3 m from a +3 nC point charge? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²)
o: Divides by r²; that gives field in N/C, not potential.
Forgets to divide by r.
Arithmetic slip: 27/0.3 is 90.
questions.note: Potential goes as 1/r; field goes as 1/r².
questions.x: Electric potential of a point charge is V = kq/r, a scalar that falls as 1/r. Here kq = (9 × 10⁹)(3 × 10⁻⁹) = 27 V·m, and dividing by 0.3 m gives 90 V. Dividing by r² instead gives 300, which is the field magnitude in N/C, not the potential.

questions.q: An electron is released from rest in an electric field. Which describes its motion?
o: It moves toward higher potential as its potential energy decreases
Correct: U = qV with q negative, so U falls as V rises.
It moves toward lower potential as its potential energy decreases
That describes a positive charge.
It moves toward higher potential as its potential energy increases
Free charges always move to lower potential energy.
It stays put because it has no initial velocity
The field exerts a force and accelerates it from rest.
questions.x: A charge released from rest moves so its potential energy U = qV decreases, converting it to kinetic energy. For a negative charge, U decreases when V increases, so an electron moves toward higher potential. Positive charges do the opposite, moving toward lower potential.

questions.q: How are equipotential surfaces oriented relative to electric field lines?
o: Parallel to them
Moving along E changes potential, so field lines cannot lie in an equipotential.
At 45° to them
There is no fixed 45° relation.
Orientation varies randomly
The perpendicular relation holds everywhere.
Perpendicular to them
Correct: no work is done moving along an equipotential, so E has no component along it.
questions.x: Moving along an equipotential changes nothing in V, so the field does no work, meaning E has no component along that surface. Therefore field lines always cross equipotentials at right angles and point toward lower potential. If they were parallel, moving along the surface would change V, a contradiction.

questions.q: Two parallel plates 2 mm apart are held at a potential difference of 10 V. What is the field between them?
o: 20 V/m
Multiplies V by d, and mm were not converted to m.
5 V/m
Uses 2 m rather than 0.002 m.
Multiplies instead of dividing.
Correct: E = V/d = 10 V/0.002 m.
questions.x: Between parallel plates the field is uniform, with magnitude E = ΔV/d. Converting 2 mm to 0.002 m gives E = 10/0.002 = 5000 V/m. Forgetting the unit conversion (using 2 m) gives 5 V/m, a factor of 1000 too small.

questions.q: Which is true at the midpoint between charges +Q and −Q?
o: E = 0 but V ≠ 0
That describes two equal like charges.
V = 0 but E ≠ 0
Correct: potentials kQ/r and −kQ/r cancel, but both fields point toward −Q.
Both V and E are zero
The fields add at this point; they do not cancel.
Both V and E are nonzero
The scalar potentials of equal and opposite charges cancel.
questions.x: Potential is a scalar: at the midpoint +Q contributes kQ/r and −Q contributes −kQ/r, which sum to zero. Field is a vector: both contributions point from +Q toward −Q, so they add and E is nonzero. The reverse case, E = 0 with V ≠ 0, describes the midpoint of two equal like charges.

questions.q: How much work must be done to bring a +2 μC charge from infinity to 0.1 m from a fixed +5 μC charge? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²)
o: 9 J
Divides by r²; energy goes as 1/r.
−0.9 J, since energy is released
Pushing like charges together requires positive external work.
Correct: W = kq₁q₂/r = (9 × 10⁹)(10 × 10⁻¹²)/0.1 = 0.9 J.
Forgets to divide kq₁q₂ by r.
questions.x: The external work to assemble two charges from infinity at constant speed equals their electric potential energy, U = kq₁q₂/r. Here (9 × 10⁹)(2 × 10⁻⁶)(5 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.09 J·m, and dividing by 0.1 m gives 0.9 J. The work is positive because like charges repel and must be pushed together.

questions.q: Two positive point charges are released from rest near each other. As they fly apart, what happens to the system's electric potential energy?
o: It decreases
Correct: like charges have U = kq₁q₂/r > 0, which falls as r grows.
It increases
Energy converts to kinetic energy; U goes down.
It stays constant
Their kinetic energy grows, so U must change.
It first increases and then decreases
For like charges U falls steadily with distance.
questions.x: For two like charges U = kq₁q₂/r is positive and shrinks as r grows. As the charges fly apart, the electric force does positive work, converting potential energy into kinetic energy, so U steadily decreases. Total energy is conserved, which rules out U staying constant while the charges speed up.

questions.q: A −3 μC charge moves from point A (V = +20 V) to point B (V = −10 V). What is the change in its electric potential energy?
o: It increases by 9 × 10⁻⁵ J
It decreases by 9 × 10⁻⁵ J
Drops the negative sign of the charge.
It increases by 3 × 10⁻⁵ J
Uses ΔV = 10 V instead of 30 V.
It decreases by 3 × 10⁻⁵ J
Wrong sign and wrong ΔV.
questions.note: Negative charges gain energy moving to lower potential.
questions.x: The change in potential energy is ΔU = qΔV, where ΔV = V_B − V_A = −10 − 20 = −30 V. With q = −3 × 10⁻⁶ C, ΔU = (−3 × 10⁻⁶)(−30) = +9 × 10⁻⁵ J. A negative charge gains potential energy moving to lower potential; dropping the sign of q gives the tempting 'decreases' answer.

questions.q: One volt is equivalent to which combination of units?
o: Coulomb per joule
Inverted relationship.
Joule per coulomb
Correct: potential is energy per unit charge.
Newton per coulomb
N/C is the unit of electric field.
Coulomb per second
C/s is the ampere.
questions.x: Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge, V = U/q, so one volt is one joule per coulomb. This is why a charge q moved through ΔV changes its energy by qΔV. N/C is a unit of field and C/s is the ampere, so neither describes potential.

questions.q: A student maps equipotential lines spaced 1 V apart. In region X adjacent lines are 0.5 cm apart; in region Y they are 2 cm apart. How do the field strengths compare?
o: The field in Y is 4 times that in X
Wider spacing means a weaker field.
They are equal because the lines are 1 V apart in both
Equal ΔV over different distances gives different E.
The field in X is 4 times that in Y
Correct: E = ΔV/d gives 200 V/m in X and 50 V/m in Y.
The field in X is 2 times that in Y
The spacing ratio is 4, not 2.
questions.x: Field strength equals how fast potential changes with distance, E = ΔV/Δx, so closely spaced equipotentials mean a strong field. In X, 1 V over 0.005 m gives 200 V/m; in Y, 1 V over 0.02 m gives 50 V/m, a ratio of 4. Equal voltage steps do not mean equal fields when the spacing differs.

questions.q: A charged particle is at rest in a uniform magnetic field. What magnetic force acts on it?
o: qB, along the field
Magnetic force needs motion; qB is not even a force.
qB, perpendicular to the field
No velocity, no magnetic force.
A force that grows with time
With v = 0 the force stays zero.
None
Correct: F = qvB sin θ is zero when v = 0.
questions.x: The magnetic force on a charge is F = qvB sin θ, so it requires the charge to be moving. A charge at rest has v = 0 and feels no magnetic force at all, no matter how strong B is. Only an electric field can push a stationary charge.

questions.q: A proton moves at 2 × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a 0.5 T magnetic field. What is the magnetic force on it?
o: Divides by B instead of multiplying.
Omits the factor of 0.5 for the field strength.
0 N
Force is zero only when v is parallel to B.
questions.x: For a charge moving perpendicular to B, sin θ = 1 and F = qvB. Here (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(2 × 10⁶)(0.5) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N. Omitting the 0.5 T factor gives 3.2 × 10⁻¹³ N, and zero would apply only to motion parallel to the field.

questions.q: An electron moves parallel to a uniform magnetic field. What is its path?
o: A circle perpendicular to the field
Circular motion requires a velocity component perpendicular to B.
A helix around the field lines
A helix needs both parallel and perpendicular velocity components.
A straight line with increasing speed
Magnetic forces never change speed, and here there is no force.
A straight line at constant speed
Correct: sin 0° = 0, so no magnetic force acts.
questions.x: The magnetic force is F = qvB sin θ, and for motion parallel to B, θ = 0 so sin θ = 0. With no force, the electron simply continues in a straight line at constant velocity. Circles need a perpendicular velocity component, and a helix needs both parallel and perpendicular components.

questions.q: A particle moves in the +x direction through a magnetic field pointing in the +y direction. If the particle is an electron, in which direction is the magnetic force?
o: Positive z direction
That is the force on a positive charge.
Positive y direction
Magnetic force is perpendicular to B, never along it.
Negative x direction
Magnetic force is perpendicular to velocity.
Negative z direction
Correct: v × B = x̂ × ŷ = +z for a positive charge; the electron's negative charge reverses it.
questions.note: Flip the right-hand-rule result for negative charges.
questions.x: The force on a moving charge is F = qv × B. For a positive charge, x̂ × ŷ = +ẑ, so the force would point in +z. An electron's negative charge reverses this, giving −z. The force is always perpendicular to both v and B, which rules out the x and y choices.

questions.q: A charged particle moves through a region containing only a uniform magnetic field. Which quantity stays constant?
o: Its velocity
Direction changes as the particle curves.
Its speed
Correct: the magnetic force is always perpendicular to v, so it does no work.
Its momentum vector
Momentum direction changes with velocity direction.
Its acceleration vector
The centripetal acceleration keeps changing direction.
questions.note: Magnetic forces do no work.
questions.x: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does zero work and cannot change kinetic energy; the speed stays constant. It does continually change the direction of motion, so velocity, momentum and the centripetal acceleration vector all change. Speed is a scalar; velocity is a vector.

questions.q: A charged particle circles in a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is doubled, what happens to the radius of its path?
o: It is halved
Inverts the relationship between r and v.
It quadruples
Squares v; r is linear in v.
It doubles
Correct: qvB = mv²/r gives r = mv/(qB), proportional to v.
It stays the same
The period stays the same; the radius does not.
questions.x: In a uniform field the magnetic force supplies the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r, so r = mv/(qB). The radius is directly proportional to speed, so doubling v doubles r. The period, T = 2πm/(qB), is independent of speed, which is the source of the 'stays the same' trap.

questions.q: In a mass spectrometer, two ions with equal charge and equal speed enter the same magnetic field. Ion 2 has twice the mass of ion 1. Compared with ion 1, ion 2's path radius is:
o: Twice as large
Correct: r = mv/(qB) is proportional to m at fixed q, v and B.
Half as large
Heavier ions are harder to deflect, so they curve less.
Four times as large
r scales linearly with m, not with m².
The same
Mass does affect the radius.
questions.x: Setting the magnetic force equal to the centripetal force gives r = mv/(qB). With equal q, v and B, the radius is directly proportional to mass, so doubling m doubles r. Heavier ions have more momentum and curve less sharply, which is how a mass spectrometer separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio.

questions.q: The magnetic field at 2 cm from a long straight current-carrying wire is B. What is the field at 4 cm?
o: Treats the wire's field as inverse-square.
Correct: B = μ₀I/(2πr) falls as 1/r.
2B
The field weakens with distance.
B
The field depends on distance from the wire.
questions.x: The magnetic field of a long straight wire is B = μ₀I/(2πr), which falls off as 1/r, not 1/r². Doubling the distance from 2 cm to 4 cm therefore halves the field. The inverse-square trap (B/4) applies to point charges and point sources, not an infinite line of current.

questions.q: What shape do the magnetic field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire take?
o: Straight lines parallel to the wire
Field lines wrap around the current; they do not run along it.
Concentric circles around the wire
Correct: the right-hand rule gives circular loops centered on the wire.
Straight lines radiating outward
That describes the electric field of a line of charge.
A uniform field along the wire's length
The field circles the wire and weakens with distance.
questions.x: Magnetic field lines around a straight current form closed concentric circles centered on the wire. The right-hand rule gives the direction: thumb along the current, fingers curl in the direction of B. Radial lines describe the electric field of a charged line, not the magnetic field of a current.

questions.q: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. How do the wires interact?
o: They attract
Correct: each wire's field exerts an ILB force on the other directed toward it.
They repel
Antiparallel currents repel; parallel currents attract.
No force acts because the wires are neutral
Magnetic forces act on moving charges even in neutral wires.
They twist to become perpendicular
Parallel wires experience forces along the line between them.
questions.note: Like currents attract, the opposite of like charges.
questions.x: Each wire sits in the circular magnetic field of the other, and the force on a current is F = IL × B. For parallel currents, the right-hand rule gives a force on each wire directed toward the other, so they attract; antiparallel currents repel. This is the reverse of electrostatics, where like charges repel.

questions.q: A straight 2 m wire carrying 3 A lies perpendicular to a 0.2 T magnetic field. What is the magnetic force on it?
o: Correct: F = ILB = (3)(2)(0.2).
Divides by L instead of multiplying.
6 N
Forgets to multiply by B = 0.2 T.
0 N
Force vanishes only when the wire is parallel to B.
questions.x: The force on a straight current-carrying wire is F = ILB sin θ, with θ the angle between the wire and the field. Perpendicular means sin θ = 1, so F = (3 A)(2 m)(0.2 T) = 1.2 N. The force would be zero only if the wire were parallel to B.

questions.q: Perpendicular electric (2000 V/m) and magnetic (0.1 T) fields are arranged so their forces on a moving charge oppose. What speed lets a charge pass undeflected?
o: Multiplies E by B instead of dividing.
Inverts the ratio; v = E/B, not B/E.
It depends on the particle's charge
q cancels in qE = qvB, so every charge with that speed passes.
Correct: qE = qvB gives v = E/B = 2000/0.1.
questions.note: Velocity selector: v = E/B.
questions.x: In a velocity selector the electric force qE and magnetic force qvB point opposite each other. A particle goes straight when they balance: qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 2000/0.1 = 2 × 10⁴ m/s. The charge cancels, so the selected speed is the same for any charge or mass.

questions.q: The tesla, the SI unit of magnetic field, is equivalent to which unit?
o: N/(A·m)
Correct: from F = ILB, B = F/(IL).
N·m/A
From F = ILB, both current and length go in the denominator.
N/C
