That is the unit of electric field.
V·s
V·s is the weber, a unit of flux; the tesla is Wb/m².
questions.x: The force on a current-carrying wire is F = ILB, so B = F/(IL), giving the tesla as N/(A·m). The weber (V·s) measures magnetic flux, which is field times area, so a tesla is a Wb/m², not a V·s. N/C is the unit of electric field.

questions.q: Conventional current in a metal wire flows in which direction?
o: The same direction as the electrons
Electrons are negative, so they drift opposite to conventional current.
From the negative to the positive terminal outside the battery
Outside a source, conventional current runs from + to −.
Perpendicular to the wire
Current flows along the conductor.
Opposite to the motion of electrons
Correct: it is defined as the direction positive charge would move.
questions.x: Conventional current is defined as the direction positive charge would flow, from high to low potential, which is from + to − through an external circuit. In metal wires the actual carriers are electrons, which are negative and drift the opposite way. The definition predates the discovery of the electron.

questions.q: A wire carries a steady 3 A current for 1 minute. How much charge passes any point in the wire?
o: Correct: Q = It = 3 A × 60 s.
3 C
Uses 1 s instead of 60 s.
Divides time by current instead of multiplying.
Divides current by time.
questions.x: Current is the rate of charge flow, I = Q/t, so Q = It. Converting 1 minute to 60 s gives Q = (3 A)(60 s) = 180 C. Using t = 1 without converting units gives the 3 C trap.

questions.q: A metal wire is stretched uniformly to twice its original length while its volume stays constant. By what factor does its resistance change?
o: Accounts for length but ignores the thinner cross-section.
Same volume does not mean same resistance.
A longer, thinner wire has more resistance, not less.
Correct: L doubles and A halves, so R = ρL/A rises 4×.
questions.x: Resistance is R = ρL/A. Stretching to twice the length at constant volume (V = LA) forces the cross-sectional area to halve. Both effects raise R: doubling L gives 2×, halving A gives another 2×, for a total of 4×. Answering 2 accounts only for length and forgets that the wire also gets thinner.

questions.q: Wire B has the same length and material as wire A but twice the diameter. How does R_B compare with R_A?
o: R_B = R_A/4
Correct: area goes as diameter², so A rises 4× and R falls 4×.
R_B = R_A/2
Treats area as proportional to diameter, not diameter².
R_B = 2R_A
Larger area lowers resistance.
R_B = 4R_A
Inverts the dependence on area.
questions.x: Resistance is R = ρL/A, and the cross-sectional area of a wire is πd²/4, so area scales with diameter squared. Doubling d makes A four times larger, which cuts R to one quarter. Answering R/2 treats area as proportional to diameter rather than its square.

questions.q: Which change would alter the resistivity (ρ) of a copper wire?
o: Raising its temperature
Correct: resistivity is a material property that depends on temperature.
Doubling its length
Length changes resistance, not resistivity.
Halving its cross-sectional area
Area changes resistance, not resistivity.
Doubling the applied voltage
An ohmic material's ρ does not depend on voltage.
questions.note: Trap: R depends on shape; ρ does not.
questions.x: Resistivity ρ is an intrinsic property of a material at a given temperature; it does not depend on the object's shape. Length and area change the resistance R = ρL/A, but not ρ itself. In metals, raising temperature increases lattice vibrations and electron scattering, which raises ρ.

questions.q: As a metal wire is heated, how does its resistance change?
o: It decreases, because electrons move faster
Faster random motion does not raise drift; more scattering raises R.
It stays the same, because resistance depends only on shape
Resistivity depends on temperature.
It increases, because lattice vibrations scatter electrons more
Correct: hotter ions vibrate more and impede electron drift.
It drops to zero above a critical temperature
Superconductivity occurs below a critical temperature, not above.
questions.x: In a metal, current is carried by electrons drifting through a lattice of ions. Heating increases ion vibrations, which scatter electrons more often and impede their drift, so resistivity and resistance rise with temperature. Faster random thermal motion does not increase the net drift that carries current.

questions.q: A material has resistivity 2 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m. What is its conductivity?
o: Flips the exponent's sign but does not invert the coefficient.
Inverts the coefficient but keeps the negative exponent.
Correct: σ = 1/ρ = 1/(2 × 10⁻⁸).
2 × 10⁻⁸ S/m, the same value as ρ
Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity, not equal to it.
questions.x: Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity, σ = 1/ρ. Inverting 2 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m means inverting both the coefficient and the power of ten: (1/2) × 10⁸ = 0.5 × 10⁸ = 5 × 10⁷ S/m. Inverting only the exponent or only the coefficient is a common slip.

questions.q: Which 0.1 M aqueous solution conducts electricity best?
o: NaCl
Gives only 2 ions per formula unit.
Acetic acid
A weak acid; only a small fraction ionizes.
CaCl₂
Correct: it dissociates into 3 ions per formula unit, the most charge carriers here.
Glucose
A nonelectrolyte; it forms no ions.
questions.note: Solution conductivity tracks the concentration of mobile ions.
questions.x: Solution conductivity depends on the concentration and charge of mobile ions. At equal molarity, CaCl₂ fully dissociates into three ions (Ca²⁺ and 2 Cl⁻), carrying more total charge than NaCl's two ions. Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte that barely ionizes, and glucose produces no ions at all.

questions.q: For an ohmic resistor, what does a graph of voltage (y-axis) versus current (x-axis) look like?
o: A straight line with slope 1/R
That would be I versus V.
An upward-curving parabola
That shape fits power versus current, P = I²R.
A straight line through the origin with slope R
Correct: V = IR is linear with slope equal to resistance.
A horizontal line
That would mean voltage is independent of current.
questions.x: Ohm's law, V = IR, is a linear relation with zero intercept, so plotting V against I gives a straight line through the origin whose slope is R. Plotting I against V would instead give slope 1/R. A curved V–I graph signals a non-ohmic device, such as a diode or a filament whose resistance changes as it heats.

questions.q: Wires A and B are made of the same metal and carry the same current, but B has half the cross-sectional area of A. How does the electron drift speed in B compare with A?
o: Half as fast
Inverts the relationship; a narrower wire needs faster drift.
Twice as fast
Correct: I = nqAv_d, so halving A at fixed I and n doubles v_d.
Four times as fast
v_d is inversely proportional to A, not to A².
The same
Same current through a smaller area requires a higher drift speed.
questions.x: Current relates to carrier motion by I = nqAv_d, where n is the carrier density and v_d the drift speed. With the same metal (same n) and same current, v_d is inversely proportional to A, so halving the area doubles the drift speed. The same charge per second must squeeze through a smaller cross-section.

questions.q: Resistors of 2 Ω, 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in series. What is the equivalent resistance?
o: That is the parallel combination.
4 Ω
That is the average, not the sum.
Correct: series resistances add directly.
Multiplies the resistances instead of adding them.
questions.x: In series, the same current flows through every resistor and their voltage drops add, so the resistances simply add: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 Ω. A series combination is always larger than the largest individual resistor. The 1.1 Ω value comes from using the parallel formula.

questions.q: Three 6 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
o: That is the series total.
2 Ω
Correct: n identical resistors in parallel give R/n = 6/3.
6 Ω
Adding parallel paths lowers the resistance.
That is 1/R_eq, not R_eq.
questions.x: Parallel resistors combine by 1/R_eq = Σ 1/R. For three identical 6 Ω resistors, 1/R_eq = 3/6, so R_eq = 2 Ω. Adding parallel paths always lowers the total, so the result must be smaller than 6 Ω; 0.5 Ω is the trap of forgetting to take the final reciprocal.

questions.q: A 12 V battery drives current through a 2 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor in series. What is the voltage across the 4 Ω resistor?
o: 8 V
Correct: I = 12/6 = 2 A, and V = IR = 2 × 4 = 8 V.
Each series element gets only part of the total voltage.
4 V
That is the voltage across the 2 Ω resistor.
6 V
Splits the voltage equally, ignoring the unequal resistances.
questions.note: Series voltage divides in proportion to resistance.
questions.x: In series, the same current passes through each resistor: I = 12 V / (2 + 4) Ω = 2 A. The drop across the 4 Ω resistor is IR = 8 V, and across the 2 Ω resistor it is 4 V, which add to 12 V. Voltage divides in proportion to resistance, not equally.

questions.q: A 12 V battery is connected across a 3 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor wired in parallel. What total current does the battery supply?
o: 6 A
Treats the resistors as in series (12/9).
4 A
That is the current in the 3 Ω branch only.
2 A
That is the current in the 6 Ω branch only.
questions.x: Each parallel branch sees the full battery voltage, so branch currents are found separately: 12/3 = 4 A and 12/6 = 2 A. The battery supplies their sum, 6 A, consistent with R_eq = 2 Ω. Treating the resistors as series (12/9) is the main trap.

questions.q: A 24 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 12 Ω resistors. What is the current through the 12 Ω resistor?
o: 3 A
That is the total current, which splits between the branches.
2 A
That is the current through the 6 Ω branch.
Splits the 3 A equally; parallel branches share voltage, not current.
1 A
Correct: the pair is 4 Ω, total 8 Ω, I = 3 A; the pair has 12 V, so 12/12 = 1 A.
questions.x: First reduce the parallel pair: 6 × 12/(6 + 12) = 4 Ω, so the total is 8 Ω and the battery supplies 24/8 = 3 A. The 4 Ω series resistor drops 12 V, leaving 12 V across the pair, so the 12 Ω branch carries 12/12 = 1 A and the 6 Ω branch 2 A. Current splits inversely to resistance, not equally.

questions.q: A resistor is added in parallel to an existing resistor connected across an ideal battery. What happens?
o: Equivalent resistance rises and battery current falls
That is what adding a resistor in series does.
Current through the original resistor falls
Its voltage is still the battery's voltage, so its current is unchanged.
Battery voltage is split between the two resistors
Parallel elements each get the full voltage.
Equivalent resistance falls and battery current rises
Correct: a new path lowers R_eq, so I = V/R_eq increases.
questions.x: Adding a parallel branch gives current another path, lowering R_eq, so the ideal battery supplies more total current, I = V/R_eq. The original resistor still has the full battery voltage across it, so its own current is unchanged. Rising resistance and falling current describe adding a resistor in series.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule, which states that current into a node equals current out, follows from conservation of what?
o: Charge
Correct: charge cannot pile up or vanish at a junction.
Energy
Energy conservation underlies the loop rule.
Momentum
Momentum does not govern circuit junctions.
Power
Power is not a conserved quantity in this sense.
questions.x: Charge is conserved and cannot accumulate at a junction in a steady circuit, so the charge flowing in per second must equal the charge flowing out. That gives the junction rule, ΣI_in = ΣI_out. The loop rule, by contrast, comes from energy conservation.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's loop rule says the voltage changes around any closed loop sum to zero. This follows from conservation of what?
o: Charge
Charge conservation gives the junction rule.
Energy
Correct: a charge returning to its starting point has no net change in potential energy.
Current
Current is not conserved around a loop with branches.
Mass
Mass is not involved in voltage changes.
questions.x: Electric potential is a single-valued function of position, so a charge that travels around a closed loop returns to the same potential and has no net change in potential energy. Thus the emf gains and IR drops around any loop must sum to zero, an expression of energy conservation. Charge conservation instead gives the junction rule.

questions.q: How should an ammeter be connected to measure the current through a resistor, and what is its ideal resistance?
o: In parallel, with infinite resistance
That describes a voltmeter.
In series, with zero resistance
Correct: it must carry the same current without changing it.
In series, with infinite resistance
Infinite resistance in series would stop the current.
In parallel, with zero resistance
This would short-circuit the resistor.
questions.x: An ammeter must carry the exact current it measures, so it is placed in series with the resistor. To avoid changing that current, its ideal resistance is zero. Placing an ammeter in parallel, especially a low-resistance one, would short the resistor and divert most of the current.

questions.q: How should a voltmeter be connected to measure the voltage across a resistor, and what is its ideal resistance?
o: In series, with zero resistance
That describes an ammeter.
In parallel, with zero resistance
This would short out the resistor.
In parallel, with infinite resistance
Correct: it reads the potential difference while drawing no current.
In series, with infinite resistance
This would block current in the branch.
questions.x: A voltmeter measures a potential difference between two points, so it is connected in parallel across the resistor. Its ideal resistance is infinite so it draws no current and does not disturb the circuit. A zero-resistance meter in parallel would short the resistor.

questions.q: A battery with an emf of 9 V and an internal resistance of 1 Ω is connected to a 2 Ω external resistor. What is the terminal voltage?
o: 9 V
Terminal voltage equals emf only when no current flows.
6 V
3 V
That is the drop across the internal resistance.
Uses I = 9/2 and ignores the internal resistance in the current.
questions.note: V_terminal = emf − Ir.
questions.x: A real battery has internal resistance r, so the current is I = emf/(R + r) = 9/3 = 3 A. Part of the emf is lost inside the battery, Ir = 3 V, so the terminal voltage is 9 − 3 = 6 V, which is also IR across the 2 Ω load. The terminal voltage equals the emf only when no current flows.

questions.q: Why are household outlets and lights wired in parallel rather than in series?
o: Parallel wiring gives a higher total resistance
Parallel wiring lowers total resistance.
Each device gets the same current
Same current is a feature of series circuits.
Each device gets the full voltage and runs independently
Correct: parallel branches share voltage, so one device off does not affect others.
One device failing turns off all the others
That happens in series circuits.
questions.x: In a parallel circuit every branch connects across the same two lines, so each device receives the full supply voltage. Branches operate independently: switching one off or having one fail does not break the path for the others. In series, devices would share the voltage and one break would shut off everything.

questions.q: A 10 Ω resistor and an unknown resistor R are in parallel across a 20 V source. The source supplies 3 A in total. What is R?
o: That is the equivalent resistance of the pair, 20/3.
Equal resistors would draw 4 A in total.
Multiplies the 20 V by the 3 A total instead of dividing.
Correct: the 10 Ω branch takes 2 A, leaving 1 A; R = 20/1.
questions.x: Parallel branches share the 20 V, so the 10 Ω branch draws 20/10 = 2 A. Total current is the sum of branch currents, leaving 3 − 2 = 1 A for R, so R = 20 V / 1 A = 20 Ω. The value 20/3 ≈ 6.7 Ω is the equivalent resistance of the pair, not the unknown resistor.

questions.q: Which quantity is the same for every resistor connected in parallel?
o: Voltage
Correct: all parallel branches connect across the same two nodes.
Current
Current is the same through series resistors.
Power
Power differs unless the resistances are equal.
Resistance
Parallel resistors can have any resistances.
questions.x: Parallel resistors are each connected between the same two nodes, so the potential difference across every one is identical. Current divides among the branches inversely with resistance, so currents and powers differ unless the resistances are equal. Equal current is the defining feature of series connection.

questions.q: A 2 A current flows through a 5 Ω resistor. How much power does the resistor dissipate?
o: Uses P = IR, which gives voltage, not power.
Correct: P = I²R = 4 × 5.
Divides R by I.
Squares R instead of I.
questions.x: Power dissipated in a resistor is P = IV, and substituting V = IR gives P = I²R. Here P = (2 A)²(5 Ω) = 20 W. The product IR = 10 is the voltage in volts, not the power, which is the most tempting slip.

questions.q: A space heater on a 120 V line draws 10 A. How much energy does it use in 1 minute?
o: 1.2 kJ
That is the energy per second.
Uses V/I = 12 as the power; that is the resistance in ohms.
4.3 MJ
Uses 1 hour (3600 s) instead of 1 minute.
72 kJ
Correct: P = IV = 1200 W; E = 1200 × 60 s.
questions.x: Electrical power is P = IV = (10 A)(120 V) = 1200 W, meaning 1200 J each second. Energy is power times time: 1200 W × 60 s = 72,000 J = 72 kJ. Forgetting to multiply by 60 s gives 1.2 kJ, and using an hour instead of a minute gives about 4.3 MJ.

questions.q: The voltage across a fixed resistor is doubled. By what factor does the power dissipated change?
o: Correct: P = V²/R, so doubling V quadruples P.
Ignores that current also doubles.
Power rises with voltage.
Power depends on voltage for a fixed resistor.
questions.x: For a fixed resistor P = V²/R, because doubling V also doubles the current (I = V/R), and P = IV. Both factors double, so power rises by 2 × 2 = 4. Answering 2 treats the current as unchanged.

questions.q: A 2 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor are wired in parallel across a battery. How does the power dissipated by the 2 Ω resistor compare with the 8 Ω resistor?
o: One-fourth as much
That is the series result, where P = I²R.
The same
Equal voltage does not mean equal power when R differs.
Twice as much
The ratio of resistances is 4, so P differs by 4.
4 times as much
Correct: same V in parallel, and P = V²/R is larger for the smaller R.
questions.note: Parallel: smaller R gets more power. Series: larger R gets more power.
questions.x: Parallel resistors share the same voltage, so the useful power formula is P = V²/R, which is inversely proportional to R. The 2 Ω resistor dissipates 8/2 = 4 times as much power as the 8 Ω resistor. In series the opposite holds: same current, P = I²R, so the larger resistor gets more power.

questions.q: A 100 W bulb runs for 10 hours. How much electrical energy does it use?
o: Uses hours as if they were seconds.
Omits a factor of 10.
3.6 MJ
Correct: 1000 W·h = 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s.
Divides watts by hours.
questions.x: Energy equals power times time. Converting hours to seconds: 10 h = 36,000 s, so E = 100 W × 36,000 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Equivalently, 100 W × 10 h = 1 kWh, and 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ. Treating hours as seconds gives only 1000 J.

questions.q: A power line delivers the same power to a town, but the transmission voltage is doubled. How does the power lost as heat in the line change?
o: It halves
Loss depends on I², not I.
It quadruples
Uses V²/R with the full line voltage, which is not the drop across the line.
It falls to one-fourth
Correct: I halves at fixed P = IV, and loss I²R falls 4×.
It does not change
Lower current reduces resistive loss.
questions.note: High-voltage transmission cuts current and I²R losses.
questions.x: To deliver a fixed power P = IV, doubling the transmission voltage halves the current. Heat lost in the line is I²R_line, so halving I cuts the loss to one quarter. Using V²/R with the transmission voltage is the trap; the voltage drop across the line itself is IR_line, which also falls.

questions.q: A 50 Ω resistor is rated for a maximum of 0.5 W. What is the largest current it can safely carry?
o: Forgets to take the square root.
Inverts P/R before the square root.
Correct: I = √(P/R) = √(0.01).
Multiplies P by R.
questions.x: Power in a resistor is P = I²R, so the maximum safe current is I = √(P/R). Here P/R = 0.5/50 = 0.01 A², giving I = 0.1 A. Stopping at 0.01 forgets the square root.

questions.q: Two bulbs are rated 60 W and 100 W for use at 120 V. Which bulb has the larger resistance?
o: The 100 W bulb
At fixed V, more power means lower resistance.
They have equal resistance
Same voltage with different power means different R.
The 60 W bulb
Correct: R = V²/P, so lower power at the same voltage means higher R.
It cannot be determined without the current
R = V²/P needs only the rated values.
questions.x: At a fixed rated voltage, P = V²/R, so R = V²/P and resistance is inversely proportional to power. The 60 W bulb has R = 14,400/60 = 240 Ω, while the 100 W bulb has 144 Ω. A brighter bulb at the same voltage draws more current because its resistance is lower.

questions.q: A 4 μF capacitor is charged to 10 V. How much charge is on each plate?
o: 0.4 μC
Divides C by V.
40 μC
Correct: Q = CV = 4 μF × 10 V.
2.5 μC
Divides V by C.
200 μC
Uses ½CV² or another squared form.
questions.x: Capacitance is the charge stored per volt, C = Q/V, so Q = CV. A 4 μF capacitor at 10 V holds 40 μC on each plate: +40 μC on one and −40 μC on the other. Dividing C by V or V by C reverses this defining relation.

questions.q: A 2 μF capacitor is charged to 100 V. How much energy does it store?
o: Correct: U = ½CV² = ½(2 × 10⁻⁶)(10⁴).
Omits the factor of ½.
Uses ½CV instead of ½CV².
Ignores the micro prefix.
questions.x: Energy stored in a capacitor is U = ½CV², from the average voltage (V/2) times the charge moved (Q = CV). Here ½(2 × 10⁻⁶ F)(100 V)² = ½(2 × 10⁻⁶)(10⁴) = 0.01 J. Omitting the ½ doubles the answer to 0.02 J.

questions.q: The plate separation of a parallel-plate capacitor is doubled. What happens to its capacitance?
o: It doubles
Capacitance falls with separation.
It quarters
C goes as 1/d, not 1/d².
It stays the same
Capacitance depends on geometry.
It halves
Correct: C = ε₀A/d is inversely proportional to d.
questions.x: For a parallel-plate capacitor, C = ε₀A/d, so capacitance is inversely proportional to plate separation. Doubling d halves C, because the same charge now produces a larger potential difference across the wider gap. The dependence is 1/d, not 1/d², which rules out quartering.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor stays connected to a battery while its plates are pulled to twice their separation. What happens to the stored charge?
o: It halves
Correct: V is fixed by the battery and C halves, so Q = CV halves.
It stays the same
Charge is fixed only if the capacitor is isolated.
It doubles
Increasing d decreases C, so Q falls.
It quarters
C goes as 1/d, so Q falls by 2, not 4.
questions.note: Connected to a battery: V constant. Isolated: Q constant.
questions.x: While a capacitor stays connected to a battery, its voltage is fixed by the battery. Doubling the plate separation halves C = ε₀A/d, so Q = CV must also halve, with charge flowing back into the battery. Charge stays constant only if the capacitor is isolated from the battery.

questions.q: A charged parallel-plate capacitor is disconnected from its battery, and then its plate separation is doubled. What happens to the stored energy?
o: It halves
That would be true at constant voltage, not constant charge.
It stays the same
Work is done pulling the attracting plates apart, so U rises.
It doubles
Correct: Q is fixed, C halves, so U = Q²/(2C) doubles.
It quadruples
U goes as 1/C, and C only halves.
questions.x: Disconnected from the battery, the capacitor's charge Q stays fixed. Doubling d halves C, and with U = Q²/(2C), the energy doubles. The extra energy comes from the work done pulling the oppositely charged plates apart against their attraction; 'halves' would apply at constant voltage instead.

questions.q: A 3 μF capacitor and a 6 μF capacitor are connected in series. What is the equivalent capacitance?
o: 9 μF
That is the parallel combination.
4.5 μF
That is the average.
18 μF
Multiplies the capacitances without dividing by their sum.
2 μF
questions.note: Capacitors combine opposite to resistors.
questions.x: Capacitors in series carry the same charge and their voltages add, so 1/C_eq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂. Here 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2, so C_eq = 2 μF, which is smaller than either capacitor. Capacitors combine in the opposite way to resistors, so adding them directly (9 μF) gives the parallel result.

questions.q: A 3 μF capacitor and a 6 μF capacitor are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent capacitance?
o: 9 μF
Correct: parallel capacitances add directly.
2 μF
That is the series combination.
3 μF
Parallel combination exceeds either capacitance.
0.5 μF
Takes a reciprocal sum unnecessarily.
questions.x: Capacitors in parallel share the same voltage, and their charges add, so the equivalent capacitance is the sum: 3 + 6 = 9 μF. Effectively, parallel connection adds plate area. The reciprocal formula, giving 2 μF, applies to capacitors in series.

questions.q: A dielectric of constant κ is slid between the plates of a charged capacitor that has been disconnected from its battery. What happens to the stored energy?
o: It increases by a factor of κ
That occurs if the battery stays connected (V fixed).
It stays the same
C changes while Q is fixed, so U changes.
It increases by a factor of κ squared
U depends on 1/C, which changes only by κ.
It decreases by a factor of κ
Correct: Q is fixed and C rises κ-fold, so U = Q²/(2C) falls by κ.
questions.x: An isolated capacitor keeps a fixed charge Q. Inserting a dielectric multiplies C by κ, and since U = Q²/(2C), the stored energy falls by a factor of κ. The field does work pulling the dielectric in, which accounts for the lost energy. With a battery connected (V fixed), U = ½CV² would rise by κ instead.

questions.q: A capacitor remains connected to a battery while a dielectric of constant κ = 3 is inserted. What happens to the charge on its plates?
o: It drops to one-third
That is what happens to V for an isolated capacitor.
It triples
Correct: C triples while the battery holds V fixed, so Q = CV triples.
It stays the same
Charge is fixed only if the capacitor is isolated.
It increases ninefold
Q scales with C, which rises by κ, not κ².
questions.x: A dielectric multiplies capacitance by κ, so C triples. With the battery still connected, V is fixed, so Q = CV also triples as the battery pushes additional charge onto the plates. If the capacitor were isolated, Q would stay fixed and V would drop to one-third instead.

questions.q: A capacitor is charged through a resistor by closing a switch. When is the current in the circuit largest?
o: When the capacitor is fully charged
A full capacitor opposes the emf and current stops.
Immediately after the switch is closed
Correct: an uncharged capacitor has no voltage, so the full emf drives current.
After one time constant
Current has already fallen to about 37% of its initial value.
The current is constant throughout
Current decays exponentially during RC charging.
questions.x: In an RC charging circuit, the current is I = (emf − V_C)/R. At the instant the switch closes, the capacitor is uncharged (V_C = 0), so the full emf drives the maximum current, emf/R. As the capacitor charges, V_C rises and the current decays exponentially toward zero.

questions.q: A 2 kΩ resistor is connected in series with a 5 μF capacitor. What is the RC time constant?
o: Ignores the kilo and micro prefixes.
10 ms
Correct: τ = RC = (2 × 10³)(5 × 10⁻⁶) = 10⁻² s.
100 ms
Prefix slip: kΩ × μF gives milliseconds, and 2 × 5 = 10, not 100.
Drops the kilo prefix: 2 Ω × 5 μF = 10⁻⁵ s.
questions.x: The RC time constant is τ = RC, the time for a charging capacitor to reach about 63% of its final charge. With R = 2 × 10³ Ω and C = 5 × 10⁻⁶ F, τ = 10 × 10⁻³ s = 10 ms. A handy shortcut: kΩ × μF gives milliseconds, so ignoring the prefixes (10 s) is the main trap.

questions.q: A circuit with a battery, a resistor and a capacitor in series has been on for a long time. What is the current through the resistor?
o: emf divided by R
That is the initial current, not the steady-state current.
Half of emf divided by R
No steady current flows through a charged capacitor.
It oscillates
Oscillation requires an inductor; RC circuits do not oscillate.
Zero
Correct: a fully charged capacitor acts as an open circuit to steady DC.
questions.x: Once a capacitor is fully charged, its voltage equals the battery's emf, so there is no net voltage across the resistor. With no potential difference driving it, the current is zero, and the capacitor acts like an open circuit in DC steady state. The value emf/R applies only at the instant the switch closes.

questions.q: How does inserting a dielectric between a capacitor's plates allow it to store more charge at a given voltage?
o: It conducts charge between the plates
A conductor would short the capacitor; dielectrics insulate.
Its molecules polarize, creating a field that partly cancels the plates' field
Correct: the reduced net field lowers V for a given Q, so C rises.
It adds free electrons to the negative plate
Dielectrics do not supply free charge.
It increases the area of the plates
Plate area is unchanged; the dielectric acts through polarization.
questions.x: A dielectric's molecules polarize in the field, with their charges lining up to create an internal field opposite the plates' field. This reduces the net field and therefore the voltage for a given charge, so C = Q/V rises by a factor of κ. A dielectric is an insulator; it does not conduct or add free charge.

questions.q: A defibrillator's 100 μF capacitor is charged to 2000 V. How much energy can it deliver?
o: Omits the factor of ½.
Uses ½CV instead of ½CV².
Ignores the micro prefix.
Correct: U = ½CV² = ½(10⁻⁴)(4 × 10⁶).
questions.x: Capacitor energy is U = ½CV². Here ½(100 × 10⁻⁶ F)(2000 V)² = ½(10⁻⁴)(4 × 10⁶) = 200 J. Omitting the ½ doubles the result to 400 J, and forgetting to square V gives only 0.1 J.

questions.q: In both galvanic and electrolytic cells, which process occurs at the anode?
o: Oxidation
Correct: the anode is always the site of oxidation (An Ox, Red Cat).
Reduction
Reduction always occurs at the cathode.
Oxidation in galvanic cells only
The definition holds for every cell type.
Neither; it depends on electrode sign
Electrode sign changes; the anode's role does not.
questions.x: Anode and cathode are defined by the reaction, not by charge sign: oxidation always occurs at the anode, and reduction at the cathode ('An Ox, Red Cat'). What changes between cell types is the electrode sign: the anode is negative in a galvanic cell and positive in an electrolytic cell.

questions.q: In a galvanic cell, in which direction do electrons flow through the external wire?
o: From cathode to anode
Reverses the direction of electron flow.
Through the salt bridge from anode to cathode
Electrons travel through the wire; ions move in the salt bridge.
From anode to cathode
Correct: electrons released by oxidation travel to the cathode for reduction.
Back and forth, alternating
A galvanic cell supplies direct current.
questions.x: In a galvanic cell, oxidation at the anode releases electrons, which travel through the external wire to the cathode, where reduction consumes them. Electrons never travel through the salt bridge; it carries ions that maintain charge balance in each half-cell. Conventional current in the wire flows the opposite way, from cathode to anode.

questions.q: What is the sign of the anode in an electrolytic cell?
o: Negative
The anode is negative in a galvanic cell, not an electrolytic one.
Neutral
The external source gives each electrode a sign.
Positive
Correct: the external source pulls electrons out of the anode, making it positive.
Positive or negative, depending on the metal
In electrolytic cells the anode is always positive.
questions.note: Anode sign: galvanic −, electrolytic +.
questions.x: In an electrolytic cell, an external power source drives a nonspontaneous reaction by pulling electrons out of the anode and pushing them into the cathode. That makes the anode positive and the cathode negative. Oxidation still occurs at the anode; only the sign is reversed relative to a galvanic cell, where the anode is negative.

questions.q: In a galvanic cell's salt bridge, which way do anions migrate?
o: Toward the cathode compartment
Cations move toward the cathode; anions go the other way.
Toward the anode compartment
Correct: anions balance the positive charge building up as metal cations form at the anode.
They do not move; only cations migrate
Both ions in the bridge migrate to keep neutrality.
Into the external wire
Ions cannot travel through the metal wire.
questions.x: As a galvanic cell runs, the anode compartment gains cations (metal is oxidized to ions) and the cathode compartment loses cations (ions are reduced to metal). To keep each solution electrically neutral, anions from the salt bridge migrate toward the anode and cations toward the cathode. Ions never travel through the external wire; only electrons do.

questions.q: In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, which electrode gains mass as the cell runs?
o: The zinc anode
Zinc is oxidized to Zn²⁺, so it loses mass.
Both electrodes
Only the cathode receives deposited metal.
Neither electrode
Reduction of Cu²⁺ deposits solid copper.
The copper cathode
Correct: Cu²⁺ is reduced and plates out as Cu(s).
questions.x: At the zinc anode, Zn(s) is oxidized to Zn²⁺(aq), which dissolves, so the anode loses mass. At the copper cathode, Cu²⁺(aq) is reduced and plates out as solid Cu, so the cathode gains mass. The rule of thumb: the anode corrodes and the cathode plates.

questions.q: In the cell notation Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s), what does the electrode on the left represent?
o: The cathode, where reduction occurs
The cathode is written on the right.
The salt bridge
The salt bridge is the double line ||.
The more positive reduction potential
The right side has the higher reduction potential in a galvanic cell.
The anode, where oxidation occurs
Correct: by convention the anode is written on the left.
questions.x: Standard cell notation writes the anode (oxidation) half-cell on the left and the cathode (reduction) half-cell on the right, with the double line || for the salt bridge. Here Zn is oxidized, and Cu²⁺, which has the higher reduction potential, is reduced on the right. A single line | marks a phase boundary.

questions.q: Which statement describes an electrolytic cell?
o: It uses electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous reaction
Correct: an external source supplies energy for a reaction with ΔG > 0.
It converts a spontaneous reaction into electrical work
That describes a galvanic cell.
It has a positive E°cell for its reaction
Its driven reaction has a negative E°cell.
It requires no external power source
An external source is what drives it.
questions.x: An electrolytic cell uses an external power source to force a nonspontaneous reaction (ΔG > 0, E°cell < 0), such as electroplating or splitting water. A galvanic cell does the reverse: a spontaneous reaction (E°cell > 0) produces electrical work. Both cells still oxidize at the anode and reduce at the cathode.

questions.q: Molten NaCl is electrolyzed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?
o: Chlorine gas
Cl₂ forms at the anode by oxidation of Cl⁻.
Hydrogen gas
No water is present in the melt to be reduced.
Sodium metal
Correct: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na at the cathode.
Oxygen gas
No oxygen-containing species is present.
questions.x: Molten NaCl contains only Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, with no water. At the cathode, the only species available to be reduced is Na⁺, giving sodium metal; at the anode, Cl⁻ is oxidized to Cl₂ gas. Hydrogen could form only if water were present to be reduced.

questions.q: A concentrated aqueous NaCl solution is electrolyzed. What forms at the cathode?
o: Hydrogen gas
Correct: water is far easier to reduce than Na⁺, so H₂ evolves.
Sodium metal
Na⁺ has a very negative reduction potential; water is reduced first.
Chlorine gas
Chlorine forms by oxidation at the anode.
Oxygen gas
Oxygen would come from oxidation at the anode.
questions.note: In water, highly active metal ions are not reduced; water is.
questions.x: In aqueous solution, the cathode reduces whichever species is easiest to reduce. Na⁺ has a very negative reduction potential (−2.71 V), so water is reduced instead, producing H₂ gas and OH⁻. This differs from molten NaCl, where no water is present and sodium metal forms.

questions.q: A 2 A current passes through a Cu²⁺ solution for 965 s. How many moles of copper are deposited? (F ≈ 96,500 C/mol)
o: 0.02 mol
That is moles of electrons; each Cu needs two.
0.01 mol
Correct: Q = 1930 C = 0.02 mol e⁻; Cu²⁺ needs 2 e⁻ each.
0.04 mol
Multiplies by 2 instead of dividing.
Divides by 2 twice.
questions.x: Faraday's law links charge to moles: Q = It = (2 A)(965 s) = 1930 C, and 1930/96,500 = 0.02 mol of electrons. Each Cu²⁺ needs two electrons to become Cu, so 0.02/2 = 0.01 mol of copper deposits. The tempting 0.02 mol is the moles of electrons, not of copper.

questions.q: Two electrolytic cells, one with Ag⁺ and one with Cu²⁺, are wired in series so the same charge passes through both. How do the moles of metal deposited compare?
o: Twice as many moles of Cu as Ag
Inverts the electron requirement.
Twice as many moles of Ag as Cu
Correct: Ag⁺ needs 1 e⁻ and Cu²⁺ needs 2 e⁻.
Equal moles of each
Equal charge gives equal moles only when n is equal.
Equal masses of each
Mass depends on molar mass and on n.
questions.x: Cells in series pass the same charge, and hence the same number of moles of electrons. Silver needs one electron per atom (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag) while copper needs two (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu), so the same electrons deposit twice as many moles of Ag. Equal masses would require equal mass per electron, which is not the case.

questions.q: The salt bridge is removed from a working galvanic cell. What happens?
o: Current increases because resistance drops
Removing the bridge opens the circuit.
Current stops almost immediately
Correct: charge builds up in each half-cell and halts electron flow.
The cell becomes electrolytic
Without an external source, it simply stops.
Nothing changes; the wire carries the current
The circuit needs ion flow to close the loop.
questions.x: A galvanic cell needs a complete circuit: electrons travel through the wire and ions through the salt bridge. Without the bridge, positive charge builds up in the anode compartment and negative charge in the cathode compartment, which quickly opposes further electron transfer. The current stops almost at once.

questions.q: In a galvanic cell's salt bridge containing KNO₃, which way do K⁺ ions move?
o: Toward the cathode compartment
Correct: they replace positive charge lost as cations are reduced at the cathode.
Toward the anode compartment
That is the direction of NO₃⁻.
Through the wire to the anode
Ions do not travel through the metal wire.
They stay put while only NO₃⁻ moves
Both ions migrate to keep both solutions neutral.
questions.x: In the cathode compartment, cations such as Cu²⁺ are removed as they are reduced, leaving excess negative charge. K⁺ ions from the salt bridge migrate into the cathode compartment to restore neutrality, while NO₃⁻ ions move toward the anode compartment, where cations are being produced. Ions never travel through the wire.

questions.q: Given these standard reduction potentials: F₂/F⁻ +2.87 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Li⁺/Li −3.05 V. Which species is the strongest oxidizing agent?
o: F₂ gas
Correct: the most positive E°red means the greatest tendency to be reduced.
Li⁺ ion
Li⁺ has the least tendency to be reduced.
Li metal
Li is a strong reducing agent, not an oxidizing agent.
Cu²⁺ ion
Its E°red is positive but much smaller than that of F₂.
questions.x: A standard reduction potential measures a species' tendency to gain electrons. The species on the left of the half-reaction with the most positive E°red, here F₂ at +2.87 V, is the strongest oxidizing agent. Li⁺, with the most negative E°red, is the weakest oxidizing agent, and Li metal is a reducing agent.

questions.q: Given these standard reduction potentials: F₂/F⁻ +2.87 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Li⁺/Li −3.05 V. Which species is the strongest reducing agent?
o: F⁻ ion
F⁻ is the weakest reducing agent here, because F₂ is so easily reduced.
Li⁺ ion
Li⁺ is already oxidized; it cannot give up more electrons.
Li metal
Correct: the most negative E°red means Li(s) is most easily oxidized.
Zn²⁺ ion
Zn²⁺ is an oxidized form and acts as a weak oxidizing agent.
questions.note: Most negative E°red: its reduced form is the best reducing agent.
questions.x: The strongest reducing agent is the reduced species (right side) of the half-reaction with the most negative E°red, because that reaction runs most readily in reverse, as oxidation. Li⁺/Li has E° = −3.05 V, so Li(s) gives up electrons most easily. Li⁺ is already oxidized and cannot lose another electron.

questions.q: Cu²⁺/Cu has E°red = +0.34 V and Zn²⁺/Zn has E°red = −0.76 V. What is E°cell for the galvanic cell built from them?
o: Ignores the negative sign on zinc's potential: 0.76 − 0.34.
Uses only the anode's potential and ignores copper's.
Doubles copper's potential for 2 electrons; E° is intensive.
Correct: E°cathode − E°anode = 0.34 − (−0.76).
questions.x: In a galvanic cell the half-reaction with the higher E°red (Cu²⁺/Cu) is the cathode, and the other (Zn²⁺/Zn) is the anode. Then E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. Potentials are not multiplied by the number of electrons, which rules out doubling copper's value.

questions.q: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag has E° = +0.80 V. What is E° for 2Ag⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Ag?
o: It doubles to +1.60 V
Multiplying a half-reaction does not multiply its potential.
It halves to +0.40 V
Dividing is also wrong; E° stays the same.
It reverses to −0.80 V
The direction did not change, so the sign stays.
It stays +0.80 V
Correct: E° is intensive and does not scale with coefficients.
questions.note: Trap: never multiply E° by stoichiometric coefficients.
questions.x: A reduction potential is an intensive property: it is energy per unit charge, not total energy. Doubling a half-reaction doubles both ΔG and the charge transferred, so their ratio, E°, stays +0.80 V. Only reversing the reaction changes the sign; multiplying by a coefficient never changes E°.

questions.q: A cell has E°cell = +1.10 V and transfers 2 electrons per reaction. What is ΔG°? (F ≈ 96,500 C/mol)
o: About −106 kJ/mol
Uses n = 1 instead of n = 2.
About −424 kJ/mol
Uses n = 4 by double-counting the electrons.
About −21 kJ/mol
Power-of-ten slip in the conversion to kJ.
About −212 kJ/mol
questions.x: Free energy and cell potential are linked by ΔG° = −nFE°. With n = 2, F = 96,500 C/mol and E° = 1.10 V, ΔG° = −2(96,500)(1.10) ≈ −212,000 J/mol ≈ −212 kJ/mol. The negative sign reflects a spontaneous reaction; using n = 1 halves the result to about −106 kJ/mol.

questions.q: A redox reaction has a positive E°cell. Which is true under standard conditions?
o: ΔG° is positive and K is less than 1
That describes a negative E°cell.
ΔG° is negative and K is less than 1
A negative ΔG° requires K > 1.
ΔG° is negative and K is greater than 1
Correct: ΔG° = −nFE° and ΔG° = −RT ln K.
ΔG° is zero and K equals 1
That corresponds to E°cell = 0.
questions.x: Cell potential, free energy and equilibrium are linked: ΔG° = −nFE° and ΔG° = −RT ln K. A positive E° gives a negative ΔG°, and a negative ΔG° means ln K > 0, so K > 1 and products are favored at equilibrium. A negative E° would give the opposite signs and K < 1.

questions.q: A redox reaction has E°cell = 0 V. What is its equilibrium constant?
o: ln 0 is undefined; K is never 0.
Correct: E° = (RT/nF) ln K, so E° = 0 requires ln K = 0.
K is very large
A large K requires a large positive E°.
K is very small
A small K requires a negative E°.
questions.x: Combining ΔG° = −nFE° and ΔG° = −RT ln K gives E° = (RT/nF) ln K. If E° = 0, then ln K = 0 and K = 1, meaning reactants and products are equally favored at standard conditions. A large K needs a positive E°, and a small K needs a negative E°.

questions.q: Cu²⁺/Cu has E°red = +0.34 V and Ag⁺/Ag has E°red = +0.80 V. Which reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions?
o: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag
Correct: Ag⁺ has the higher E°red and is reduced; E° = 0.80 − 0.34 = +0.46 V.
2Ag + Cu²⁺ → 2Ag⁺ + Cu
This reverse reaction has E° = −0.46 V.
Cu + Cu²⁺ → 2Cu
This is not a balanced redox reaction.
Ag + Cu → Ag⁺ + Cu²⁺
Both metals are oxidized; nothing is reduced.
questions.x: A spontaneous redox reaction pairs the higher-E°red species as the one reduced with the lower-E°red metal as the one oxidized. Ag⁺ (+0.80 V) is reduced and Cu (+0.34 V) is oxidized, giving E°cell = +0.46 V > 0. The reverse reaction would have E° = −0.46 V and is nonspontaneous.

questions.q: Al³⁺/Al has E°red = −1.66 V and Ni²⁺/Ni has E°red = −0.25 V. What is E°cell for a galvanic cell made from them?
o: Adds the magnitudes instead of taking the difference.
Divides by 3 for the three electrons; E° is intensive.
Doubles the potential for stoichiometry; E° is intensive.
Correct: E°cathode − E°anode = −0.25 − (−1.66).
questions.x: The cathode is the half-reaction with the higher E°red: Ni²⁺/Ni at −0.25 V; aluminum, at −1.66 V, is oxidized at the anode. E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = −0.25 − (−1.66) = +1.41 V. Electron counts (3 for Al, 2 for Ni) affect balancing, never E°, because potential is intensive.

questions.q: Why does the standard hydrogen electrode have E° = 0.00 V?
o: H⁺ has no tendency to be reduced
H⁺ is readily reduced; zero is simply a convention.
Hydrogen gas has no charge
Charge on H₂ does not set the zero of potential.
It is assigned that value as the reference point
Correct: only differences in potential are measurable, so SHE is set to zero.
Platinum is completely inert
Pt's inertness is why it is used, not why E° = 0.
questions.x: Only differences in electrode potential can be measured, so one half-reaction must serve as an arbitrary zero. By convention the standard hydrogen electrode (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ at 1 M, 1 atm) is assigned exactly 0.00 V, and all other E° values are measured against it. Its zero reflects a choice of reference, not an absence of reactivity.

questions.q: Which metal reacts with 1 M H⁺ to release H₂ gas under standard conditions?
o: Cu (E°red = +0.34 V)
Positive E°red: Cu cannot reduce H⁺.
Ag (E°red = +0.80 V)
Ag is less easily oxidized than H₂.
Zn (E°red = −0.76 V)
Correct: a negative E°red means Zn can reduce H⁺ (E° = 0).
Au (E°red = +1.50 V)
Gold is very hard to oxidize.
questions.x: A metal reduces H⁺ to H₂ if it is more easily oxidized than H₂, which means its E°red is below 0 V, the SHE reference. Zn (−0.76 V) gives E°cell = 0 − (−0.76) = +0.76 V, a spontaneous reaction. Cu, Ag and Au all have positive E°red and do not dissolve in nonoxidizing acids.

questions.q: A student pairs an unknown metal M with a standard hydrogen electrode. M acts as the anode, and the cell reads +0.44 V. What is E°red for M²⁺/M?
o: +0.44 V (above hydrogen)
If M were reduced more easily than H⁺, it would be the cathode.
Divides by n; potentials do not scale with electrons.
−0.44 V (below hydrogen)
Correct: E°cell = 0 − E°(M) = +0.44, so E°(M) = −0.44 V.
Doubles for 2 electrons; E° is intensive.
questions.x: When M is the anode, it is oxidized and the SHE (E° = 0) is the cathode. E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode gives 0.44 = 0 − E°(M), so E°(M) = −0.44 V. A metal that acts as an anode against SHE must lie below hydrogen in reduction potential, so a positive value is impossible.

questions.q: What is E°cell for any concentration cell?
o: That is the Nernst slope per decade for n = 1, not E°.
0 V
Correct: both half-cells use the same reaction, so their E° values cancel.
It equals the E°red of the metal
Identical half-reactions cancel.
It equals twice the E°red of the metal
Identical half-reactions cancel.
questions.note: Concentration cells run on Q alone; E° = 0.
questions.x: A concentration cell uses the same half-reaction in both compartments, so E°cathode − E°anode = 0. Any voltage it produces comes entirely from the concentration difference, through the Nernst term −(0.059/n) log Q. Once the concentrations equalize, Q = 1 and the voltage drops to zero.

questions.q: A concentration cell has two Cu electrodes, one in 0.01 M Cu²⁺ and one in 1 M Cu²⁺. Which electrode is the cathode?
o: The electrode in 0.01 M Cu²⁺
Oxidation occurs here, raising the dilute concentration.
Both electrodes, alternately
The current flows in one direction until equilibrium.
The electrode in 1 M Cu²⁺
Correct: reduction there lowers the high concentration toward equality.
Neither, because E° = 0
E° = 0, but E ≠ 0 when the concentrations differ.
questions.x: A concentration cell runs spontaneously in the direction that equalizes the concentrations. Reduction of Cu²⁺ at the 1 M side lowers the high concentration, making it the cathode, while oxidation of Cu at the 0.01 M side raises the low concentration. E° is zero, but E is not, because Q ≠ 1.

questions.q: A Cu concentration cell has 0.001 M Cu²⁺ in one half-cell and 1 M Cu²⁺ in the other. What is the cell voltage at 25 °C? (Use 0.06/n per decade.)
o: About 0.18 V
Uses n = 1; Cu²⁺ transfers 2 electrons.
About 0.03 V
Counts only one decade of difference.
0 V
That is E°; actual E depends on the concentration ratio.
About 0.09 V
questions.x: For a concentration cell, E = (0.06/n) log(concentrated/dilute) at 25 °C, since E° = 0. Cu²⁺ transfers n = 2 electrons, and the ratio is 1/0.001 = 10³, three decades. So E = (0.06/2) × 3 = 0.09 V. Using n = 1 would double this to 0.18 V.

questions.q: In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, [Cu²⁺] in the cathode compartment is increased. What happens to the cell voltage?
o: It increases
Correct: Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] decreases, so E = E° − (0.06/n) log Q rises.
It decreases
More reactant pushes the reaction forward and raises E.
It stays at E°
E equals E° only at standard concentrations.
It drops to zero
Zero voltage occurs only at equilibrium.
questions.x: The Nernst equation is E = E° − (0.06/n) log Q, where Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] for Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Raising [Cu²⁺], a reactant, lowers Q, which raises E. This follows Le Châtelier's principle: more reactant increases the driving force for the forward reaction.

questions.q: As a galvanic cell discharges, what happens to its voltage?
o: It stays at E° until the reactants run out
E changes continuously as Q changes.
It decreases toward zero as Q approaches K
Correct: products build up, raising Q, until E = 0 at equilibrium.
It increases as products accumulate
Rising Q lowers E.
It becomes negative after equilibrium
A cell stops at equilibrium; it does not reverse on its own.
questions.x: As a cell discharges, reactants are consumed and products accumulate, so Q rises. Through the Nernst equation, E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q, the voltage falls steadily rather than holding at E°. When Q reaches K, the reaction is at equilibrium, E = 0, and the cell is dead.

questions.q: A Zn/Cu cell (E° = 1.10 V) has [Zn²⁺] = 1 M and [Cu²⁺] = 0.01 M. What is the cell voltage at 25 °C? (Use 0.06/n per decade.)
o: Uses log Q with the wrong sign; Q > 1 lowers E.
Uses n = 1 instead of n = 2.
Ignores the nonstandard concentrations.
questions.x: The Nernst equation is E = E° − (0.06/n) log Q. For Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 1/0.01 = 100, so log Q = 2 and E = 1.10 − (0.06/2)(2) = 1.04 V. A low reactant concentration makes Q > 1, which lowers E; flipping the sign gives the 1.16 V trap.

questions.q: A battery is completely dead. Which describes its chemistry?
o: E° has fallen to zero
E° is a fixed constant; E is what reaches zero.
ΔG is large and positive
A large positive ΔG would drive the reverse reaction.
The reaction has reached equilibrium, so E = 0 and ΔG = 0
Correct: Q = K, so there is no driving force left.
Q is much smaller than K
Then the reaction would still proceed forward.
questions.note: Trap: E° never changes; E reaches 0.
questions.x: A battery delivers current only while its reaction has a driving force, ΔG < 0 and E > 0. As it runs, Q rises toward K; when Q = K the reaction is at equilibrium, so ΔG = 0 and E = 0. E° is a fixed standard-state constant and does not change as the battery discharges.

questions.q: As a concentration cell operates, what happens to the concentrations in its two half-cells?
o: They converge until they are equal
Correct: oxidation raises the dilute side; reduction lowers the concentrated side.
The difference between them grows
The cell runs to reduce the gradient, not enlarge it.
They stay the same; only electrons move
Redox at each electrode changes ion concentrations.
Both rise steadily
One side rises while the other falls.
questions.x: A concentration cell runs because of a concentration difference, and its reaction reduces that difference. Oxidation at the dilute electrode adds ions there, and reduction at the concentrated electrode removes ions. The concentrations converge until they are equal, at which point Q = 1 and the voltage is zero.

questions.q: Two hydrogen electrodes (1 atm H₂) are in solutions at pH 1 and pH 4. What is the voltage of this concentration cell at 25 °C? (Use 0.06/n per decade.)
o: About 0.09 V
Applies n = 2 without squaring [H⁺] in Q.
About 0.18 V
Correct: [H⁺] differs by 10³; 0.06 V per decade for H⁺ gives 0.06 × 3.
About 0.30 V
Adds the pH values (1 + 4 = 5 decades) instead of taking their difference.
0 V
That is E°; unequal [H⁺] produces a voltage.
questions.x: The half-reaction 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ has n = 2, but Q contains [H⁺]², so E = (0.06/2) log([H⁺]conc/[H⁺]dil)² = 0.06 log(ratio). pH 1 versus pH 4 is a 10³ ratio, giving 0.06 × 3 = 0.18 V. Using n = 2 without squaring the concentrations gives the 0.09 V trap.

questions.q: A tenfold increase in Q changes a cell's voltage at 25 °C by about how much for a one-electron reaction?
o: It lowers E by about 59 mV
Correct: E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q with n = 1.
It raises E by about 59 mV
Higher Q lowers E.
It lowers E by about 590 mV
One decade is 59 mV, not 590 mV.
It lowers E by about 30 mV
That is the value for n = 2.
questions.x: The Nernst equation at 25 °C is E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q. A tenfold increase in Q raises log Q by 1, so for n = 1, E falls by about 59 mV. Increasing Q means more products relative to reactants, which reduces the driving force, so E falls rather than rises.

questions.q: In a discharging lead–acid battery, what compound forms at both electrodes?
o: PbO₂
PbO₂ is consumed at the cathode during discharge.
Pb
Pb is consumed at the anode during discharge.
PbSO₄
Correct: Pb is oxidized and PbO₂ is reduced, both to lead(II) sulfate.
H₂SO₄
Sulfuric acid is consumed during discharge.
questions.x: In a lead–acid battery during discharge, the Pb anode is oxidized to Pb²⁺ and the PbO₂ cathode is reduced from Pb⁴⁺ to Pb²⁺. In both cases the Pb²⁺ combines with sulfate from the sulfuric acid, so PbSO₄ forms on both electrodes. Recharging reverses both reactions.

questions.q: In a nickel–cadmium battery during discharge, what happens to cadmium?
o: It is reduced at the cathode
The nickel compound is reduced at the cathode.
It is oxidized at the anode
Correct: Cd → Cd(OH)₂ releases electrons to the external circuit.
It is reduced at the anode
Reduction never occurs at the anode.
It acts only as an inert conductor
Cadmium is an active reactant.
questions.x: In a NiCd battery, cadmium metal is oxidized at the anode to Cd(OH)₂, releasing electrons into the external circuit. At the cathode, the nickel oxyhydroxide (NiO(OH)) is reduced. Oxidation always occurs at the anode, so cadmium cannot be reduced there.

questions.q: As a battery ages, its emf is nearly unchanged but its voltage under load drops. What best explains this?
o: Its E° has decreased
E° is a fixed thermodynamic constant.
Its internal resistance has increased
Correct: V = emf − Ir falls as r rises.
Its external load resistance has increased
A larger load would raise terminal voltage.
Its electrodes have become more conductive
More conductivity would reduce, not increase, internal losses.
questions.x: Terminal voltage under load is V = emf − Ir. The emf is set by the cell's chemistry and changes little with age, but internal resistance r rises as electrodes and electrolyte degrade. A larger Ir drop means lower voltage whenever current flows, although an unloaded reading still shows nearly the full emf.

questions.q: While a rechargeable battery is being recharged, what is the electrode that served as the anode during discharge?
o: Still the anode, where oxidation occurs
Reversing the reaction reverses which electrode oxidizes.
The cathode, where reduction now occurs
Correct: charging reverses each electrode's reaction, so the former anode is reduced.
A salt bridge
Electrodes do not become salt bridges.
Inactive during charging
Both electrodes react while charging.
questions.note: A recharging battery is an electrolytic cell.
questions.x: Recharging uses an external source to drive the discharge reaction in reverse, making the battery an electrolytic cell. The electrode that was oxidized during discharge is now reduced, so it becomes the cathode. Anode and cathode are defined by the reaction occurring, not by a fixed physical electrode.

questions.q: Two identical 1.5 V cells are connected in parallel to a load. Compared with one cell, what does this arrangement provide?
o: 3.0 V with the same run time
That describes cells in series.
0.75 V with a longer run time
Parallel identical sources do not divide the voltage.
The same 1.5 V but a longer run time
Correct: parallel cells share the current, keeping 1.5 V while doubling capacity.
3.0 V with a longer run time
Parallel connection does not add voltage.
questions.x: Identical cells in parallel share the same two terminals, so the output voltage stays at 1.5 V. The load current is split between them, so each cell supplies half as much, and the pair lasts about twice as long. Connecting the cells in series would add voltages to 3.0 V without increasing capacity.

questions.q: A phone battery is rated at 2000 mAh. If the phone draws a steady 250 mA, how long does the battery last?
o: 8 hours
Correct: 2000 mAh ÷ 250 mA = 8 h.
0.125 hours
Divides current by capacity.
80 hours
Decimal slip: 2000/250 = 8, not 80.
4 hours
Arithmetic slip; 250 × 8 = 2000.
questions.x: A battery's mAh rating is its charge capacity: current times time. Running time is capacity divided by current: 2000 mAh ÷ 250 mA = 8 h. Units guide the operation: mAh divided by mA leaves hours.

questions.q: As a lead–acid battery discharges, how does the density of its electrolyte change?
o: It increases
Sulfuric acid is used up, not produced, during discharge.
It stays the same
Discharge changes the acid concentration.
It first increases then decreases
Acid is consumed steadily during discharge.
It decreases
Correct: dense H₂SO₄ is consumed and water is produced.
questions.x: During discharge, both electrodes react with sulfuric acid to form PbSO₄, and water is produced: Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O. Consuming dense H₂SO₄ and producing water makes the electrolyte steadily less dense. This is why a hydrometer can measure a lead–acid battery's state of charge.

questions.q: How does a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell differ from an ordinary battery?
o: It oxidizes O₂ at the anode
O₂ is reduced at the cathode; H₂ is oxidized at the anode.
It needs an external power source to run
A fuel cell is galvanic; its reaction is spontaneous.
Its reactants are supplied continuously from outside
Correct: H₂ and O₂ are fed in, so it runs as long as fuel flows.
Its electrons flow from cathode to anode
As in all galvanic cells, electrons flow from anode to cathode.
questions.x: A fuel cell is a galvanic cell whose reactants, H₂ and O₂, are supplied continuously from outside rather than sealed inside. H₂ is oxidized at the anode and O₂ reduced at the cathode, with electrons flowing from anode to cathode as in any galvanic cell. It runs as long as fuel is supplied.

questions.q: In circuit models of a neuron, the lipid bilayer and the ion channels are represented by which elements?
o: Bilayer as a resistor, channels as capacitors
Reversed: channels carry current, the bilayer stores charge.
Bilayer as a capacitor, channels as resistors
Correct: the thin bilayer separates charge; channels conduct ions.
Bilayer as a battery, channels as wires
Batteries model ion gradients, not the bilayer itself.
Both as batteries
Batteries represent equilibrium potentials of ions.
questions.x: In the equivalent circuit model of a membrane, the thin, insulating lipid bilayer separates charge across it and acts as a capacitor. Ion channels let current flow and are modeled as resistors (conductances), each in series with a battery representing that ion's equilibrium potential. Reversing these roles is the main trap.

questions.q: How does myelin change the electrical properties of an axon segment it wraps?
o: It increases capacitance and decreases resistance
That would slow conduction and increase leak.
It increases both capacitance and resistance
Greater plate separation lowers capacitance.
It decreases both capacitance and resistance
Insulation raises resistance.
It decreases membrane capacitance and increases membrane resistance
Correct: thicker insulation separates charge farther and blocks leak.
questions.note: Less charge to move and less leak: faster conduction.
questions.x: Myelin wraps many membrane layers around the axon, effectively increasing the distance between the capacitor's 'plates'. Since C is inversely proportional to separation, capacitance falls, so less charge is needed to change the voltage. The insulation also raises membrane resistance and reduces ion leak, letting signals travel farther and faster.

questions.q: At body temperature, [K⁺] inside a cell is 10 times [K⁺] outside. What is the K⁺ equilibrium potential? (Use 61 mV per decade for z = +1.)
o: About +61 mV, inside positive
Inside high K⁺ makes the inside negative at equilibrium.
About −610 mV
One decade gives 61 mV, not 610 mV.
About −61 mV, inside negative
Correct: E = 61 log(out/in) = 61 log(0.1) = −61 mV.
0 mV
Unequal concentrations produce a nonzero potential.
questions.x: The Nernst equation for an ion of charge z is E = (61/z) log([out]/[in]) at body temperature. With [in] = 10 × [out], E_K = 61 log(0.1) = −61 mV. Since K⁺ tends to leak out down its gradient, the inside becomes negative at equilibrium, ruling out the +61 mV answer.

questions.q: Extracellular Ca²⁺ is 10,000 times its intracellular level. What is the Ca²⁺ equilibrium potential at body temperature? (Use 61 mV per decade for z = +1.)
o: About +244 mV
Ignores z = 2 in the denominator.
About −122 mV, inside negative
High outside Ca²⁺ makes the inside positive at equilibrium.
About +122 mV, inside positive
About +61 mV
Uses one decade instead of four.
questions.x: The Nernst equation is E = (61/z) log([out]/[in]). For Ca²⁺, z = 2 and the ratio is 10⁴, so E = 30.5 × 4 ≈ +122 mV. The sign is positive because Ca²⁺ tends to flow in, making the inside positive at equilibrium. Forgetting to divide by z doubles the result to +244 mV.

questions.q: A neuron rests at −70 mV, and E_Na is +60 mV. Which describes the net electrochemical force on Na⁺?
o: Strongly outward
Na⁺ would move out only if Vm were above E_Na.
Strongly inward
Correct: Vm is 130 mV below E_Na, so Na⁺ is driven into the cell.
Zero, since the cell is at rest
Rest is a steady state, not equilibrium for Na⁺.
Weakly outward due to the electrical gradient
Both the chemical and electrical gradients push Na⁺ inward.
questions.x: The net driving force on an ion is Vm − E_ion. At −70 mV, the membrane is 130 mV below E_Na = +60 mV, so both the concentration gradient (more Na⁺ outside) and the negative interior pull Na⁺ inward. Resting is a steady state maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, not equilibrium for Na⁺.

questions.q: Extra K⁺ channels open in a resting neuron. How does the membrane potential change?
o: It becomes more positive, moving toward E_Na
That results from opening Na⁺ channels.
It becomes more negative, moving toward E_K
Correct: higher K⁺ conductance pulls Vm toward E_K (about −90 mV).
It stays the same, since K⁺ is already at equilibrium
At rest Vm is slightly above E_K, so K⁺ still flows out.
It reverses to a positive value
K⁺ efflux makes the inside more negative.
questions.x: The membrane potential is a conductance-weighted average of the ions' equilibrium potentials. Opening more K⁺ channels increases K⁺ conductance, pulling Vm toward E_K (about −90 mV), so the cell hyperpolarizes. At rest Vm sits slightly above E_K, so K⁺ still has a net outward drive.

questions.q: Sound traveling through air is best described as which type of wave?
o: A transverse mechanical wave
Gases cannot support the shear needed for transverse waves; that describes a wave on a string.
A longitudinal mechanical wave
Correct: air molecules oscillate parallel to the direction the compression travels.
A transverse electromagnetic wave
Sound needs a material medium; electromagnetic waves do not.
A longitudinal electromagnetic wave
Sound is mechanical, and electromagnetic waves in vacuum are transverse.
questions.note: Trap: sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
questions.x: Sound is a pressure disturbance: molecules are pushed together and pulled apart along the line the wave travels, which makes it longitudinal. Because it needs particles to carry it, it is mechanical. Gases and liquids cannot resist shear, so they cannot carry transverse waves; only EM waves cross a vacuum.

questions.q: A 680 Hz tone travels through air where the speed of sound is 340 m/s. What is its wavelength?
o: Correct: λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.5 m.
2 m
Inverted the ratio: f/v gives 2, which has units of 1/m, not m.
1 m
That is the wavelength of a 340 Hz tone, not 680 Hz.
Divided by twice the frequency; λ = v/f with no extra factor.
questions.x: For any wave, v = fλ. The medium sets the speed, so wavelength is speed divided by frequency: 340/680 = 0.5 m. A quick check is that doubling frequency in the same medium halves wavelength, so 340 Hz would give 1 m and 680 Hz gives half of that.

questions.q: A sound wave passes from air into water. Which property of the wave stays the same?
o: Wavelength
Wavelength changes because speed changes while frequency is fixed.
Speed
Sound moves about four times faster in water than in air.
Intensity
Some energy reflects at the boundary, so transmitted intensity changes.
Frequency
Correct: frequency is set by the source, so it is unchanged at the boundary.
questions.note: At any boundary, frequency is fixed; v and λ change together.
questions.x: Frequency is set by the source: every compression arriving at the boundary must launch one compression on the other side, so cycles per second cannot change. Speed is set by the new medium, so wavelength (λ = v/f) changes with it. Intensity also changes because part of the energy reflects.

questions.q: The speed of sound in a medium is proportional to √(B/ρ). Why does sound travel faster in steel than in air even though steel is far denser?
o: Denser media always carry sound faster
Higher density alone lowers speed; v ∝ 1/√ρ at fixed stiffness.
Steel's stiffness (bulk modulus) is greater by a much larger factor than its density
Correct: B rises far more than ρ from air to steel, so √(B/ρ) is larger.
Steel molecules move faster thermally than air molecules
Sound speed in solids is set by elastic stiffness, not thermal speed.
Sound in steel is transverse, which is always faster
The comparison holds for longitudinal waves; transverse waves in solids are slower.
questions.x: Wave speed in any medium is √(stiffness/inertia). Density alone would slow sound, but solids resist compression enormously: steel's bulk modulus exceeds air's by about a million times while its density is only several thousand times larger. The stiffness wins, so sound travels about 15 times faster in steel.

questions.q: What happens to the speed of sound in air as the air temperature rises?
o: It decreases
Reversed: warmer gas carries sound faster, not slower.
It stays the same
Sound speed in a gas depends on temperature.
It increases
Correct: faster-moving molecules transmit compressions more quickly (v ∝ √T).
It increases only if pressure also rises
At fixed composition, temperature alone sets sound speed in an ideal gas.
questions.x: In a gas, compressions are passed along by molecular collisions, so sound speed tracks the molecules' thermal speed, v ∝ √T (absolute temperature). Warmer air carries sound faster, about 0.6 m/s more per °C near room temperature. Pressure alone does not matter for an ideal gas because it raises B and ρ by the same factor.

questions.q: A listener moves from 2 m to 4 m away from a small speaker radiating equally in all directions. By what factor does the sound intensity change?
o: It becomes 1/2 as large
Treated intensity as falling with 1/r instead of 1/r².
It becomes 1/8 as large
Cubed the distance ratio; spreading over a sphere gives 1/r².
It becomes 1/4 as large
Correct: I ∝ 1/r², so doubling r divides I by 4.
It stays the same
Energy spreads over a larger sphere, so intensity drops.
questions.x: A point source spreads its power over a sphere of area 4πr², so I = P/(4πr²) and intensity falls as 1/r². Doubling the distance spreads the same power over four times the area, giving one quarter the intensity. The 1/r dependence describes pressure amplitude, not intensity.

questions.q: A machine raises the sound level in a room from 60 dB to 90 dB. By what factor did the intensity increase?
o: Treated decibels as linear in intensity.
Correct: each 10 dB is a factor of 10, so 30 dB is 10³.
Took the ratio of the decibel values (90/60).
Multiplied 30 dB by 10; each 10 dB multiplies intensity by 10.
questions.x: The decibel scale is logarithmic: β = 10 log(I/I₀). Every +10 dB multiplies intensity by 10, so +30 dB is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000. The tempting error is treating the 30 dB difference as a simple factor; decibel differences correspond to intensity ratios, not intensity differences.

questions.q: One trumpet produces 70 dB at a listener. A second identical trumpet joins, playing equally loudly. What is the new sound level?
o: 140 dB
Decibels do not add arithmetically; intensities do.
80 dB
That would need ten times the intensity, not two.
About 76 dB
That is a factor of 4 in intensity (two doublings).
About 73 dB
Correct: doubling intensity adds 10 log 2 ≈ 3 dB.
questions.note: Doubling intensity adds 3 dB; ×10 adds 10 dB.
questions.x: Intensities add, not decibel values. Two equal sources double the intensity, and the level rises by 10 log 2 ≈ 3 dB, giving about 73 dB. Getting 80 dB would require ten equal trumpets, and adding the dB values (140 dB) ignores the logarithmic scale.

questions.q: A sound wave's pressure amplitude is tripled at constant frequency. By what factor does its intensity change?
o: Correct: intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, 3² = 9.
Assumed intensity is linear in amplitude.
Cubed the amplitude ratio instead of squaring it.
Took a square root; intensity grows with the square of amplitude.
questions.x: Wave energy, like that of an oscillator, scales with the square of amplitude, so I ∝ A². Tripling the pressure amplitude multiplies intensity by 3² = 9. This also means a sound level change of 20 log 3 ≈ 9.5 dB, not 10 log 3.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches perceived qualities of sound to physical properties?
o: Pitch to frequency; loudness to intensity
Correct: higher frequency sounds higher; greater intensity sounds louder.
Pitch to intensity; loudness to frequency
Swapped the two relationships.
Pitch to wave speed; loudness to wavelength
Speed is set by the medium and is the same for all pitches in air.
Pitch to amplitude; loudness to wave speed
Amplitude governs loudness, and speed does not set loudness.
questions.x: Perception maps onto physics: pitch is our sense of frequency, and loudness is our sense of intensity (which depends on amplitude squared). In a given medium all frequencies travel at the same speed, so speed cannot encode pitch, which is why a distant band's music stays in tune.

questions.q: A source emitting a steady tone moves away from a stationary listener. Compared with the emitted tone, the listener hears:
o: a lower frequency
Correct: wavefronts are stretched behind a receding source, so fewer reach the ear per second.
a higher frequency
That happens when source and observer approach each other.
the same frequency but lower intensity
Distance changes intensity, but motion also shifts frequency.
a higher speed of sound
Sound speed depends on the medium, not on source motion.
questions.x: A receding source emits each wavefront from a point farther away than the last, stretching the spacing between wavefronts behind it. Longer wavelength at the same sound speed means fewer crests per second reach the listener, so the frequency heard is lower. The speed of sound itself is set by the air, not the source.

questions.q: A siren emitting 1000 Hz moves at 34 m/s directly toward a stationary listener (speed of sound 340 m/s). What frequency does the listener hear?
o: About 1110 Hz
About 909 Hz
Used v + vs in the denominator, which applies to a receding source.
Ignored the Doppler shift from the moving source.
About 1210 Hz
Applied a 10% shift twice; the source alone gives about an 11% increase.
questions.x: For a source approaching a stationary listener, f′ = f·v/(v − vs). Wavefronts are compressed, so the denominator shrinks: 340/306 ≈ 1.11, giving about 1110 Hz. Using v + vs is the receding case and gives a lower frequency.

questions.q: In Doppler ultrasound of an artery, echoes return at a higher frequency than the transmitted beam. What does this indicate?
o: Blood is flowing away from the transducer
Receding blood would lower the echo frequency.
Blood is flowing perpendicular to the beam
Perpendicular flow produces almost no Doppler shift.
The tissue has a higher speed of sound than blood
A speed difference alone does not change the echo frequency.
Blood is flowing toward the transducer
Correct: reflectors approaching the probe raise the echo frequency.
questions.x: Doppler ultrasound bounces sound off moving red blood cells. Cells moving toward the probe act as an approaching receiver and then an approaching source, so the echo returns at a higher frequency; cells moving away lower it. The size of the shift is proportional to velocity times cos θ, so flow perpendicular to the beam gives almost no shift.

questions.q: A bat flying toward a cave wall emits a 40 kHz call. How does the frequency of the echo it hears compare with 40 kHz?
o: Higher, shifted twice: once at the wall and once at the bat
Correct: the wall receives a raised frequency, then acts as a source the moving bat approaches.
Higher, shifted only once because the wall is stationary
The bat moves both as emitter and as receiver, so two shifts add.
Equal, since the wall reflects the same frequency it receives
The wall receives an already-shifted frequency and the bat moves toward the echo.
Lower, because the echo travels back toward the bat
Approach raises frequency; direction of the echo does not reverse that.
questions.note: Moving reflector or moving receiver both count; echoes are double-shifted.
questions.x: An echo off a reflector involves two Doppler steps. The wall receives the call as a stationary observer of an approaching source, so it hears a raised frequency. It then re-emits that frequency, and the bat, now a moving observer approaching the source, raises it again. Both shifts are upward because the bat and wall are closing.

questions.q: A train horn's frequency is 1100 Hz as the train approaches and 900 Hz after it passes a listener. Speed of sound is 340 m/s. What is the train's approximate speed?
o: About 68 m/s
Used the full 200 Hz difference as one shift; each direction shifts about 100 Hz.
About 34 m/s
Correct: the shift is about ±10% of 1000 Hz, so vs ≈ 0.1 × 340 m/s.
About 17 m/s
Used half the shift; Δf/f = 100/1000 = 0.1, and 0.1 × 340 m/s is 34 m/s.
About 200 m/s
Equated the frequency difference in Hz with a speed.
questions.note: Small-speed Doppler: Δf/f ≈ v/c.
questions.x: When source speed is small compared with sound speed, the fractional shift is Δf/f ≈ vs/v. The true frequency is about 1000 Hz, midway between 1100 and 900, and each one-way shift is about 100 Hz, or 10%. So vs ≈ 0.1 × 340 = 34 m/s. Using the full 200 Hz gap counts the shift twice.

questions.q: What produces a sonic boom?
o: A source emitting sound above 20 kHz
That is ultrasound, which is simply inaudible, not explosive.
A source at exactly the resonant frequency of air
Air has no single resonant frequency; resonance is not the cause.
A source moving faster than the speed of sound
Correct: wavefronts pile into a cone-shaped shock wave behind a supersonic source.
A source accelerating while below the speed of sound
Acceleration alone does not stack wavefronts into a shock.
questions.x: A source moving faster than sound outruns its own wavefronts, so they pile up along a cone (the Mach cone) and form a shock wave with a sudden pressure jump. The boom is heard whenever that cone sweeps past a listener, not only at the moment the sound barrier is crossed. High frequency alone just makes ultrasound.

questions.q: Two tuning forks of 440 Hz and 444 Hz sound together. What beat frequency is heard?
o: 442 Hz
That is the average tone heard, not the beat rate.
4 Hz
Correct: beat frequency = |f₁ − f₂| = 4 Hz.
884 Hz
Added the frequencies instead of subtracting.
2 Hz
Halved the difference; beats occur at the full difference.
questions.x: Two close frequencies alternately reinforce and cancel, so loudness rises and falls at the beat frequency |f₁ − f₂|. Here that is 4 Hz. The tone you hear is near the average (442 Hz), but the pulsing rate is the difference, which is why musicians tune until the beats vanish.

questions.q: A guitar string sounded with a 256 Hz fork gives 3 beats per second. Tightening the string slightly increases the beat rate. What was the string's original frequency?
o: 253 Hz
Raising 253 Hz toward 256 Hz would reduce the beats, not increase them.
256 Hz
Equal frequencies give zero beats, not 3 per second.
262 Hz
Doubled the beat count; f differs from 256 Hz by 3 Hz.
259 Hz
Correct: tightening raises f; beats grew, so f was already above 256 Hz.
questions.x: 3 beats/s means the string is at 253 or 259 Hz. Tightening raises the string's frequency. If it started at 253 Hz, raising it would approach 256 Hz and slow the beats; since the beats sped up, it must have started above 256 Hz, at 259 Hz, and moved farther away.

questions.q: A pipe open at both ends is 0.5 m long. With sound speed 340 m/s, what is its fundamental frequency?
o: 170 Hz
Used λ = 4L, which applies to a pipe closed at one end.
680 Hz
Used λ = L; the fundamental fits half a wavelength in an open pipe.
340 Hz
Correct: open-open fundamental λ = 2L = 1 m, so f = 340 Hz.
85 Hz
Used λ = 8L; no harmonic of an open pipe fits that way.
