questions.x: A pipe open at both ends has pressure nodes (displacement antinodes) at each end, so the fundamental fits half a wavelength: λ = 2L = 1 m. Then f = v/λ = 340 Hz. Using λ = 4L is the closed-pipe condition, which would give half this frequency.

questions.q: A pipe closed at one end and open at the other is 0.25 m long. With sound speed 340 m/s, what is its fundamental frequency?
o: 680 Hz
Used λ = 2L, which is the open-open condition.
Used λ = L; a closed pipe holds only a quarter wavelength at its fundamental.
340 Hz
Correct: closed-open fundamental λ = 4L = 1 m, so f = 340 Hz.
170 Hz
Used λ = 8L; the fundamental is a quarter wavelength, λ = 4L.
questions.x: A pipe closed at one end has a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so the fundamental fits only a quarter wavelength: λ = 4L = 1 m and f = 340 Hz. An open pipe of the same length would have λ = 2L and twice the frequency.

questions.q: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental of 200 Hz. Which frequency is NOT one of its resonances?
o: 400 Hz
Correct: closed-open pipes support only odd harmonics, so 2 × 200 Hz is absent.
600 Hz
600 Hz is the third harmonic, which a closed pipe supports.
1000 Hz is the fifth harmonic, an odd multiple.
1400 Hz is the seventh harmonic, an odd multiple.
questions.note: Closed at one end: odd harmonics only.
questions.x: With a node at one end and an antinode at the other, a closed pipe can only fit odd numbers of quarter wavelengths: L = nλ/4 with n = 1, 3, 5... So its resonances are odd multiples of the fundamental, 200, 600, 1000, 1400 Hz. Even multiples like 400 Hz would need a node or antinode at both ends.

questions.q: A string fixed at both ends is 0.6 m long, and waves travel on it at 240 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?
o: 400 Hz
Used λ = L; the fundamental fits half a wavelength between the ends.
100 Hz
Used λ = 4L, the condition for a pipe closed at one end.
144 Hz
Multiplied v by L instead of dividing v by 2L.
200 Hz
Correct: λ = 2L = 1.2 m, so f = 240/1.2 = 200 Hz.
questions.x: A string fixed at both ends has nodes at each end, so the fundamental is half a wavelength long: λ = 2L = 1.2 m. With v = 240 m/s, f = v/λ = 200 Hz. The quarter-wavelength (4L) rule belongs only to systems with one open end.

questions.q: Wave speed on a string is √(T/μ). If a violinist quadruples the tension in a string, its fundamental frequency:
o: doubles
Correct: v ∝ √T doubles, and with fixed length λ is unchanged, so f doubles.
quadruples
Frequency scales with √T, not T.
halves
Higher tension speeds up waves, raising pitch.
stays the same
Fixed λ with larger v means larger f.
questions.x: For a string of fixed length, the allowed wavelengths are fixed by its ends (λ = 2L/n), so frequency changes only through wave speed. Since v = √(T/μ), quadrupling tension doubles v and therefore doubles f. Frequency is not proportional to tension itself, only to its square root.

questions.q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its third harmonic. How many nodes are present, counting the fixed ends?
o: Correct: three half-wavelength loops need four nodes including both ends.
Counted loops (antinodes) instead of nodes.
Only the fundamental has just the two end nodes.
Doubled the harmonic number; nodes = n + 1.
questions.x: The nth harmonic on a fixed-fixed string has n loops (antinodes), each half a wavelength long. Each loop is bounded by nodes, and neighboring loops share nodes, so there are n + 1 nodes including both ends. The third harmonic therefore has 4 nodes and 3 antinodes.

questions.q: On a standing wave, what is the distance between adjacent nodes?
o: One wavelength
That is the distance between every other node.
A quarter wavelength
That is the node-to-adjacent-antinode distance.
Two wavelengths
Nodes are far closer together than that.
Half a wavelength
Correct: nodes repeat every λ/2.
questions.x: A standing wave is two identical waves traveling opposite ways. Points of zero motion (nodes) recur every half wavelength, with antinodes halfway between, a quarter wavelength from each node. Two nodes a full wavelength apart are every other node, not adjacent.

questions.q: Resonance in a physical system occurs when:
o: a periodic driving force matches the system's natural frequency
Correct: energy is added in step with each cycle, so amplitude grows large.
the driving force has a very large amplitude at any frequency
Large forcing off resonance still gives small responses.
the system has no natural frequency
Resonance requires a natural frequency to match.
damping is increased
Damping reduces the resonant amplitude.
questions.x: Every oscillating system has natural frequencies set by its mass and stiffness. A driving force at one of these frequencies pushes in step with the motion each cycle, so energy accumulates and the amplitude becomes large, limited only by damping. Driving hard at another frequency still yields a small response.

questions.q: A tuning fork of 500 Hz is held over a tube closed at the bottom. Resonance occurs at air column lengths of 17 cm and 51 cm. What is the speed of sound?
o: Took the 34 cm spacing as a full wavelength instead of half.
85 m/s
Used 17 cm as the wavelength; the first resonance is λ/4.
Correct: successive resonances differ by λ/2 = 34 cm, so λ = 0.68 m and v = 500 × 0.68.
Used 51 cm as the wavelength; successive resonances differ by λ/2.
questions.note: Spacing between successive resonance lengths is always λ/2.
questions.x: In a tube closed at the bottom, resonances occur at L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4..., so successive resonance lengths differ by λ/2. Here 51 − 17 = 34 cm = λ/2, so λ = 0.68 m and v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m/s. Using the spacing difference also cancels any end correction.

questions.q: An organ pipe open at both ends is tuned in a cool hall. When the hall warms, what happens to its fundamental frequency?
o: It decreases
Warmer air speeds up sound, which raises f for a fixed length.
It stays the same because the pipe length is unchanged
Fixed length fixes λ, but f also depends on sound speed.
It shifts to only odd harmonics
The open-open boundary conditions, not temperature, set which harmonics exist.
It increases
Correct: sound speed rises with temperature while λ = 2L is fixed, so f = v/2L rises.
questions.x: An open-open pipe has λ = 2L, fixed by its length, so f = v/(2L). Warming the air raises the speed of sound, so every resonant frequency rises and the organ goes sharp. The pipe's boundary conditions, not temperature, decide which harmonics exist.

questions.q: After inhaling helium, a person's voice sounds higher pitched. What is the main reason?
o: Helium makes the vocal folds vibrate at a much higher rate
Fold vibration rate changes little; the tract's filtering shifts.
Helium's lower density increases sound intensity
Intensity affects loudness, not pitch.
Sound in helium has a shorter wavelength at each frequency
Faster speed gives a longer wavelength at a given frequency.
Faster sound in helium raises the resonant frequencies of the vocal tract
Correct: the tract's length fixes λ, so higher v shifts its resonances up.
questions.x: The vocal folds set the voice's fundamental, but the vocal tract acts as a resonating tube whose resonances (formants) shape the sound. The tract's dimensions fix the resonant wavelengths, so in helium, where sound is roughly three times faster, f = v/λ rises. The voice's timbre shifts upward even though fold vibration barely changes.

questions.q: Ultrasound used in medical imaging refers to sound with frequencies:
o: below about 20 Hz
That is infrasound, below the lower limit of hearing.
between 20 Hz and 20 kHz
That is the audible range.
in the radio band of the electromagnetic spectrum
Ultrasound is mechanical sound, not electromagnetic radiation.
above about 20 kHz
Correct: ultrasound lies above the upper limit of human hearing.
questions.x: Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Sound below that range is infrasound and above it is ultrasound; medical ultrasound typically uses 1 to 20 MHz. Ultrasound is still a mechanical pressure wave in tissue, not electromagnetic radiation.

questions.q: A sonographer switches from a 3 MHz to a 10 MHz transducer. What trade-off results?
o: Deeper penetration but coarser resolution
This reverses both effects of raising frequency.
Finer resolution and deeper penetration
Attenuation rises with frequency, so penetration drops.
Finer resolution but shallower penetration
Correct: shorter wavelength resolves smaller detail, but high frequencies are absorbed faster.
No change, because the speed in tissue is the same
Speed is the same, but wavelength and attenuation change.
questions.x: In tissue v ≈ 1540 m/s, so raising frequency shortens wavelength, and shorter wavelength resolves finer detail. But attenuation in tissue rises roughly in proportion to frequency, so high-frequency beams are absorbed before reaching deep structures. That is why 10 MHz probes image superficial structures and 3 MHz probes image the abdomen.

questions.q: An ultrasound echo returns 130 μs after the pulse is sent. Sound travels at about 1540 m/s in soft tissue. How deep is the reflecting boundary?
o: About 10 cm
Correct: round trip 1540 × 130×10⁻⁶ ≈ 0.2 m; half of that is 0.1 m.
About 20 cm
Forgot the pulse travels to the boundary and back.
About 5 cm
Halved the distance twice.
About 1 cm
Misplaced a power of ten in the microsecond conversion.
questions.note: Echo ranging: depth = v·t/2.
questions.x: The echo time covers the trip to the boundary and back, so depth = v·t/2. The total path is 1540 m/s × 1.3×10⁻⁴ s ≈ 0.2 m, so the reflector is about 0.1 m (10 cm) deep. Forgetting the factor of 2 doubles the depth.

questions.q: Why is a gel applied between an ultrasound probe and the skin?
o: It slows the sound to improve resolution
Resolution depends on wavelength in tissue, not the coupling layer.
It converts sound into electromagnetic waves the skin can absorb
Ultrasound stays mechanical throughout.
It removes air, whose acoustic impedance mismatch would reflect most of the sound
Correct: matching impedances lets sound enter tissue instead of bouncing off an air gap.
It increases the frequency of the transmitted beam
The transducer sets frequency; the gel does not change it.
questions.x: How much sound reflects at a boundary depends on the mismatch in acoustic impedance (density times sound speed). Air's impedance is thousands of times smaller than tissue's, so even a thin air gap reflects nearly all the beam. The gel has an impedance close to skin, displacing the air so sound passes into the body.

questions.q: Why can astronauts on a spacewalk not hear each other speak directly, even in close proximity?
o: Sound travels too slowly in a vacuum to arrive
Sound does not travel through a vacuum at all.
Low temperature in space freezes sound frequencies
Temperature does not stop sound; lack of a medium does.
Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium to travel
Correct: there are almost no particles in space to carry compressions.
Cosmic radiation destructively interferes with sound
Radiation does not cancel mechanical waves.
questions.x: Sound travels by particles pushing on neighboring particles, so it requires a material medium. Space is a near vacuum with too few particles to carry compressions, so speech cannot travel directly between helmets. Radio, an electromagnetic wave, needs no medium, which is why astronauts use it.

questions.q: A small speaker produces 40 dB at 1 m. Treating it as a point source with no absorption, what is the sound level at 10 m?
o: 20 dB
Correct: intensity falls by 10² = 100, which is a 20 dB drop.
4 dB
Divided the decibel value by 10 as if it were linear in distance.
30 dB
Assumed a 1/r drop in intensity rather than 1/r².
0.4 dB
Divided by 100 as if decibels were proportional to intensity.
questions.x: Going from 1 m to 10 m, a point source's intensity falls by (10)² = 100. Each factor of 10 in intensity is 10 dB, so a factor of 100 is a 20 dB drop: 40 − 20 = 20 dB. Decibel values are never divided or multiplied by ratios; intensity ratios become additive dB changes.

questions.q: The threshold intensity of hearing is 10⁻¹² W/m². What is the sound level of a 10⁻⁵ W/m² sound?
o: 7 dB
Forgot the factor of 10 in the decibel definition.
70 dB
Correct: β = 10 log(10⁻⁵/10⁻¹²) = 10 × 7 = 70 dB.
50 dB
Used the exponent 5 rather than the ratio 10⁷.
120 dB
Computed 10 log(1/10⁻¹²), the level of a 1 W/m² sound, ignoring the actual 10⁻⁵ W/m².
questions.x: Sound level is β = 10 log(I/I₀) with I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m². The ratio here is 10⁻⁵/10⁻¹² = 10⁷, whose log is 7, so β = 70 dB. A useful shortcut: every power of ten above threshold adds 10 dB.

questions.q: A researcher compares a 1 kHz and a 5 kHz tone sent through the same thick foam panel. Which result is most likely?
o: The 5 kHz tone loses a larger fraction of its intensity
Correct: absorption in most materials increases with frequency.
The 1 kHz tone loses a larger fraction of its intensity
Lower frequencies generally penetrate materials better.
Both lose the same fraction because attenuation is frequency independent
Attenuation in real media depends on frequency.
The 5 kHz tone gains intensity through resonance
A passive panel cannot add energy to the wave.
questions.x: In real materials, part of a sound wave's energy turns into heat during each oscillation, so higher frequencies, with more cycles per meter, lose more energy over the same thickness. Absorption therefore generally rises with frequency, which is why bass passes through walls while treble is muffled. A passive panel cannot add energy.

questions.q: A wave on a rope has a period of 0.02 s. What is its frequency?
o: Gave the period as if it were the frequency.
50 Hz
Correct: f = 1/T = 1/0.02 = 50 Hz.
20 Hz
Mixed up 0.02 with 0.05; 1/0.02 is 50.
500 Hz
Off by a factor of 10 in taking the reciprocal.
questions.x: Period and frequency are reciprocals: f = 1/T. One cycle every 0.02 s means 50 cycles each second, or 50 Hz. Checking units helps: seconds per cycle inverted gives cycles per second.

questions.q: A student shakes a taut rope twice as fast while tension stays constant. What happens to the waves on the rope?
o: Speed doubles; wavelength is unchanged
Wave speed depends on tension and mass density, not on shaking rate.
Wavelength halves; speed is unchanged
Correct: the rope sets v, so doubling f halves λ.
Both speed and wavelength double
Wave speed is fixed by the rope's tension and density, so it cannot double.
Wavelength doubles; speed is unchanged
With v fixed, λ = v/f decreases as f increases.
questions.x: Wave speed on a rope is set by the medium, v = √(T/μ), not by how the wave is generated. Shaking faster raises the frequency, so with v fixed the wavelength λ = v/f must shrink. Doubling f halves λ.

questions.q: Two points on a traveling wave are separated by half a wavelength. What is their phase difference?
o: That corresponds to a quarter wavelength.
Correct: a full wavelength is 360°, so λ/2 is 180°.
That is a full wavelength; such points move in step.
Points half a wavelength apart move opposite each other.
questions.x: One full wavelength corresponds to a full cycle, 360° of phase. Phase difference is proportional to separation: Δφ = 360° × Δx/λ, so λ/2 gives 180°. Points 180° apart always move in opposite directions; points a whole wavelength apart move together.

questions.q: What does a traveling mechanical wave carry from one place to another?
o: Energy, without net transport of the medium
Correct: particles oscillate about fixed positions while energy moves on.
Matter, carried along at the wave speed
Medium particles return to their equilibrium positions.
Both energy and a net flow of matter
Waves do not cause a net flow of the medium.
Neither energy nor matter, only a shape
Waves do carry energy; that is why loud sounds can do work.
questions.x: In a traveling wave, each particle of the medium oscillates about its equilibrium position and passes energy to its neighbor. The disturbance and its energy travel along, but the medium itself has no net displacement. A cork on water bobs up and down as waves pass rather than riding with them.

questions.q: A pulse traveling along a rope reflects from an end tied firmly to a wall. How does the reflected pulse compare with the incident pulse?
o: It is inverted
Correct: a fixed end exerts a reaction force that flips the pulse (a 180° phase change).
It is upright with the same orientation
An upright reflection occurs at a free end.
It is doubled in amplitude
Reflection cannot add energy; amplitude stays the same or less.
It travels back faster
Speed is set by the same rope, so it is unchanged.
questions.x: At a fixed end, the rope cannot move, so the wall pulls opposite to the incoming displacement and launches an inverted pulse, a 180° phase change. At a free end the rope overshoots and the pulse returns upright. In both cases speed is unchanged because the pulse returns along the same rope.

questions.q: Two identical speakers emit the same tone in phase. A listener stands where the path difference to the speakers is 1.5 wavelengths. What does the listener hear?
o: A maximum, due to constructive interference
Constructive interference needs a whole-number path difference.
A minimum, due to destructive interference
Correct: a half-integer path difference puts the waves 180° out of phase.
A tone at 1.5 times the original frequency
Interference changes amplitude, not frequency.
Beats at 1.5 Hz
Beats need two different frequencies; these are identical.
questions.x: Two in-phase sources interfere constructively where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths and destructively where it is a half-integer number (0.5λ, 1.5λ...). A 1.5λ difference shifts one wave by 180° relative to the other, so they cancel. Interference changes amplitude, never frequency.

questions.q: Two waves of equal amplitude A overlap exactly in phase. What is the amplitude of the resulting wave?
o: A
Ignored the second wave's contribution.
2A
Correct: superposition adds displacements, and in phase they add fully.
Complete cancellation occurs only for waves 180° out of phase.
4A
Intensity rises by 4, but amplitude only doubles.
questions.x: By superposition, overlapping displacements add point by point. Two equal waves in phase add crest to crest, giving amplitude 2A. Because intensity goes as amplitude squared, the intensity is four times that of one wave, a common source of the tempting 4A choice.

questions.q: Why can you hear someone talking around a doorway corner even though you cannot see them?
o: Sound travels faster than light around obstacles
Light is far faster; the difference is wavelength, not speed.
Light cannot reflect off walls
Light does reflect; it just diffracts negligibly through a doorway.
Sound wavelengths are comparable to the doorway width, so sound diffracts strongly
Correct: diffraction is large when wavelength is similar to the opening size.
Sound is a transverse wave and bends more
Sound in air is longitudinal; bending depends on wavelength.
questions.x: Diffraction, the spreading of waves around edges, is significant when the wavelength is comparable to the opening. Speech wavelengths are roughly 0.3 to 3 m, similar to a doorway, so sound bends around it. Visible light wavelengths are under a micrometer, so light passes through nearly in straight lines and you cannot see around the corner.

questions.q: A student plots resonant frequency against 1/L for open-open pipes of different lengths, using the fundamental each time. The best-fit line through the origin has slope 170 m/s. What is the speed of sound?
o: Read the slope as v directly, ignoring the factor of 2.
Correct: f = v/(2L), so the slope of f vs 1/L is v/2.
85 m/s
Divided the slope by 2 instead of multiplying.
Used the closed-pipe relation f = v/(4L).
questions.x: For an open-open pipe, f = v/(2L) = (v/2)(1/L). Plotting f against 1/L gives a straight line through the origin with slope v/2. So v = 2 × 170 = 340 m/s. Reading the slope directly as v forgets the factor of 2 in λ = 2L.

questions.q: In an electromagnetic wave traveling through vacuum, how are the electric and magnetic fields oriented?
o: Perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
Correct: EM waves are transverse, with E, B and propagation mutually perpendicular.
Parallel to each other and to the direction of travel
That would make the wave longitudinal; EM waves are transverse.
Parallel to each other, perpendicular to the direction of travel
E and B are perpendicular to each other, not parallel.
Perpendicular to each other, with E along the direction of travel
Neither field points along the propagation direction.
questions.x: An EM wave is a self-sustaining pair of oscillating fields: a changing E field produces B, and a changing B produces E. In vacuum both fields are perpendicular to each other and to the propagation direction, making the wave transverse; E × B points along the direction of travel.

questions.q: Which list orders electromagnetic radiation from shortest to longest wavelength?
o: Microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays
This is longest to shortest, the reverse order.
X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves
Correct: wavelength increases as energy decreases down this list.
Ultraviolet, X-rays, visible, microwaves, infrared
X-rays are shorter than UV, and infrared is shorter than microwaves.
Visible, ultraviolet, infrared, X-rays, microwaves
Visible lies between UV and IR, and X-rays are among the shortest.
questions.note: Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns: radio to gamma, long to short.
questions.x: All EM radiation obeys c = fλ and E = hf, so shorter wavelength means higher frequency and higher photon energy. From short to long: gamma, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio. UV and IR bracket the visible band, UV on the violet (short) side and IR on the red (long) side.

questions.q: Which color of visible light has the longest wavelength?
o: Violet
Violet is near 400 nm, the short-wavelength end.
Green
Green sits in the middle, around 500–550 nm.
Blue
Blue is near 450 nm, shorter than red.
Red
Correct: red is near 700 nm, the long-wavelength end of the visible band.
questions.x: Visible light runs from about 400 nm (violet) to about 700 nm (red), in the order of the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet from long to short. Red has the longest wavelength and lowest photon energy; violet has the shortest wavelength and highest energy.

questions.q: What is the frequency of light with a vacuum wavelength of 600 nm? (c = 3×10⁸ m/s)
o: 5×10¹⁴ Hz
Correct: f = c/λ = 3×10⁸ / 6×10⁻⁷ = 5×10¹⁴ Hz.
2×10⁻¹⁵ Hz
Computed λ/c, which is the period in seconds, not the frequency.
Multiplied c by λ instead of dividing.
5×10⁵ Hz
Used 600 m instead of 600 nm (6×10⁻⁷ m).
questions.x: Frequency and vacuum wavelength are linked by c = fλ, so f = c/λ. Converting first is essential: 600 nm = 6×10⁻⁷ m, and 3×10⁸/6×10⁻⁷ = 5×10¹⁴ Hz. Visible light frequencies are always around 10¹⁴ to 10¹⁵ Hz, a good sanity check.

questions.q: Photon A has a wavelength of 300 nm and photon B has a wavelength of 600 nm. How does A's energy compare with B's?
o: Twice as large
Correct: E = hc/λ, so halving λ doubles E.
Half as large
Energy is inversely, not directly, proportional to wavelength.
Four times as large
E depends on 1/λ, not 1/λ².
Equal, since both travel at c
Same speed, but energy depends on frequency.
questions.x: Photon energy is E = hf = hc/λ, so it is inversely proportional to wavelength. Halving λ from 600 to 300 nm doubles the energy. All photons travel at c in vacuum, so speed carries no information about energy; frequency does.

questions.q: What is the energy of a photon with frequency 5×10¹⁴ Hz? (h ≈ 6.6×10⁻³⁴ J·s)
o: Divided h by f instead of multiplying.
Off by one power of ten in multiplying the exponents.
Correct: E = hf = 6.6×10⁻³⁴ × 5×10¹⁴ = 3.3×10⁻¹⁹ J.
Divided f by h; energy is the product hf.
questions.x: Planck's relation E = hf gives a single photon's energy. Multiplying 6.6×10⁻³⁴ by 5×10¹⁴ gives 33×10⁻²⁰ = 3.3×10⁻¹⁹ J, or about 2 eV, typical for visible light. Visible photons always carry energies of order 10⁻¹⁹ J, which helps catch exponent slips.

questions.q: Using E (eV) ≈ 1240/λ (nm), what is the energy of a 620 nm photon?
o: 2 eV
Correct: 1240/620 = 2 eV.
0.5 eV
Inverted the ratio: 620/1240.
4 eV
That would be a 310 nm photon.
620 eV
Gave the wavelength value as an energy.
questions.x: Since E = hc/λ and hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm, a photon's energy in eV is 1240 divided by its wavelength in nm. For 620 nm, that is exactly 2 eV. The relation is inverse, so halving the wavelength to 310 nm would double the energy to 4 eV.

questions.q: Which type of radiation is ionizing?
o: Infrared
IR photons are well under 1 eV, enough only to excite vibrations.
Microwaves
Microwave photons are far too low in energy to ionize.
X-rays
Correct: X-ray photons carry keV energies, enough to eject electrons from atoms.
Radio waves
Radio photons have the lowest energies in the spectrum.
questions.x: Ionizing radiation carries enough energy per photon (roughly 10 eV or more) to knock electrons out of atoms and break bonds. X-ray photons carry thousands of eV, far above that threshold. Radio, microwave and infrared photons carry well under 1 eV, so even intense beams only heat tissue; intensity does not make a photon ionizing.

questions.q: Light passes from air into glass. Which property of the light remains unchanged?
o: Speed
Light slows to c/n in glass.
Frequency
Correct: frequency is fixed by the source and is continuous across the boundary.
Wavelength
Wavelength shrinks by the factor n in glass.
Direction, for all angles of incidence
Oblique rays bend at the surface.
questions.x: At a boundary, the wave on each side must oscillate together, so frequency is fixed by the source. Light slows to v = c/n in glass, so its wavelength shrinks to λ₀/n. Oblique rays also change direction (refraction), so only frequency is truly conserved.

questions.q: Light travels at 2×10⁸ m/s in a certain plastic. What is the plastic's index of refraction? (c = 3×10⁸ m/s)
o: Computed v/c; n is always at least 1.
Used the speed in the plastic as if it were n.
Multiplied the speeds instead of dividing.
Correct: n = c/v = 3/2 = 1.5.
questions.x: The index of refraction is defined as n = c/v, how many times slower light moves in the material than in vacuum. Here n = 3×10⁸/2×10⁸ = 1.5. Because light in a material never travels faster than c, n is at least 1, so a value like 0.67 signals an inverted ratio.

questions.q: Light of vacuum wavelength 600 nm enters glass with n = 1.5. What is its wavelength in the glass?
o: 900 nm
Multiplied by n; wavelength shrinks in a denser medium.
600 nm
Frequency is unchanged, but wavelength is not.
267 nm
Divided by n²; wavelength scales with 1/n.
400 nm
Correct: λ = λ₀/n = 600/1.5 = 400 nm.
questions.x: Entering a medium, frequency stays fixed but speed drops to c/n, so wavelength scales the same way: λ = λ₀/n = 600/1.5 = 400 nm. The light's color, which depends on frequency, does not change even though its wavelength in glass does.

questions.q: A 1 mW laser emits photons of energy 2×10⁻¹⁹ J each. About how many photons does it emit per second?
o: Correct: (10⁻³ J/s)/(2×10⁻¹⁹ J) = 5×10¹⁵ per second.
Divided photon energy by power, inverting the ratio.
Used 1 W instead of 1 mW.
Multiplied power by photon energy.
questions.x: Power is energy per second, and each photon carries a fixed energy, so photons per second = P/E. Here (1×10⁻³ J/s)/(2×10⁻¹⁹ J) = 5×10¹⁵ photons/s. Even a weak laser emits an enormous number of photons because each carries so little energy.

questions.q: In vacuum, how does the speed of a gamma ray compare with that of a radio wave?
o: They are equal
Correct: all electromagnetic radiation travels at c in vacuum.
The gamma ray is faster because it has more energy
Energy depends on frequency, not on speed.
The radio wave is faster because its wavelength is longer
λ and f trade off so that fλ = c for all EM waves.
It depends on the intensity of each wave
Intensity does not change the speed of light in vacuum.
questions.x: In vacuum every electromagnetic wave travels at c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s regardless of frequency, wavelength or intensity. Differences across the spectrum are in f and λ, which trade off so fλ = c. Higher photon energy reflects higher frequency, not higher speed.

questions.q: A microwave oven uses radiation of wavelength 12 cm. What is its frequency? (c = 3×10⁸ m/s)
o: 25 GHz
Used 1.2 cm; 12 cm is 0.12 m.
250 MHz
Used 1.2 m; 12 cm is 0.12 m.
36 MHz
Multiplied c by λ instead of dividing.
2.5 GHz
questions.x: Using c = fλ with λ in meters: 12 cm = 0.12 m, so f = 3×10⁸/0.12 = 2.5×10⁹ Hz = 2.5 GHz. That frequency is why microwave ovens and Wi-Fi share a band. Most errors come from unit conversion, so convert to meters before dividing.

questions.q: An FM station broadcasts at 100 MHz. What is the wavelength of its signal? (c = 3×10⁸ m/s)
o: Inverted the ratio f/c.
Used 10 MHz instead of 100 MHz.
3×10¹⁶ m
Multiplied c by f.
3 m
Correct: λ = c/f = 3×10⁸/10⁸ = 3 m.
questions.x: Wavelength is λ = c/f. For f = 100 MHz = 10⁸ Hz, λ = 3×10⁸/10⁸ = 3 m. Radio waves have wavelengths from meters to kilometers, which is why their antennas are large compared with optical components.

questions.q: In a Young's double-slit experiment, red light is replaced by blue light with everything else unchanged. What happens to the bright fringes?
o: They spread farther apart
That would happen with a longer wavelength.
They stay in the same places
Fringe positions depend on wavelength.
They vanish because blue light cannot interfere
All coherent light interferes.
They move closer together
Correct: fringe spacing ≈ λL/d, and blue has a shorter wavelength.
questions.x: In the double-slit pattern, bright fringes sit where d sin θ = mλ, and for small angles the spacing is Δy = λL/d. Fringe spacing is proportional to wavelength, so switching from red (about 650 nm) to blue (about 450 nm) squeezes the fringes closer together. Any coherent light interferes.

questions.q: Light of 500 nm passes through two slits 0.1 mm apart onto a screen 2 m away. What is the spacing between adjacent bright fringes?
o: 1 mm
Lost a factor of 10 converting 0.1 mm to 10⁻⁴ m.
Divided by L instead of multiplying.
10 cm
Used d = 0.01 mm; the slits are 0.1 mm apart.
1 cm
questions.x: For small angles, adjacent bright fringes are separated by Δy = λL/d. Converting to meters: λ = 5×10⁻⁷ m, d = 0.1 mm = 10⁻⁴ m, L = 2 m. So Δy = (5×10⁻⁷ × 2)/10⁻⁴ = 10⁻² m = 1 cm. Most wrong answers come from converting 0.1 mm incorrectly.

questions.q: In a double-slit setup, the slits are moved closer together. What happens to the interference pattern?
o: The fringes move closer together
That happens when d increases.
The fringes spread farther apart
Correct: spacing ≈ λL/d, so smaller d gives wider spacing.
The fringes stay the same
Spacing depends inversely on slit separation.
The pattern changes color
Color is set by the light's wavelength, not slit spacing.
questions.x: Fringe spacing Δy = λL/d is inversely proportional to slit separation. Moving the slits closer (smaller d) spreads the bright fringes farther apart, while widening the separation crowds them together. Wavelength sets the color, which slit geometry cannot change.

questions.q: Monochromatic light passes through a single slit. If the slit is made narrower, the central bright band:
o: becomes narrower
Narrower openings diffract more, not less.
stays the same width but dims
It dims, but its width also grows.
splits into two bands
A single slit still gives one central maximum.
becomes wider
Correct: the first minimum is at sin θ = λ/a, so smaller a spreads the band.
questions.x: For a single slit of width a, the first dark fringe lies at sin θ = λ/a. A narrower slit makes λ/a larger, pushing the first minima outward, so the central maximum widens even as it dims because less light passes. This inverse relation between aperture size and spread is the essence of diffraction.

questions.q: In single-slit diffraction (slit width a), what does the condition a sin θ = mλ, with m = 1, 2, 3..., locate?
o: Bright fringes
That is the meaning of d sin θ = mλ for a double slit, not a single slit.
The center of the central maximum
The central maximum is at θ = 0, which is m = 0, excluded here.
Dark fringes
Correct: for a single slit, this condition gives the minima.
Angles of complete polarization
Polarization is not set by slit diffraction conditions.
questions.note: Same equation, opposite meaning: double slit maxima, single slit minima.
questions.x: In a single slit, the condition a sin θ = mλ (m = 1, 2, 3...) means the slit can be divided into pairs of strips whose waves cancel, producing dark fringes. The double-slit equation d sin θ = mλ has the same form but gives bright fringes. The central maximum at θ = 0 is excluded from the single-slit minima.

questions.q: Why does a soap bubble show swirling colors in white light?
o: Soap molecules absorb some colors and emit others
The colors come from interference, not emission.
The film disperses light like a prism
A thin film is too thin to separate colors by dispersion.
Light reflected from the film's front and back surfaces interferes
Correct: thickness sets the path difference, so different colors reinforce at different places.
Diffraction around the bubble's edge
The colors appear across the whole film, not just at edges.
questions.x: Light reflects from both the outer and inner surfaces of the thin film, and the two reflected waves interfere. Whether a color is reinforced depends on the extra path through the film (about 2nt) and on phase flips at reflection. Because thickness varies across the bubble, different colors are reinforced in different places, producing the swirls.

questions.q: A coating with n = 1.25 is put on glass (n = 1.5) to minimize reflection of 500 nm light at normal incidence. What is the minimum coating thickness?
o: 100 nm
Correct: both reflections flip phase, so cancellation needs 2t = λ/(2n); t = 500/(4×1.25).
125 nm
Used the vacuum wavelength without dividing by n.
200 nm
Used t = λ/(2n), which gives reinforcement here.
83 nm
Used the glass index 1.5 instead of the coating index.
questions.note: Count phase flips: reflection off a higher-n medium adds a half wave.
questions.x: Count phase flips first: air to coating (1.0 to 1.25) and coating to glass (1.25 to 1.5) both reflect off a higher index, so both reflections flip and the flips cancel. Destructive interference then needs the round trip 2t to equal half a wavelength in the coating: 2t = λ/(2n), so t = 500/(4 × 1.25) = 100 nm.

questions.q: Increasing the number of lines per millimeter on a diffraction grating, at fixed wavelength, causes the bright maxima to:
o: move to smaller angles
That follows from a larger line spacing d.
spread to larger angles
Correct: d sin θ = mλ, and more lines per mm means smaller d.
remain at the same angles
Angles depend on line spacing.
merge into one central spot
Smaller spacing separates maxima more, not less.
questions.x: A grating's maxima obey d sin θ = mλ, where d is the spacing between lines. More lines per millimeter means smaller d, so sin θ = mλ/d grows and each order appears at a larger angle. That is why finer gratings spread spectra more widely and resolve colors better.

questions.q: Why are X-rays, rather than visible light, used to determine atomic arrangements in crystals by diffraction?
o: X-rays travel faster than visible light
All EM radiation travels at c in vacuum.
X-rays are absorbed only by electrons in bonds
X-rays scatter off all of an atom's electrons.
Visible light cannot be diffracted
Visible light diffracts, but its wavelength is far larger than atomic spacing.
X-ray wavelengths are comparable to the spacing between atoms
Correct: diffraction is strong when wavelength matches the spacing of the scattering lattice.
questions.x: Diffraction produces a measurable pattern only when the wavelength is comparable to the spacing of the scatterers. Atoms in crystals are about 0.1 to 0.3 nm apart, matching X-ray wavelengths, while visible light (400 to 700 nm) is thousands of times too long to resolve such spacing. All EM waves move at c in vacuum, so speed is irrelevant.

questions.q: Which kind of wave cannot be polarized?
o: A visible light wave
Light is transverse and can be polarized.
A radio wave
Radio waves are transverse EM waves and can be polarized.
A sound wave in air
Correct: sound in air is longitudinal, so it has no transverse direction to select.
A transverse wave on a string
Any transverse wave can be polarized.
questions.x: Polarization describes the direction of oscillation perpendicular to travel, so only transverse waves can be polarized. Light, radio waves and string waves are transverse. Sound in air is longitudinal: its oscillation is along the direction of travel, so there is no perpendicular orientation for a filter to select.

questions.q: Unpolarized light of intensity I passes through a polarizer, then through a second polarizer whose axis is 60° from the first. What intensity emerges?
o: Applied cos²60° but skipped the initial halving of unpolarized light.
Ignored the 60° angle at the second polarizer.
Correct: first polarizer gives I/2; Malus gives (I/2)cos²60° = (I/2)(1/4).
Used sin²60° instead of cos²60°.
questions.x: An ideal polarizer passes half of unpolarized light, leaving I/2 polarized along its axis. Then Malus's law, I = I₀cos²θ, applies at the second polarizer: cos²60° = 1/4, so the output is (I/2)(1/4) = I/8. Malus's law applies only to already polarized light, so the first halving cannot be skipped.

questions.q: Two polarizers are crossed at 90°, so no light passes. A third polarizer is inserted between them at 45°. Unpolarized light of intensity I enters. What emerges?
o: Correct: I/2, then × cos²45° = I/4, then × cos²45° = I/8.
The middle filter rotates the polarization, so some light now passes.
Stopped after the middle polarizer; the last one halves it again.
Ignored both 45° losses.
questions.x: The first polarizer passes I/2. The 45° middle filter passes cos²45° = 1/2 of that, I/4, and re-polarizes the light along 45°. The final filter is now 45° from that new direction, not 90°, so it passes another half: I/8. Each polarizer resets the polarization direction, which is why inserting a filter can increase transmission.

questions.q: Polarized sunglasses reduce glare from a lake surface mainly because:
o: they absorb all ultraviolet light
UV blocking does not explain glare reduction.
reflected light is partially polarized horizontally, and the lenses block that direction
Correct: the lenses' vertical axis absorbs the horizontally polarized glare.
they reflect all light from horizontal surfaces
Polarizers transmit or absorb by direction; they do not selectively reflect.
reflected light has a longer wavelength that the lenses absorb
Reflection does not shift wavelength.
questions.x: Light reflecting off a horizontal surface like water becomes partially polarized with its electric field mostly horizontal (fully so at Brewster's angle). Polarized sunglasses have a vertical transmission axis, so they absorb much of this horizontally polarized glare while transmitting other light. They work by absorption along one direction, not by reflection.

questions.q: Circularly polarized light can be described as two perpendicular linear components that are:
o: equal in amplitude and in phase
In-phase components give linear polarization at 45°.
equal in amplitude and 90° out of phase
Correct: the field vector then rotates at constant length.
unequal in amplitude and in phase
This gives linear polarization at some other angle.
equal in amplitude and 180° out of phase
A 180° shift also gives linear polarization.
questions.x: Any polarization can be built from two perpendicular linear components. If they are in phase or 180° out of phase, the resultant oscillates along a fixed line (linear polarization). If they have equal amplitude and are 90° out of phase, the resultant field keeps constant length and rotates, tracing a circle.

questions.q: A light ray strikes a flat mirror at 35° from the normal. At what angle from the normal does it reflect?
o: Gave the angle from the mirror surface, not the normal.
Doubled the angle; that is the angle between incident and reflected rays.
Correct: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
Subtracted from 180°; reflection angles are measured from the normal.
questions.x: The law of reflection says the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, with both measured from the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface). So a ray at 35° reflects at 35°. A common slip is measuring from the surface, which gives the complement, 55°.

questions.q: What kind of image does a flat (plane) mirror form?
o: Real, inverted, and the same size
A plane mirror's rays do not actually converge, so the image is not real.
Virtual, upright, and smaller
Plane mirror magnification is exactly 1.
Real, upright, and larger
Plane mirrors neither enlarge nor form real images.
Virtual, upright, and the same size
Correct: the image appears behind the mirror, as far behind as the object is in front.
questions.x: A plane mirror reflects rays so they appear to diverge from a point behind the mirror, as far behind as the object is in front. No light actually reaches that point, so the image is virtual. Its magnification is +1: upright and the same size, though left-right reversed relative to facing the object.

questions.q: A light ray passes from air into glass at an angle to the normal. How does it bend?
o: Toward the normal
Correct: entering a higher index slows light, so θ₂ < θ₁.
Away from the normal
That happens going from higher to lower index.
It does not bend because frequency is unchanged
Fixed frequency, but changing speed still bends oblique rays.
It reflects completely
Total internal reflection cannot occur going into a higher index.
questions.x: Snell's law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, means that entering a higher-index medium makes sin θ₂ smaller, so the ray bends toward the normal. Physically, the side of the wavefront that enters the glass first slows down, pivoting the wave. Total internal reflection can occur only when traveling toward a lower index.

questions.q: Light in air strikes glass (n = 1.5) at 30° from the normal. What is the sine of the refraction angle?
o: Multiplied sin 30° by 1.5, as if going from glass into air.
Ignored the change in index.
Used 1/1.5 without the sin 30° factor.
questions.x: Apply Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, so sin θ₂ = (1.0 × 0.5)/1.5 = 1/3. The smaller sine confirms the ray bends toward the normal as it enters the denser glass. Multiplying by 1.5 instead of dividing reverses the direction of travel.

questions.q: Light inside glass (n = 1.5) hits a glass-air surface at 30° from the normal. What is the sine of the angle of the ray in air?
o: Divided by 1.5, as if going from air into glass.
Ignored the change in index.
Correct: 1.5 sin 30° = 1 · sin θ₂, so sin θ₂ = 0.75.
A sine cannot exceed 1; forgot the sin 30° factor.
questions.x: Snell's law from glass to air gives 1.5 sin 30° = 1.0 sin θ₂, so sin θ₂ = 0.75 and the ray bends away from the normal (about 49°). Because 30° is below glass's critical angle (about 42°), the ray escapes rather than totally reflecting. A sine must stay at or below 1.

questions.q: What is the critical angle for light going from a material with n = 2 into air?
o: Used cos θc = 1/2 instead of sin θc.
That corresponds to n = √2, not 2.
90° is the refraction angle at the critical angle, not θc itself.
Correct: sin θc = n₂/n₁ = 1/2, so θc = 30°.
questions.x: The critical angle is the incidence angle at which the refracted ray would travel along the surface (90°). From n₁ sin θc = n₂ sin 90°, sin θc = n₂/n₁ = 1/2, so θc = 30°. Ninety degrees is the refraction angle at that point, not the critical angle itself.

questions.q: Which conditions are both required for total internal reflection?
o: Light travels toward higher n, and the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle
Going into higher n, light always refracts; no critical angle exists.
Light travels toward lower n, and the incidence angle is below the critical angle
Below θc, light still partially transmits.
The surface is silvered, at any angle
Mirror reflection is not total internal reflection.
Light travels toward lower n, and the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle
Correct: a critical angle exists only toward a lower index.
questions.x: Total internal reflection requires that the light be traveling from higher to lower index, because only then can Snell's law demand a sine greater than 1. It also requires the incidence angle to exceed the critical angle, sin θc = n₂/n₁. Below θc, part of the light refracts out and only part reflects.

questions.q: In an optical fiber used in endoscopy, light stays inside the core because:
o: the cladding has a higher index than the core
Then no critical angle would exist at the core-cladding boundary.
the core has a higher index than the cladding, giving total internal reflection
Correct: rays striking the boundary beyond θc reflect back into the core.
the cladding is a metal mirror
Fibers use dielectric cladding, not metal coatings.
light is polarized and cannot leave the core
Polarization does not confine light in a fiber.
questions.x: An optical fiber has a core with a higher index than its cladding. Rays traveling along the fiber strike the core-cladding boundary at large angles beyond the critical angle, so they are totally reflected back into the core and zigzag along it with little loss. If the cladding had the higher index, no critical angle would exist.

questions.q: Diamond (n ≈ 2.4) sparkles more than glass (n ≈ 1.5) of the same cut. What property of diamond explains this?
o: Its larger critical angle lets more light escape directly
Higher n gives a smaller critical angle, not larger.
Its smaller critical angle traps more light by total internal reflection
Correct: sin θc = 1/n is smaller, so more internal rays reflect before escaping.
Light travels faster in diamond than in glass
Higher n means slower light in diamond.
Diamond emits light when struck by photons
The sparkle is from reflection and dispersion, not emission.
questions.x: Since sin θc = 1/n, a higher index gives a smaller critical angle: about 25° for diamond versus 42° for glass. In diamond, many more internal rays exceed θc and are totally reflected, bouncing around inside until they exit through the top facets. Its strong dispersion then spreads that light into colors.

questions.q: White light passes through a glass prism. Violet light bends more than red light because:
o: glass has a slightly higher index for shorter wavelengths
Correct: this wavelength dependence of n is dispersion.
violet photons travel faster in glass
Higher n for violet means it travels slower.
violet light has a longer wavelength
Violet has the shortest visible wavelength.
red light reflects off the prism faces
Both colors refract; they differ in bending, not reflection.
questions.x: In glass, the index of refraction is slightly higher for shorter wavelengths, a property called dispersion. Violet light therefore travels a bit slower and bends more at each prism surface than red, separating white light into a spectrum. A higher index always means slower light, not faster.

questions.q: Which color of light is deviated the least by a glass prism?
o: Violet
Violet bends the most.
Blue
Blue bends more than red because n is larger for shorter λ.
Green
Green lies between red and violet in deviation.
Red
Correct: red has the lowest index in glass, so it bends least.
questions.x: Because of dispersion, glass has its lowest index for the longest visible wavelengths. Red light, at the long end, is slowed least and bent least, so it is deviated least by a prism, while violet is deviated most. The order of deviation follows the order of wavelength.

questions.q: The sky looks blue on a clear day mainly because:
o: air molecules absorb red light and emit blue
Scattering, not absorption and re-emission at new colors, causes the blue.
the ocean reflects blue light upward
The sky is blue over deserts too.
blue light travels faster through air
All visible colors travel at nearly the same speed in air.
air molecules scatter short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones
Correct: Rayleigh scattering grows roughly as 1/λ⁴.
questions.x: Air molecules are much smaller than visible wavelengths, so they scatter light by Rayleigh scattering, whose strength varies as 1/λ⁴. Blue light (about 450 nm) is scattered several times more than red (about 700 nm), so scattered skylight looks blue. The same effect leaves the direct sun reddish at sunset.

questions.q: A swimming pool is 2 m deep. Viewed from directly above, how deep does it appear? (n of water = 4/3)
o: Multiplied by n; water makes objects look shallower, not deeper.
Correct: apparent depth ≈ real depth / n = 2 ÷ 4/3.
2 m
Refraction at the surface changes apparent depth.
1 m
Divided by 2 rather than by n.
questions.x: Light from the pool bottom bends away from the normal as it leaves the water, so to an observer above the rays seem to come from a shallower point. For near-vertical viewing, apparent depth ≈ real depth × (n_observer/n_object) = 2 × (1/(4/3)) = 1.5 m. Objects underwater always look closer to the surface than they are.

questions.q: Students measure refraction angles as light enters an unknown liquid from air. A graph of sin θ(air) on the y-axis versus sin θ(liquid) on the x-axis is linear with slope 1.4. What does the slope represent?
o: The reciprocal of the liquid's index
That would be the slope with the axes swapped.
The critical angle of the liquid
A slope here is a ratio of sines, not an angle.
The liquid's index of refraction
Correct: sin θ(air) = n·sin θ(liquid), so the slope equals n.
The speed of light in the liquid, in units of 10⁸ m/s
Speed in the liquid is c/n ≈ 2.1×10⁸ m/s, not the slope.
questions.x: Snell's law for light entering the liquid from air is (1.0) sin θ(air) = n sin θ(liquid). Plotting sin θ(air) against sin θ(liquid) gives a line through the origin whose slope is exactly n, here 1.4. Swapping the axes would give a slope of 1/n.

questions.q: Light reflects off a glass surface (n = 1.5) while traveling in air. Compared with the incident wave, the reflected wave has:
o: no phase shift
No shift occurs on reflection off a lower-index medium.
a 90° phase shift
Reflection gives either 0° or 180°, not 90°.
a 180° phase shift
Correct: reflection off a higher-index medium inverts the wave, like a fixed rope end.
a shorter wavelength
The reflected wave stays in air, so λ is unchanged.
questions.x: When light reflects off a medium with a higher index, the reflected wave is inverted, a 180° phase shift, just like a rope pulse reflecting from a fixed end. Reflecting off a lower-index medium gives no shift. These phase flips are crucial in thin-film interference calculations.

questions.q: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 cm. What is its focal length?
o: 40 cm
Equated focal length with radius of curvature.
20 cm
Correct: f = R/2 for a spherical mirror.
80 cm
Doubled R instead of halving it.
−20 cm
Concave mirrors converge light and have positive f.
questions.x: For a spherical mirror, parallel rays converge (concave) or appear to diverge (convex) from a focal point halfway between the mirror and its center of curvature, so f = R/2. A concave mirror with R = 40 cm has f = +20 cm. The sign is positive because the focus is real, in front of the mirror.

questions.q: What type of image does a convex mirror form of a real object?
o: Real, inverted, and smaller
Convex mirrors cannot bring reflected rays to a real focus.
Virtual, upright, and larger
That describes a concave mirror with the object inside f.
Virtual, upright, and smaller
Correct: diverging mirrors always give reduced, upright virtual images.
Real or virtual, depending on object distance
For a convex mirror, the image is virtual at every distance.
questions.x: A convex mirror spreads reflected rays so they appear to come from behind it, so the image is always virtual. Because its focal length is negative, the mirror equation always gives a negative image distance and a magnification between 0 and 1: upright and smaller. That wide, reduced view is why convex mirrors are used for car side mirrors.

questions.q: A person holds their face closer to a concave makeup mirror than its focal length. What image do they see?
o: Real, inverted, and enlarged
That occurs for objects between f and 2f.
Real, inverted, and reduced
That occurs for objects beyond 2f (center of curvature).
Virtual, upright, and enlarged
Correct: inside f, a concave mirror acts as a magnifier.
Virtual, upright, and reduced
That describes a convex mirror.
questions.x: When an object is inside the focal length of a concave mirror, reflected rays diverge and appear to come from a point behind the mirror. The image is therefore virtual, upright and enlarged, which is how a makeup or shaving mirror works. Moving beyond f produces real, inverted images instead.

questions.q: An object is 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image and what is the magnification?
o: 30 cm in front of the mirror; m = −2
6 cm in front of the mirror; m = −0.4
Added 1/10 and 1/15 instead of subtracting.
30 cm behind the mirror; m = +2
Positive i for a mirror is in front, giving a real, inverted image.
5 cm in front of the mirror; m = −1/3
Subtracted distances (15 − 10) instead of reciprocals.
questions.x: Use 1/f = 1/o + 1/i: 1/i = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30, so i = +30 cm. For mirrors, positive i means a real image in front of the mirror. Magnification m = −i/o = −2: inverted and twice the size, as expected for an object between f and 2f.

questions.q: An object stands exactly at 2f in front of a converging lens. What image forms?
o: Virtual, upright, enlarged, on the same side
That requires the object inside f.
Real, inverted, reduced, between f and 2f
That happens for objects beyond 2f.
No image; rays emerge parallel
That happens for an object at the focal point.
Real, inverted, same size, at 2f on the other side
Correct: 1/i = 1/f − 1/2f = 1/2f, so i = 2f and m = −1.
questions.x: With the thin lens equation, an object at o = 2f gives 1/i = 1/f − 1/(2f) = 1/(2f), so the image is at 2f on the far side. Magnification m = −i/o = −1, so the image is real, inverted and the same size. Objects farther than 2f give reduced images; objects between f and 2f give enlarged ones.

questions.q: An object is 10 cm from a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. Describe the image.
o: Real, inverted, 20 cm on the far side, magnified 2×
The negative i means the image is virtual, not real.
Virtual, upright, 6.7 cm from the lens, magnified 0.67×
Added the reciprocals instead of subtracting.
Virtual, upright, 20 cm from the lens on the object's side, magnified 2×
Real, inverted, 10 cm on the far side, same size
Used the 2f result; this object is inside f.
questions.x: Thin lens: 1/i = 1/f − 1/o = 1/20 − 1/10 = −1/20, so i = −20 cm. A negative image distance for a lens means a virtual image on the same side as the object. Then m = −i/o = −(−20)/10 = +2, upright and doubled, the magnifying-glass case of an object inside f.

questions.q: Regardless of object position, a single diverging lens forms images of real objects that are:
o: virtual, upright, and reduced
Correct: diverging lenses spread rays, which appear to come from a smaller upright image.
real, inverted, and reduced
Diverging lenses cannot converge rays to a real image of a real object.
virtual, upright, and enlarged
Enlarged virtual images come from converging lenses with the object inside f.
real or virtual depending on distance
A diverging lens gives a virtual image at every object distance.
questions.x: A diverging lens has negative f, so for any real object 1/i = 1/f − 1/o is negative and the image is virtual. The image always lies between the lens and its focal point, so |i| < o and the magnification is between 0 and +1: upright and reduced. That is why diverging lenses cannot project images or magnify.

questions.q: An object is 10 cm from a diverging lens with focal length −10 cm. Where is the image?
o: At infinity
That would require 1/f − 1/o = 0, true only for a converging lens with o = f.
5 cm from the lens, on the object's side
Correct: 1/i = −1/10 − 1/10 = −1/5, so i = −5 cm (virtual).
5 cm on the far side of the lens
The negative sign means same side as the object, a virtual image.
20 cm from the lens, on the object's side
Added distances instead of reciprocals.
questions.x: With f = −10 cm and o = 10 cm, 1/i = 1/f − 1/o = −1/10 − 1/10 = −1/5, so i = −5 cm. The negative sign marks a virtual image on the object's side. Magnification is −i/o = +0.5, upright and half size, as diverging lenses always give.

questions.q: Using the thin lens equation with standard signs, a lens gives a positive image distance. What does this indicate?
o: A virtual image on the same side as the object
That is indicated by a negative image distance.
A real image on the opposite side of the lens from the object
Correct: for lenses, positive i means light actually converges there.
The lens must be diverging
A diverging lens gives negative i for real objects.
The image is upright
Real single-lens images are inverted (m = −i/o < 0).
questions.x: For lenses, light passes through to the far side, so a positive image distance means rays actually converge there: a real image that could be projected on a screen. Negative i means a virtual image on the object's side. A single lens's real image is inverted, since m = −i/o is negative.

questions.q: An optical system has a magnification of −3. What does this tell you about the image?
o: It is upright and three times larger
Upright images have positive magnification.
It is inverted and three times larger than the object
Correct: the negative sign means inverted; |m| = 3 means 3× size.
It is inverted and one-third the object's size
|m| = 3 means larger, not smaller.
It is virtual and three times larger
Negative m for a single element signals a real, inverted image.
questions.x: Magnification m = h_image/h_object = −i/o. Its magnitude gives the size ratio, and its sign gives orientation: negative means inverted, positive means upright. So m = −3 is inverted and three times taller; for a single mirror or lens, an inverted image is also real.

questions.q: A converging lens has a focal length of 25 cm. What is its power?
o: +25 diopters
Used f in centimeters instead of meters.
+0.04 diopters
Inverted using centimeters (1/25).
−4 diopters
Converging lenses have positive power.
+4 diopters
Correct: P = 1/f in meters = 1/0.25 m.
questions.x: Lens power is P = 1/f with f in meters, measured in diopters. A focal length of 25 cm is 0.25 m, so P = +4 D. Converging lenses have positive f and positive power; forgetting to convert to meters gives values off by 100.

questions.q: Two thin lenses of +5 D and −2 D are placed in contact. What is the focal length of the combination?
o: About 14 cm
Added the magnitudes (7 D) and ignored the negative sign.
3 m
Took the power in diopters as the focal length in meters.
About 33 cm
Correct: powers add to +3 D, so f = 1/3 m.
About −50 cm
Used only the diverging lens.
questions.note: Lenses in contact: add powers, not focal lengths.
questions.x: For thin lenses in contact, powers add: P = +5 + (−2) = +3 D. The focal length is the reciprocal, f = 1/3 m ≈ 33 cm, and the combination is converging. Focal lengths themselves do not add; only their reciprocals do.

questions.q: An object is 20 cm in front of lens 1 (f = 10 cm). Lens 2 (f = 10 cm) is 40 cm beyond lens 1. Describe the final image.
o: Real, inverted, same size, 20 cm beyond lens 2
Two inversions cancel; the final image is upright.
Virtual, upright, same size, 20 cm before lens 2
The first image is 20 cm before lens 2, a real object at 2f, giving a real image.
Real, upright, twice the size, 40 cm beyond lens 2
Each stage has m = −1, so total size is unchanged.
Real, upright, same size, 20 cm beyond lens 2
Correct: each lens images at 2f with m = −1, so total m = (−1)(−1) = +1.
questions.note: Multiply magnifications in a lens system.
questions.x: Treat the image of lens 1 as the object for lens 2. Lens 1: object at 2f gives an image 20 cm past lens 1 with m₁ = −1. That image is 20 cm before lens 2, again at 2f, so lens 2 forms an image 20 cm beyond it with m₂ = −1. Total m = m₁m₂ = +1: real, upright and same size, because two inversions cancel.

questions.q: In myopia (nearsightedness), where do distant objects focus, and which lens corrects it?
o: Behind the retina; a converging lens
That describes hyperopia.
In front of the retina; a diverging lens
Correct: the eye is too strongly converging, so a negative lens pushes the focus back.
In front of the retina; a converging lens
Adding convergence would move the focus farther forward.
Behind the retina; a diverging lens
Hyperopia needs added convergence, not divergence.
questions.x: In myopia the eye is too strongly converging (often too long), so light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina. A diverging (negative) lens spreads incoming rays slightly, pushing the focus back onto the retina. Adding a converging lens would move the focus even farther forward.

questions.q: A farsighted (hyperopic) patient has trouble focusing on near objects. Which lens corrects this?
o: A diverging lens
That corrects myopia.
A cylindrical lens only
Cylindrical lenses correct astigmatism.
A plane glass plate
A flat plate has zero power and corrects nothing.
A converging lens
Correct: the eye converges too weakly, so a positive lens adds power.
questions.x: In hyperopia the eye converges too weakly (often too short), so images of near objects would focus behind the retina. A converging (positive) lens adds focusing power to bring the image forward onto the retina. Diverging lenses correct the opposite problem, myopia.

questions.q: Presbyopia, common after age 45, results mainly from:
o: an eyeball that is too long
That is a common cause of myopia.
an irregularly curved cornea
That causes astigmatism.
loss of lens flexibility, reducing accommodation
Correct: a stiffer lens cannot round up enough for near focus.
loss of rod cells in the retina
Photoreceptor loss affects sensitivity, not focusing.
questions.x: Accommodation depends on the elastic lens rounding up when the ciliary muscle contracts. With age the lens stiffens, so it cannot become curved enough for near vision, and the near point recedes: presbyopia. Unlike myopia (eyeball shape) or astigmatism (corneal shape), it is a loss of focusing range, corrected with reading lenses.

questions.q: A myopic person's far point is 50 cm. What lens power lets them see distant objects clearly (ignore lens-eye distance)?
o: Correct: the lens must image infinity at 50 cm (virtual), so f = −0.5 m.
Myopia needs a diverging (negative) lens.
Gave the focal length in meters as the power.
Used centimeters instead of meters.
questions.x: A myopic eye sees clearly only out to its far point, 50 cm. The corrective lens must take an object at infinity and form a virtual image at the far point: 1/f = 1/∞ + 1/(−0.5 m), so f = −0.5 m and P = −2 D. Myopia always needs negative power.

questions.q: A hyperopic person's near point is 100 cm. What lens power lets them read at 25 cm (ignore lens-eye distance)?
o: Treated the image as at infinity, ignoring the 100 cm near point.
Added 1/1 instead of subtracting for the virtual image.
Hyperopia needs a converging, positive lens.
Correct: object at 0.25 m, virtual image at −1 m: P = 1/0.25 − 1/1 = 4 − 1.
questions.x: The lens must take a book at 25 cm and form a virtual image at the near point, 100 cm, where the eye can focus. With i = −1 m: P = 1/o + 1/i = 1/0.25 + 1/(−1) = 4 − 1 = +3 D. The image term is negative because it is virtual, on the same side as the book.

questions.q: Where does most of the refraction of light entering the human eye occur?
o: At the lens
The lens fine-tunes focus but sits between media of similar index.
At the retina
The retina detects light; it does not focus it.
At the air-cornea surface
Correct: the index jump from air (1.0) to cornea (about 1.38) is the largest in the eye.
In the vitreous humor
Light travels straight through this uniform gel.
questions.x: Refraction at a surface depends on the change in index across it. Light goes from air (1.00) to cornea (about 1.38), the largest jump in the eye, so the cornea supplies roughly two thirds of the eye's focusing power. The lens sits between fluids of similar index, so it bends light less but is adjustable.

questions.q: The image formed on the retina of a healthy eye is:
o: virtual and upright
Virtual images cannot be projected onto a surface like the retina.
real and upright
A single converging system forms inverted real images.
real and inverted
Correct: the eye's converging optics form a real, inverted image; the brain interprets it.
virtual and inverted
The retinal image must be real to be detected.
questions.x: The cornea and lens act as a converging system that brings light from each object point to a real focus on the retina, so the image is real. Like any single converging system forming a real image, it is inverted. The brain interprets the inverted image so we perceive the world upright.

questions.q: When the eye shifts focus from a distant mountain to a nearby book, the ciliary muscle contracts. What happens to the lens?
o: It becomes more rounded, shortening its focal length
Correct: higher curvature gives more power for near objects.
It flattens, lengthening its focal length
Flattening occurs for distant viewing when the ciliary muscle relaxes.
It moves forward without changing shape
Human accommodation works by changing lens shape.
It becomes more rounded, lengthening its focal length
More curvature means more power, which is a shorter focal length.
questions.x: For near objects the eye needs more power. Contracting the ciliary muscle relaxes tension on the zonular fibers, letting the elastic lens round up. Greater curvature means greater power and a shorter focal length. For distant viewing the muscle relaxes, the fibers pull taut and the lens flattens.

questions.q: A glass converging lens (n = 1.5) is moved from air into water (n = 1.33). What happens to its focal length?
o: It decreases
Smaller index difference means weaker bending, not stronger.
It increases
Correct: lens power depends on (n_lens − n_medium), which shrinks in water.
It stays the same since its shape is unchanged
Focal length depends on both shape and the surrounding index.
It changes sign and becomes diverging
The glass index still exceeds water's, so it stays converging.
questions.x: By the lensmaker's equation, power is proportional to (n_lens − n_medium) times the curvature terms. In air that factor is 0.5; in water it drops to about 0.17, so the lens bends light much less and its focal length grows roughly threefold. Since glass's index still exceeds water's, the lens remains converging.

questions.q: To use a converging lens as a magnifying glass, where must the object be placed?
o: Exactly at the focal point
The image goes to infinity; there is no finite enlarged image.
Inside the focal length
Correct: this gives an upright, enlarged virtual image.
Beyond 2f
That gives a reduced, inverted real image.
Exactly at 2f
That gives an inverted image of the same size.
questions.x: A converging lens forms a virtual, upright, enlarged image only when the object lies inside the focal length, because then 1/f − 1/o is negative. At exactly f the rays emerge parallel and the image is at infinity; beyond f the images are real and inverted. Magnifying glasses always hold the object inside f.

questions.q: A microscope uses a 40× objective and a 10× eyepiece. What is the total magnification?
o: Added the magnifications instead of multiplying.
Correct: magnifications of lenses in series multiply.
Divided the objective by the eyepiece.
Subtracted the magnifications.
questions.x: In a compound microscope the objective forms a magnified real image, which the eyepiece then magnifies again. Each stage scales the previous image, so total magnification is the product: 40 × 10 = 400×. Adding the two values ignores that magnifications compound.

questions.q: For a simple glass converging lens, how does the focal length for red light compare with that for blue light?
o: Shorter for red
Blue, with the higher index, focuses closer.
Equal, since focal length depends only on shape
Focal length also depends on n, which varies with wavelength.
Red has no focal point
All colors focus; they just focus at different distances.
Longer for red
Correct: glass has a lower index for red, so red bends less and focuses farther away.
questions.note: This color-dependent focus is chromatic aberration.
questions.x: Because of dispersion, glass has a slightly lower index for red than for blue. By the lensmaker's equation, lower n means less power, so red light bends less and comes to focus farther from the lens than blue. This wavelength-dependent focus is chromatic aberration, which achromatic doublets correct.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes real and virtual images?
o: A real image is always upright; a virtual image is always inverted
Single-element real images are inverted and virtual images upright.
A real image can be projected onto a screen; a virtual image cannot
Correct: light actually converges at a real image location.
Only mirrors form real images
Converging lenses also form real images.
Virtual images are always smaller than the object
Magnifying glasses produce enlarged virtual images.
questions.x: A real image forms where light rays actually converge, so placing a screen there shows the image. A virtual image is where rays only appear to come from, so no screen can capture it. Orientation and size depend on the setup: magnifying glasses give enlarged virtual images, and converging lenses as well as mirrors make real ones.

questions.q: In a ray diagram for a thin lens, which ray passes through without changing direction?
o: A ray through the center of the lens
Correct: at the center the two surfaces are nearly parallel, so the ray is undeflected.
A ray parallel to the principal axis
It refracts through (or away from) the focal point.
A ray through the near focal point
It emerges parallel to the axis.
Every ray at a small angle to the axis
Only the central ray is undeflected.
questions.x: Near the optical center, a thin lens's two surfaces are nearly parallel, like a thin flat plate, so a ray through the center continues undeviated. A ray parallel to the axis refracts through (or away from) the focal point, and a ray through the focal point exits parallel. These three rays build every thin lens ray diagram.

questions.q: The top half of a converging lens is covered with black tape while it projects a real image of a candle. What happens to the image?
o: The top half of the image disappears
Each image point is formed by rays through the whole lens, not one half.
The whole image remains but is dimmer
Correct: every part of the lens receives light from every point of the object.
The bottom half of the image disappears
No part of the image is lost; only brightness drops.
The image becomes virtual
Covering part of the lens does not change its focal length.
questions.x: Each point of the object sends rays to every part of the lens, and all those rays converge on the same image point. Covering half the lens removes half the rays for every image point but leaves rays from the uncovered half to form the complete image. The result is a full image with roughly half the brightness.

questions.q: With standard sign conventions, which spherical mirror has a negative focal length?
o: A convex mirror
Correct: diverging mirrors have virtual focal points behind the mirror, so f < 0.
A concave mirror
Concave mirrors converge light and have f > 0.
A plane mirror
A plane mirror has an infinite focal length.
Any mirror forming a real image
Real images come from concave mirrors with positive f.
questions.x: Sign conventions make f positive when the focal point is real. A concave mirror converges parallel rays to a real focus in front, so f > 0. A convex mirror diverges them so they only appear to come from a focus behind it, so f < 0. A plane mirror has no focus at a finite distance.

questions.q: A student records object distance o and image distance i for a lens and plots 1/i versus 1/o. The line has slope −1 and y-intercept 0.05 cm⁻¹. What is the focal length?
o: 2 cm
Misplaced the decimal; 1/0.05 is 20, not 2.
20 cm
Correct: 1/i = −1/o + 1/f, so the intercept 1/f = 0.05 cm⁻¹.
Gave 1/f as f.
−20 cm
A positive intercept means positive f, a converging lens.
questions.x: Rearranging 1/o + 1/i = 1/f gives 1/i = −(1/o) + 1/f, a line with slope −1 and y-intercept 1/f. An intercept of 0.05 cm⁻¹ means f = 1/0.05 = 20 cm, and the positive value indicates a converging lens. Linearizing data this way lets one fit pick out f from many measurements.

questions.q: A leaf looks green under sunlight because chlorophyll:
o: absorbs green light and reflects red and blue
An object looks the color it reflects, not the color it absorbs.
emits green light by fluorescence
Leaf color under daylight is mainly reflected light.
refracts sunlight into a green beam
Leaf color comes from absorption, not refraction.
absorbs red and blue light and reflects green
Correct: the perceived color is the light not absorbed.
questions.x: An object's color is the light it sends to your eye, which is the light it does not absorb. Chlorophyll absorbs strongly in the red and blue regions to drive photosynthesis and reflects much of the green, so leaves look green. Saying it absorbs green confuses absorbed with reflected light.

questions.q: A dye solution absorbs strongly near 450 nm (blue). What color does the solution appear in white light?
o: Blue
The solution absorbs blue, so blue is missing from the transmitted light.
Violet
Violet is near the absorbed band, not complementary to it.
Orange-yellow
Correct: removing blue leaves its complementary color, orange-yellow.
Colorless
Absorption in the visible range always produces color.
questions.x: A solution's color is the complement of what it absorbs, because the eye sees the remaining wavelengths. Removing blue (about 450 nm) from white light leaves light dominated by the complementary orange-yellow. Assuming the solution looks the color it absorbs is the classic trap.

questions.q: By the Beer-Lambert law (A = εbc), what happens to absorbance if the sample's concentration doubles in the same cuvette?
o: It doubles
Correct: absorbance is directly proportional to concentration.
It is halved
Transmittance falls with concentration; absorbance rises.
It quadruples
The relationship is linear, not squared.
It stays the same
More absorbing molecules in the path means more absorbance.
questions.x: The Beer-Lambert law, A = εbc, makes absorbance directly proportional to concentration at fixed path length and wavelength. Doubling c doubles A. Transmittance, by contrast, falls exponentially, since A = −log T, which is why A rather than T is plotted for calibration curves.

questions.q: A sample has an absorbance of 2. What percentage of incident light is transmitted?
o: Treated absorbance as a linear fraction.
Took T = 1/A.
That corresponds to A = 1.
Correct: A = −log T, so T = 10⁻² = 1%.
questions.x: Absorbance is logarithmic: A = −log T, so T = 10^(−A). An absorbance of 1 transmits 10%, and each additional unit cuts transmission by another factor of 10, so A = 2 transmits 1%. Treating absorbance as a linear fraction gives the tempting wrong answers.

questions.q: A chemist measures standards and plots a linear calibration line: A = 0.20 at 1 mM and A = 0.80 at 4 mM. An unknown reads A = 0.50. What is its concentration?
o: 2.5 mM
Correct: slope is 0.20 per mM through the origin, so c = 0.50/0.20.
2.0 mM
Guessed by eye; the line has slope 0.20 per mM, so 0.50/0.20 = 2.5 mM.
0.4 mM
Divided slope by absorbance, inverting the ratio.
10 mM
Divided 0.50 by 0.05 instead of 0.20 per mM.
questions.x: Beer-Lambert behavior gives a straight calibration line. The slope is (0.80 − 0.20)/(4 − 1) = 0.20 per mM, and the line passes through the origin. Solving A = 0.20 × c for A = 0.50 gives c = 2.5 mM. Interpolating along the line, rather than guessing a midpoint, is the key step.

questions.q: As the number of conjugated double bonds in a molecule increases, its UV-Vis absorption maximum:
o: shifts to shorter wavelength
Conjugation lowers the energy gap, which lengthens λmax.
stays fixed because only the functional group matters
Extending conjugation clearly shifts λmax.
disappears
Conjugated systems absorb more strongly, not less.
shifts to longer wavelength
Correct: the HOMO-LUMO gap narrows, so lower-energy photons are absorbed.
questions.x: Each added conjugated double bond spreads the π system over more atoms, raising the HOMO and lowering the LUMO, so the energy gap shrinks. A smaller gap means lower-energy, longer-wavelength photons are absorbed. Highly conjugated molecules such as β-carotene therefore absorb visible light and appear colored.

questions.q: Absorption of infrared radiation by a molecule primarily causes:
o: electronic transitions to higher orbitals
That requires UV-visible photons.
nuclear spin flips
Those are driven by radio waves in NMR.
bond vibrations such as stretching and bending
Correct: IR photon energies match vibrational transitions.
ionization of the molecule
IR photons carry far too little energy to ionize.
questions.x: Infrared photons have energies matching the spacing between vibrational levels of bonds, so IR absorption excites stretching and bending modes. Electronic transitions require higher-energy UV-visible photons, and nuclear spin flips need far lower-energy radio waves. That is why IR spectra identify functional groups by their bond vibrations.

questions.q: An IR spectrum shows a very broad absorption from 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ overlapping a strong peak near 1710 cm⁻¹. Which functional group is most likely present?
o: Carboxylic acid
Correct: a very broad hydrogen-bonded O–H plus a C=O near 1710 cm⁻¹ marks COOH.
Ketone
A ketone has the C=O peak but no broad O–H absorption.
Alcohol
An alcohol lacks the C=O peak near 1710 cm⁻¹.
Amine
N–H peaks are sharper and near 3300–3500 cm⁻¹, with no C=O.
questions.x: Carboxylic acids show two signatures together: an extremely broad O–H stretch from about 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹, broadened by strong hydrogen-bonded dimers, and a C=O stretch near 1700 to 1720 cm⁻¹. A ketone has the carbonyl but no O–H, and an alcohol has an O–H band (narrower, near 3300) but no carbonyl.

questions.q: A sharp, medium-strength IR peak appears near 2250 cm⁻¹. Which bond is most consistent with this?
o: O–H
O–H absorbs broadly near 3200–3550 cm⁻¹.
C=O
Carbonyls absorb near 1700 cm⁻¹.
C–H (sp³)
sp³ C–H stretches appear just below 3000 cm⁻¹.
C≡N
Correct: nitriles absorb in the triple-bond region near 2250 cm⁻¹.
questions.x: Triple bonds are stiff, so they vibrate at high frequencies in a region with few other absorptions, about 2100 to 2260 cm⁻¹. A sharp medium peak near 2250 cm⁻¹ fits a C≡N nitrile stretch. O–H and C–H stretches appear above about 2850 cm⁻¹, and C=O near 1700 cm⁻¹.

questions.q: UV-visible spectroscopy probes which kind of molecular transition?
o: Vibrational transitions of bonds
Those are probed by IR.
