Electronic transitions of valence electrons
Correct: UV-Vis photons promote electrons, often π → π*, to higher orbitals.
Nuclear spin transitions
Those are probed by NMR with radio waves.
Changes in mass-to-charge ratio
That is mass spectrometry, which does not use absorbed light.
questions.x: UV and visible photons carry a few eV, matching gaps between electronic energy levels, so absorption promotes valence electrons, commonly π → π* or n → π*. Vibrational transitions need lower-energy IR photons, spin flips need radio waves, and mass spectrometry does not involve light absorption.

questions.q: In NMR spectroscopy, what form of electromagnetic radiation flips nuclear spins in the applied magnetic field?
o: Infrared
IR excites bond vibrations.
Radio waves
Correct: spin-state energy gaps in a magnet correspond to radiofrequency photons.
Ultraviolet
UV excites electrons, far above spin-flip energies.
X-rays
X-rays far exceed nuclear spin-flip energies.
questions.x: In a strong magnetic field, nuclei like ¹H have spin states separated by a tiny energy gap. Photons matching that gap are in the radiofrequency range (hundreds of MHz), so NMR uses radio waves to flip spins. IR, UV and X-ray photons carry far more energy than this transition needs.

questions.q: In the ¹H NMR spectrum of an ethyl group (CH₃CH₂–) attached to an atom with no hydrogens, the CH₃ signal is split into a:
o: triplet
Correct: n + 1 rule with the two neighboring CH₂ protons gives 3 lines.
quartet
That is the CH₂ signal, split by three CH₃ protons.
doublet
A doublet needs exactly one neighboring proton.
singlet
The CH₃ has two neighboring protons, so it is split.
questions.x: The n + 1 rule says a signal is split into n + 1 peaks by n equivalent protons on adjacent carbons. The CH₃ has two neighboring CH₂ protons, so it appears as a triplet; the CH₂, with three neighbors, appears as a quartet. Splitting reports neighbors, not the group's own protons.

questions.q: In ¹H NMR, a proton on a carbon bonded to an electronegative oxygen appears:
o: upfield (lower ppm), because it is shielded
Electronegative neighbors deshield protons, not shield them.
at 0 ppm, like TMS
TMS protons are highly shielded; a C–H next to O is not.
only as a singlet
Chemical shift and splitting are separate features.
downfield (higher ppm), because it is deshielded
Correct: oxygen pulls electron density away, exposing the proton to more of the field.
questions.x: Electrons around a proton shield it from the applied field. An electronegative atom like oxygen withdraws electron density, deshielding nearby protons so they resonate at higher frequency, which appears downfield at higher ppm (about 3.3 to 4 ppm for H–C–O). Shielded protons, like those of TMS, appear upfield near 0 ppm.

questions.q: The ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) shows three signals. What are the relative integrations?
o: Integration reflects proton count, not the number of signals.
The OH carries one proton and the CH₂ carries two.
Correct: integration is proportional to the number of equivalent protons.
The three groups have different numbers of protons.
questions.x: In ¹H NMR, the area under each signal is proportional to the number of protons producing it. Ethanol's CH₃, CH₂ and OH groups carry 3, 2 and 1 protons, so the integrations are 3 : 2 : 1. Integration counts protons; splitting, a separate feature, counts neighbors.

questions.q: A mass spectrum shows a molecular ion peak at m/z 122 and a peak of nearly equal height at m/z 124. Which element does the compound most likely contain?
o: Chlorine
Chlorine gives an M+2 peak about one-third the height of M.
Nitrogen
Nitrogen affects odd or even molecular mass, not a strong M+2 peak.
Bromine
Correct: ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br are about equally abundant, giving M and M+2 peaks of similar height.
Oxygen
¹⁸O is rare, so oxygen gives only a tiny M+2 peak.
questions.x: Isotope patterns reveal halogens. Bromine is about 50% ⁷⁹Br and 50% ⁸¹Br, so a molecule with one Br shows M and M+2 peaks of nearly equal height. Chlorine is about 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl, giving an M+2 peak about one third the height of M, which rules it out here.

questions.q: Which of these analytical techniques does NOT rely on a molecule absorbing electromagnetic radiation?
o: Infrared spectroscopy
IR measures absorption of infrared photons.
NMR spectroscopy
NMR measures absorption of radiofrequency photons.
Mass spectrometry
Correct: it ionizes molecules and sorts ions by mass-to-charge ratio.
UV-Vis spectroscopy
UV-Vis measures absorption of ultraviolet and visible photons.
questions.x: IR, UV-Vis and NMR are all absorption spectroscopies: each measures which photon energies a molecule absorbs. Mass spectrometry instead ionizes molecules, often fragments them, and separates the ions by mass-to-charge ratio using electric or magnetic fields. It reveals molecular mass and structure without absorbing light.

questions.q: A fluorescent dye absorbs at 490 nm. Compared with the absorbed light, the emitted light most likely has:
o: a shorter wavelength
Emission cannot exceed the absorbed photon's energy in ordinary fluorescence.
the same wavelength
Some energy is always lost to vibrational relaxation first.
a longer wavelength
Correct: energy is lost to vibrational relaxation before emission, so emitted photons have less energy.
a higher frequency
Lower energy means lower frequency.
questions.x: After absorbing a photon, a fluorescent molecule quickly loses some energy through vibrational relaxation in the excited state before emitting. The emitted photon therefore has less energy, lower frequency and longer wavelength than the absorbed one, a difference called the Stokes shift. Here emission would fall above 490 nm, toward green.

questions.q: Which pairing of radiation type with molecular transition, in order of increasing photon energy, is correct?
o: Radio: rotation; microwave: nuclear spin; IR: electronic; UV: vibration
Swaps several pairings; IR excites vibrations and UV excites electrons.
Radio: nuclear spin; microwave: rotation; IR: vibration; UV: electronic
Correct: each region's photon energy matches progressively larger energy gaps.
Radio: nuclear spin; microwave: electronic; IR: rotation; UV: vibration
Electronic transitions need far more energy than microwaves supply.
Radio: vibration; microwave: rotation; IR: nuclear spin; UV: electronic
Vibrations need IR, and spin flips need radio waves.
questions.x: Photon energy rises from radio to microwave to infrared to ultraviolet, and each region matches a progressively larger molecular energy gap. Nuclear spin flips in a magnet are tiny (radio), molecular rotations are next (microwave), bond vibrations larger (IR), and electronic transitions largest (UV-Vis). Pairing higher-energy radiation with smaller gaps reverses this logic.

questions.q: Lens aberration in which rays striking the outer edge of a spherical lens focus at a different point than central rays is called:
o: chromatic aberration
That results from different wavelengths focusing at different points.
astigmatism
That comes from unequal curvature in different directions.
spherical aberration
Correct: it comes from the lens's spherical shape, not from color.
dispersion
Dispersion is the wavelength dependence of n that causes chromatic aberration.
questions.x: A spherical surface is only an approximation to the ideal focusing shape, so rays hitting the outer edge of a lens bend too much and focus closer than central rays. This blurring is spherical aberration and occurs even with one wavelength. Chromatic aberration, by contrast, comes from different colors focusing at different points.
